Ch. 4 — Tissues, Integument and Homeostasis

Week 6 · study page · 40 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 47 flashcards · 2 diagrams, 21 labels · Two of his six named topics live here — tissues and integument. One chapter, one bank: Canvas lists Ch. 4 under two module titles across Weeks 5 and 6, but Whalen wrote a single study guide for it — 74 objectives in three groups (tissues, skin, homeostasis) — and examines it whole. Its three sections were taught over three lectures (Wed 09/09, Mon 09/14, Wed 09/16), all consolidated on the Week 6 page, which is where the bank is written from. He named tissues and integument but not homeostasis; the homeostasis third is banked anyway, because the guide is one document and homeostasis was the Unit 1 essay answer.

1Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

What are the four primary tissue types?

Answer: c

Epithelial covers surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands; connective binds, supports, stores and transports; muscle produces movement; nervous conducts impulses. Option a lists epithelial shapes and layer counts, not tissue types. Options b and d list kinds of connective tissue as if they were peers of the four.

2Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Every epithelium has two features in common. Which pair?

Answer: a

The free surface may be specialised for protection, secretion or absorption; the basement membrane is a noncellular layer binding the epithelium to the connective tissue beneath and helping it resist stretching. Matrix and ground substance belong to connective tissue, not epithelium — that swap is the trap in options c and d.

3Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which epithelium lines the air sacs of the lungs, and why that one?

Answer: a

Structure follows function, which is a study-guide objective in its own right. Flattened, scale-like squamous cells in a single layer are thin enough for O2 and CO2 to diffuse across easily — the same reason they line blood vessels, where the smooth surface also reduces friction. Stratified epithelium is for protection, because the extra thickness makes passage harder.

4Ch. 44.1
  • textbook

Shape and layer count are independent axes. Which pairing with its location is right?

Answer: b

Stratified squamous lines the mouth, esophagus and vagina and forms the outer layer of skin — everywhere abrasion happens. Option a is that same location under the wrong name. The small intestine is simple columnar, with goblet cells and fingerlike folds for absorption. Stratified columnar is rare — urethra, and the esophagus–stomach junction.

5Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

What is the difference between an exocrine and an endocrine gland?

Answer: c

Exo = out: secretion travels down a duct to a body surface, cavity or organ — digestive-enzyme glands, milk glands, and the skin's oil and sweat glands. Endo = inside: no ducts; hormones are released into the spaces just outside the cells and diffuse into the bloodstream. Both are epithelial tissue — a gland is epithelium that secretes a product — which rules out option a.

6Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

What makes connective tissue unlike the other three tissue types?

Answer: b

All connective tissues are cells embedded in an extracellular matrix of protein fibres plus a noncellular ground substance — and the character of any particular connective tissue comes from its matrix, not its cells. The book's image is fruit suspended in a gelatin dessert. Option a is true of cartilage only, not of connective tissue generally — bone and blood are richly vascular.

7Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which fibre type is correctly described?

Answer: d

Collagen resists pulling; elastic fibres contain random coils and stretch and recoil, so they are common in skin, lungs and blood vessels; reticular fibres are thin, branching strands of collagen that form networks supporting soft organs such as the liver and spleen. All three are made by the same cell: the fibroblast, which also lays down collagen to close a wound.

8Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Loose and dense connective tissue differ in what?

Answer: a

Both are connective tissue proper; the difference is the ratio. Loose has many cells and fewer, loosely woven fibres — areolar (the universal packing material) and adipose (fat storage). Dense has large amounts of tightly woven fibres forming strong bands — ligaments, tendons and the dermis. Option b separates the specialised connective tissues from each other, not loose from dense.

9Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

A ligament and a tendon differ in what they connect. Which is right?

Answer: a

Both are dense connective tissue. Ligament: bone to bone. Tendon: muscle to bone. Worth knowing that Table 4.2 states the pair in reverse order — "attaches bone to bone (ligaments) or bone to muscle (tendons)" — which is easy to misread as saying the opposite of the text. Whalen added the tissue subtype: dense regular fibrous connective tissue.

10Ch. 44.1
  • textbook

A skier tears knee cartilage and also breaks a bone in the same fall. Which heals faster, and why?

Answer: b

Cartilage has no blood vessels and no nerves — nutrients reach chondrocytes by diffusion from nearby capillaries, which is slow, so it heals slowly. Bone is living, actively metabolising tissue with a good blood supply, and heals promptly. That single contrast is the chapter's own answer to its ski-injury question. Option d gets bone right for the wrong reason.

11Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which cartilage type is in the intervertebral disks and the knee's cushioning layer?

Answer: c

Fibrocartilage has fewer cells than hyaline or elastic and a matrix full of collagen — built to withstand pressure. Hyaline is the most abundant, at the ends of long bones and in the nose, ribs, larynx and trachea. Elastic is the most flexible, in the external ear. There is no such thing as reticular cartilage — reticular names a fibre type.

12Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why is blood classified as connective tissue?

Answer: b

Connective tissue is cells in a matrix, and blood fits: the formed elements — red cells, white cells and platelets — are suspended in the liquid matrix plasma. Students routinely miss this because blood has no visible fibres — its "fibres" are soluble proteins, visible only when it clots. Ground substance can be solid (bone), fluid (blood) or gelatinous (cartilage).

13Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Skeletal and cardiac muscle are both striated. What separates them?

Answer: a

Skeletal is voluntary with many nuclei per cell; cardiac is involuntary with typically one, in branching cells joined by specialised junctions. Striations come from the orderly arrangement of actin and myosin, which both have — so option b cannot separate them, and all muscle is excitable and contractile. Smooth muscle is the only one that is neither striated nor voluntary, and its cells taper.

14Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Neuroglia do what?

Answer: b

Neuroglia are far more numerous than neurons — the visual point of Figure 4.4 is how much of the field they occupy — and they support, insulate and protect neurons, increase the rate at which neurons conduct, and supply them with nutrients from nearby vessels. Options a, c and d all describe the neuron: cell body, dendrites for receiving, one axon for conducting away.

15Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which junction forms a leakproof seal, and where would you expect it?

Answer: c

Tight junctions attach neighbouring membranes so securely that nothing leaks between the cells — exactly what the intestinal and urinary linings need, so that digestive juices and urine cannot pass through the epithelium. Adhesion junctions (desmosomes) are rivets for tissues that stretch. Gap junctions are small holes letting ions pass, synchronising heart and smooth muscle.

16Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which pairing of body cavity to its contents is right?

Answer: d

The ventral cavity splits into the thoracic and abdominal cavities, separated by the diaphragm; the thoracic then splits into the pleural cavities (lungs) and the pericardial cavity (heart). Options a and b are that pair swapped. The dorsal cavity splits into the cranial cavity (brain) and the spinal cavity (spinal cord).

17Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which membrane lines passageways that open to the exterior?

Answer: a

Four membranes, four locations: mucous lines passages open to the outside (respiratory, digestive, reproductive, urinary); serous lines the thoracic and abdominal cavities and their organs; synovial lines freely movable joint cavities; cutaneous is the skin — the only one that is thick, relatively waterproof and comparatively dry. The chapter gives them half a page and the deck one and a half slides: cheap marks, easy to skip.

18Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

What is the difference between an organ and an organ system?

Answer: b

An organ is a structure of two or more different tissues working together for a specific function. An organ system is a group of organs with a common function — trachea, bronchi and lungs make the respiratory system. There are 11 major organ systems. Option a is close enough to be tempting and wrong on the first half: one tissue is a tissue, not an organ.

19Ch. 44.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which organ system's listed functions include synthesising vitamin D?

Answer: c

Figure 4.7 lists four for the integumentary system: protects underlying tissues · provides skin sensation · helps regulate body temperature · synthesises vitamin D. Modified cholesterol in the skin's outer layer is converted by UV, then modified further in the liver and kidneys before it can stimulate calcium and phosphorus absorption — which is the hook into Chapter 5.

20Ch. 44.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why is the epidermis's outermost layer dead?

Answer: b

The epidermis has no blood vessels. The deepest layer divides rapidly and pushes older cells toward the surface; on the way they flatten and die because they no longer receive nourishment from the dermis, and keratin gradually replaces their cytoplasmic contents. It takes two weeks to a month from a cell's formation to its shedding, at 30,000 to 40,000 cells a minute.

21Ch. 44.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

What does keratin do for the skin?

Answer: b

Keratin is the tough, water-resistant fibrous protein that replaces the cytoplasm of epidermal cells as they move outward, and it is what prevents excessive water loss from the tissues beneath. Nails are the same protein, harder. Option a is melanin's job; option c is the basement membrane's.

22Ch. 44.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why can a nicotine patch work through intact skin?

Answer: b

The epidermis is a water-resistant barrier, but its cells have lipid membranes — so a drug dissolved in a lipid solvent can cross them, diffuse into the connective tissue beneath and be absorbed into the blood. This is a study-guide objective in its own right. Common uses: birth-control and menopausal hormones, nicotine, motion-sickness drugs.

23Ch. 44.2
  • textbook

Why are tattoos permanent?

Answer: a

The epidermis sheds continuously; the dermis does not wear away. Ink injected into the dermal layer therefore stays. The same fact explains why getting a tattoo hurts — the dermis is laced with nerves and sensory receptors, where the epidermis has none. Note the chapter's own wobble: the summary upgrades "does not wear away" to "nondividing", which is a different claim.

24Ch. 44.2
  • textbook

A blister forms after a shoe rubs a heel. What has happened?

Answer: b

Nutrients reach the avascular epidermis by passing out of dermal vessels and diffusing upward through tissue fluid. Where the skin is traumatised, that fluid accumulates between the two layers, separating them — a blister. Option a is acne, in a different structure entirely. Almost every clinical detail in this section hangs off one fact: the dermis has vessels, the epidermis has none.

25Ch. 44.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Two people have very different skin colours. What differs between them?

Answer: c

All people have about the same number of melanocytes. What differs is which form of melanin they produce — a yellow-to-red form or the commoner black-to-brown one — and the size and number of the pigment granules, determined genetically. The melanin is then taken up by surrounding epidermal cells, colouring the whole epidermis. Blood flow and oxygenation are the second factor.

26Ch. 44.2
  • textbook

Why do lips look blue in extreme cold?

Answer: b

The body shunts blood away from the skin to the core, which reduces oxygen supply to the small surface vessels. Well-oxygenated blood is ruby red; poorly oxygenated blood is a much deeper red that reads as bluish through thin skin — and the skin of the lips is thin. The same mechanism explains dark circles under the eyes after too little sleep.

27Ch. 44.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Tanning is protective. What is the catch?

Answer: b

Melanocytes respond to UV by increasing melanin production, and melanin absorbs UV before it reaches deeper cells — genuinely protective. But the buildup is not instantaneous, and that gap is when the damage is done. Whalen's deck makes the same point on slide 60. The skin does need some UV for vitamin D, so the answer is not zero exposure.

28Ch. 44.2
  • textbook

Which skin cancer is least common and most dangerous, and where does it arise?

Answer: c

Melanoma arises in melanocytes, is the least common and most dangerous, and unlike the two carcinomas it often metastasises — first to lymph nodes, later to vital organs. Survival is about 90% if found before it spreads and about 14% after. Option d puts melanocytes in the wrong layer: they sit at the base of the epidermis, not in the dermis.

29Ch. 44.2
  • textbook

What does the ABCD rule stand for?

Answer: b

Asymmetry — most melanomas are irregular in shape. Border — often diffuse and unclear. Colour — mottled brown, black, red, white and blue. Diameter — growths over 5 mm (about 0.2 in.) are threatening. The chapter's prevention advice pairs with it: SPF 15 or higher, applied about 45 minutes beforehand, reapplied after swimming, used even when overcast.

30Ch. 44.2
  • textbook

An oil gland opens where?

Answer: b

Onto the hair follicle — and that is the whole mechanism of acne. If the duct is blocked, sebum and dead cells clog it: a plugged follicle is a whitehead; when the sebum mixes with melanin it darkens into a blackhead — so melanin, not dirt, is what makes it dark; a ruptured follicle spilling into the epidermis is a pimple. Acne is not caused by poor hygiene or by chocolate.

31Ch. 44.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

What is the principal function of sweat glands?

Answer: b

Sweat is largely water plus some salts, lactic acid, vitamin C and metabolic wastes such as urea — so option a is a real but secondary function, which is exactly why it is the distractor. The principal function is temperature regulation by evaporation. Option c is the oil (sebaceous) gland, and option d is the wax gland, a modified sweat gland in the external ear canal.

32Ch. 44.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

What makes a goose bump?

Answer: a

The arrector pili is a tiny smooth muscle in the dermis attached to the hair follicle; its contraction pulls on the follicle and makes the hair stand up, and the small mound of flesh at the base is the goose bump. It is associated with fear and cold — and in the cold it is a genuine heat-conserving response, piloerection, trapping an insulating layer of air.

33Ch. 44.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which best defines homeostasis?

Answer: b

The word means "to stay the same", but conditions inside never actually do. Homeostatic mechanisms dampen fluctuations around a set point to keep conditions within a range — homeostasis is dynamic, not static. Options a and d are the static misreading the chapter explicitly rejects, and it is the whole point of its exercise question about exercise.

34Ch. 44.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Name the three components of a homeostatic mechanism in order.

Answer: a

A receptor detects the change and reports it; a control center holds the set point, integrates the input and selects a response — in most systems it is in the brain; an effector, often a muscle or gland, carries the response out. For temperature: thermoreceptors → hypothalamus → sweat glands, dermal vessels, skeletal muscles. The study guide asks for this template with examples.

35Ch. 44.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

What does "negative" mean in negative feedback?

Answer: b

It is a direction, not a value judgement. A negative feedback mechanism slows or reverses a variation from the normal value and returns it to normal — and reaching the normal value is itself the feedback that shuts the response off. Positive feedback promotes continued change in the same direction and does not promote homeostasis. The chapter's own end-of-chapter question tests exactly this.

36Ch. 44.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

You walk into a 38 °C room. What does the hypothalamus order?

Answer: a

Sweat so that evaporation sheds heat, and dilate the dermal vessels so more heat is released to the air — which is why you look flushed during hard exercise. Also relaxation of the arrector pili, keeping damp hair against the skin, and behavioural responses like seeking shade. Options b, c and d each mix in a cold response; constriction, piloerection and shivering all conserve or make heat.

37Ch. 44.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why does the body constrict dermal blood vessels in the cold?

Answer: a

Reduced flow to the extremities conserves heat for the internal organs — "cold hands, warm heart". It is also why fingers and toes are the first tissue to suffer frostbite: the body is trading the extremities for the core, and they pay. The other cold responses are decreased sweating, piloerection, raised metabolic rate, shivering, and behavioural ones.

38Ch. 44.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

At what core temperature does the chapter put the hyperthermia crisis?

Answer: b

At about 42 °C (107 °F) the heartbeat becomes irregular, blood oxygen drops, the liver ceases to function, and unconsciousness and death soon follow; few survive 43 °C (110 °F). The other numbers are the hypothermia side: 35 °C (95 °F) or below is hypothermia, 33 °C (91.4 °F) brings loss of consciousness, and at 30 °C (86 °F) temperature regulation is fully shut down.

39Ch. 44.3
  • textbook

Elderly people are at greater risk than children in a heat wave. Which part of the loop has failed?

Answer: c

Sweating is the main effector for shedding heat, and its activity declines with age. The receptors and hypothalamus still work, but the loop cannot close at the effector stage, so temperature keeps climbing. Children's sweat glands are fully active, so their loop still closes. This is the chapter's own Stop and Think, and it is a model of how an exam asks about the three components.

40Ch. 44.3
  • textbook

You exercise and your breathing rate, blood pressure and heart rate all rise. Is homeostasis failing?

Answer: b

Exercising muscle consumes oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and heat faster than at rest, so leaving the rates unchanged is what would let the internal environment drift. What is held constant is the composition of the extracellular fluid, not the rate of the machinery maintaining it — homeostasis is dynamic. Option c gets the right instinct attached to the wrong verdict.

1Ch. 4short answer4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Name the four tissue types and give, for each, its function and one location.

Model answer

Epithelial. Covers body surfaces, lines cavities and organs, and forms glands. Every epithelium has a free surface and a basement membrane. Example: simple squamous lining the air sacs of the lungs, where flatness lets gases diffuse. Connective. Binds and supports, and also stores fat, transports, and takes part in immunity. It is the most abundant and most widely distributed tissue, and the only one that is mostly matrix rather than cells. Example: tendon, dense connective tissue joining muscle to bone. Muscle. Cells (muscle fibers) that contract when stimulated, producing body movement and moving substances through the body. All muscle is excitable and contractile. Example: cardiac muscle in the wall of the heart. Whalen's deck adds two functions the text omits — muscle also stores glycogen and generates heat. Nervous. Conducts nerve impulses from one part of the body to another. Two cell types: neurons (cell body, dendrites, one axon) and the far more numerous neuroglia, which support, insulate, protect and nourish them. Example: the brain.

Four types, each with a function and a location, is the base. Naming epithelium's two shared features, connective tissue's matrix, muscle's two properties and nervous tissue's two cell types is what takes it to full marks. The deck's glycogen-and-heat addition is a lecture-only point.

2Ch. 4short answer4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Describe the three types of cartilage — where each is, and what it is built for.

Model answer

All cartilage is tough but flexible specialised connective tissue. Its cells, chondrocytes, sit in spaces in the matrix called lacunae, and it has no blood vessels and no nerves — nutrients reach the cells by diffusion from nearby capillaries, which is why cartilage heals slowly where bone heals promptly. Hyaline cartilage — the most abundant, and the weakest. Cells in a matrix of collagen fibres and a bluish-white gel-like ground substance; commonly called gristle. At the ends of long bones, where it lets one bone slide over another (articular cartilage), and in the nose, ribs, larynx and trachea. Elastic cartilage — more flexible than hyaline because of large amounts of wavy elastic fibres. In the external ear, giving strength and elasticity. Fibrocartilage — the toughest; fewer cells than the other two, with a matrix full of collagen fibres, and built to withstand pressure. Forms the cushioning layer in the knee joint, the outer part of the intervertebral disks, and the pubic symphysis.

Three types with a location and a distinguishing property each. Opening with what all cartilage shares — chondrocytes in lacunae, avascular, slow to heal — earns the first marks, and the hyaline superlatives (weakest and most abundant) are the pair Whalen asked for twice in the skeletal lecture.

3Ch. 4short answer4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Compare the three muscle tissue types on four features.

Model answer

Skeletal. Voluntary. Cells are long cylinders with several nuclei each, arranged in parallel bundles, and show obvious striations from the orderly arrangement of actin and myosin. Usually attached to bone, so contraction moves a body part. Joined to its neighbours by nothing — fibers contract end to end. Cardiac. Involuntary. Cells are short and branching, with typically one nucleus, and are striated. Found only in the wall of the heart, where contraction pumps blood. Joined by intercalated discs carrying gap junctions, which strengthen the tissue and speed conduction through the heart. Smooth. Involuntary. Cells are short and spindle-shaped, tapering at each end, with one nucleus, and have no striations because the myofilaments are not arranged in sarcomeres. In the walls of blood vessels and airways (contraction reduces flow), and of the stomach, intestines and bladder (mixing, propelling, eliminating). Joined by gap junctions. The useful summary: two are striated and two are involuntary, and they are not the same two — smooth is the only one that is neither, and cardiac is striated but involuntary.

Four features across three types: cell shape and nuclei, striations, voluntary or not, and location. The closing line about "not the same two" shows the comparison rather than three separate descriptions. Note the chapter's own inconsistency: Table 4.3 says cardiac has "one nucleus" flatly, while the text says "typically only one".

4Ch. 4short answer4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

List the functions of the skin, and describe its layers.

Model answer

The integumentary system is the skin plus its derivatives — hair, nails, sweat glands, oil glands, wax glands. Functions. Protection — a physical barrier against bacteria and harmful particles, UV radiation, and physical and chemical insult; it also contains macrophages that fight infection actively. Preventing water loss — the water-resistant protein keratin in the outer cells. Temperature regulation — sweating and changes in blood flow to the skin. Vitamin D production — modified cholesterol converted by UV, then further modified in liver and kidneys, where it stimulates calcium and phosphorus absorption. Sensation — receptors for temperature, touch, pressure and pain. Layers. Epidermis — the thin outer layer, several layers of epithelial cells, avascular, with its deepest layer dividing rapidly and pushing cells outward; on the way they flatten, fill with keratin and die, and are shed at 30,000–40,000 a minute, the whole journey taking two weeks to a month. Dermis — much thicker, mostly connective tissue, and the layer that holds the blood vessels, nerves, sensory structures, hair follicles, oil glands and sweat gland ducts. It does not wear away, which is why tattoos are permanent. Hypodermis — loose connective tissue anchoring the skin to what lies beneath; it cushions blows, insulates, and holds about half the body's fat stores. It is not usually considered part of the skin.

Five functions and three layers. The single most load-bearing fact is that the dermis has blood vessels and the epidermis has none — say it and blisters, tattoos, the dying epidermal cells and transdermal patches all follow. Noting that the hypodermis is not part of the skin is a free mark the chapter sets up.

5Ch. 4short answer4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Explain thermoregulation as a negative feedback loop, naming the three components and what happens in both directions.

Model answer

The components. Receptors — thermoreceptors in the skin sensing surface temperature, and deep receptors sensing the temperature of the blood. Control center — the hypothalamus, whose set point is about 37 °C (98.6 °F), varying slightly between people. Effectors — sweat glands, the blood vessels of the dermis, the arrector pili muscles and the skeletal muscles. Too hot. Thermoreceptors detect the rise and message the hypothalamus, which sends impulses to increase sweat gland secretion — evaporation sheds heat — and to dilate the dermal blood vessels, releasing more heat to the air (the flushed look during exercise). The arrector pili relax, keeping damp hair against the skin, and the brain may add behavioural responses such as seeking shade. Too cold. Skin thermoreceptors detect the drop; the hypothalamus orders decreased sweating, constriction of dermal vessels (conserving heat for the core — and why fingers and toes get frostbite first), contraction of the arrector pili to trap insulating air (piloerection), a raised metabolic rate, and shivering — repeated skeletal muscle contraction. Plus behavioural responses. Why it is negative feedback: the effect produced — cooling, or warming — is relayed back, and reaching the set point is itself what shuts the corrective mechanism off. Temperature therefore oscillates around the set point rather than sitting on it, exactly like a house thermostat. Failures: hyperthermia (heat stroke) — crisis at about 42 °C, rarely survivable at 43 °C; hypothermia — 35 °C or below, unconsciousness at 33 °C, regulation fully shut down at 30 °C.

Three components named and mapped, then both branches with at least three effectors each, then the sentence explaining why it counts as negative feedback. The temperatures are worth having. A common half-answer gives only sweating and shivering — Figure 4.13 shows only two effectors per branch, and the text lists more.

6Ch. 4short answer4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Compare the three cell junction types, giving an example of each and saying why that tissue needs it.

Model answer

Tight junctions. The membranes of neighbouring cells are attached so securely that they form a leakproof seal — nothing passes between the cells. Found in the linings of the urinary tract and the intestines, where the seal is what stops urine or digestive juices leaking through the epithelium into the tissue beneath. Adhesion junctions, also called desmosomes. Less rigid — they work like rivets holding adjacent tissue layers together. The plasma membranes do not actually touch; they are bound by intercellular filaments attached to a thickening in the membrane, so the cells stay connected but can still slide slightly. Common in tissues that must withstand stretching — skin, heart muscle, the opening of the uterus. Gap junctions. Small holes connecting the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, letting certain small molecules and ions flow directly from one to the next. In cardiac and smooth muscle they synchronise electrical activity and therefore contraction, which is how the heart wall contracts as one and how peristalsis works. The pattern: each junction suits the function of its tissue — seal where nothing may leak, rivet where the tissue stretches, hole where cells must act together.

Three junctions, each with what it does structurally, an example tissue, and why that tissue needs it. The study guide asks to "compare and contrast, providing examples", so the closing pattern sentence is answering the question as asked rather than listing three definitions.

1Ch. 4label the diagramThe skin, in cross-section

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Epidermis

    The thin outer layer, several layers of epithelial cells. Avascular — its deepest layer divides and pushes cells up, and they flatten, fill with keratin and die on the way because they lose their supply of nutrients.

  2. 2name it

    Dermis

    The much thicker inner layer. Mostly connective tissue, and the layer that holds the blood vessels, nerves, glands and follicles. It does not wear away, which is why tattoos are permanent.

  3. 3name it

    Hypodermis

    Loose connective tissue anchoring the skin to what lies beneath. Holds about half the body's fat. Not usually counted as part of the skin.

  4. 4name it

    Hair shaft

    The part projecting above the surface. Hair is keratin, made the same way the epidermis is — cells divide, get pushed away from their supply, die, and the keratin remains.

  5. 5name it

    Hair follicle

    The structure the root sits in, extending down into the dermis or hypodermis. Nerve endings around it are sensitive enough to notice a slight movement of the shaft.

  6. 6name it

    Arrector pili

    A tiny smooth muscle attached to the follicle. Contraction raises the hair — a goose bump — and in the cold it is piloerection, trapping an insulating layer of air.

  7. 7name it

    Oil (sebaceous) gland

    Secretes sebum — fats, cholesterol, proteins and salts — onto the hair follicle, not onto the surface. Block that duct and you get acne.

  8. 8name it

    Sweat gland

    Produces sweat — mostly water with salts, lactic acid, vitamin C and urea. Its principal function is temperature regulation by evaporation.

  9. 9name it

    Sweat gland duct and pore

    Carries the secretion to the surface, where it can evaporate.

  10. 10name it

    Sensory corpuscle

    One of the structures for detecting temperature, touch, pressure and pain. They are components of the nervous system.

  11. 11name it

    Melanocyte

    A spiderlike pigment cell at the base of the epidermis. It makes melanin and distributes it in granules to the keratinocytes above, where it absorbs UV. Everyone has about the same number — the form of melanin and the size and number of granules is what differs.

  12. 12name it

    Adipocytes

    Fat cells filling the hypodermis. They cushion blows and insulate, and they are why liposuction works on this layer and not a deeper one.

2Ch. 4label the diagramThe four tissue types

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Free surface

    Every epithelium has one. It may be specialised for protection, secretion or absorption, and nothing is attached to it.

  2. 2name it

    Epithelial tissue

    Tightly packed cells with very little matrix. Covers surfaces, lines cavities and organs, and forms glands. This panel is simple columnar.

  3. 3name it

    Basement membrane

    A noncellular layer binding the epithelium to the connective tissue beneath and helping it resist stretching. Nutrition diffuses across it, because epithelium is avascular.

  4. 4name it

    Connective tissue

    Cells scattered in a matrix — the opposite arrangement, and the only tissue type whose identity comes from its matrix rather than its cells. This panel is areolar.

  5. 5name it

    Matrix

    Protein fibres plus ground substance. Collagen resists pulling, elastic fibres recoil, reticular fibres form supportive networks — and fibroblasts make all three. Ground substance may be solid (bone), fluid (blood) or gelatinous (cartilage).

  6. 6name it

    Skeletal muscle

    Long cylindrical fibers, striations, and many nuclei along the periphery. The only voluntary muscle.

  7. 7name it

    Smooth muscle

    Short, spindle-shaped with tapered ends, one nucleus, no striations — its myofilaments are not arranged in sarcomeres. Involuntary.

  8. 8name it

    Neuron

    Cell body, many dendrites receiving signals, and one axon carrying the impulse away. Generates and conducts the nerve impulse.

  9. 9name it

    Neuroglia

    Far more numerous than neurons. They support, insulate, protect and nourish neurons and speed conduction.

1Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The four tissue types and what each does

Back

Epithelial — covers, lines, forms glands. Connective — binds, supports, stores fat, transports, immunity. Muscle — movement. Nervous — conducts impulses.

2Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The two features every epithelium has

Back

A free surface (specialised for protection, secretion or absorption) and a basement membrane — a noncellular layer binding it to connective tissue and resisting stretch.

3Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The three epithelial shapes, and what each is for

Back

Squamous — flat, scale-like; diffusion (lung air sacs, blood vessels). Cuboidal — cube-shaped; secretion and absorption (kidney tubules, glands). Columnar — elongated; absorption and secretion (small intestine, with goblet cells).

4Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook

Simple vs stratified

Back

Simple — one layer. Stratified — more than one, and usually protective, because the thickness makes passage harder. Shape and layer count are independent axes — learn Table 4.1 as a 3 × 2 grid.

5Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Exocrine vs endocrine gland

Back

Exocrine — secretes through ducts onto surfaces, into cavities or organs (digestive enzymes, milk, oil, sweat). Endocrine — ductless; hormones diffuse into the bloodstream. Both are epithelium.

6Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

What makes connective tissue different from every other tissue?

Back

It is mostly matrix, not cells — and a given connective tissue's character comes from its matrix. Matrix = protein fibres + ground substance (solid in bone, fluid in blood, gelatinous in cartilage).

7Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The three fibre types, and who makes them

Back

Collagen — ropelike, resists pulling. Elastic — coiled, stretches and recoils (skin, lungs, vessels). Reticular — thin branching collagen networks supporting liver and spleen. All three made by fibroblasts.

8Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Fibroblasts

Back

The connective tissue cell that produces all three fibre types and repairs tears — after a cut they move to the wound and lay down collagen that closes it and gives the epidermis a surface to grow back over.

9Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Loose connective tissue — the two kinds

Back

Areolar — the universal packing material between tissues; lets muscles slide, anchors skin. Adipose — cells specialised for fat storage; also insulates and cushions organs.

10Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Dense connective tissue — where

Back

Ligaments (bone to bone), tendons (muscle to bone) and the dermis. Large amounts of tightly woven fibres in strong bands. Whalen's subtype: dense regular fibrous connective tissue.

11Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook

Why does cartilage heal so slowly?

Back

It has no blood vessels and no nerves. Nutrients reach the chondrocytes in their lacunae by diffusion from nearby capillaries. Bone is vascular and heals promptly.

12Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The three cartilages

Back

Hyaline — most abundant, weakest; long-bone ends, nose, ribs, larynx, trachea. Elastic — most flexible, wavy elastic fibres; external ear. Fibrocartilage — toughest, built for pressure; knee, intervertebral disks, pubic symphysis.

13Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why is blood connective tissue?

Back

Cells suspended in an extracellular matrix — the liquid matrix is plasma, and the formed elements are red cells, white cells and platelets. Its "fibres" are soluble proteins, visible only when it clots.

14Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth muscle

Back

Skeletal — voluntary, striated, many nuclei, long cylinders. Cardiac — involuntary, striated, one central nucleus, branching, intercalated discs. Smooth — involuntary, no striations, tapered ends, one nucleus.

15Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Neuron vs neuroglia

Back

Neuron — generates and conducts impulses; cell body, branched dendrites (receive), one axon (conducts away). Neuroglia — far more numerous; support, insulate, protect, nourish neurons and speed conduction.

16Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The three cell junctions

Back

Tight — leakproof seal (intestine, urinary tract). Adhesion / desmosome — rivets that allow slight sliding (skin, heart muscle, cervix). Gap — small holes passing ions, synchronising contraction (cardiac, smooth muscle).

17Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Organ vs organ system

Back

Organ — two or more different tissues working together for a specific function. Organ system — a group of organs with a common function. 11 major organ systems.

18Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The ventral cavity and its subdivisions

Back

Ventral → thoracic and abdominal, separated by the diaphragm. Thoracic → pleural cavities (lungs) and pericardial cavity (heart). Abdominal → digestive, urinary and reproductive systems.

19Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The dorsal cavity and its subdivisions

Back

Dorsal → cranial cavity (brain) and spinal cavity (spinal cord).

20Ch. 4flashcard4.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The four membranes

Back

Mucous — lines passages open to the exterior. Serous — lines the thoracic and abdominal cavities and their organs. Synovial — lines freely movable joint cavities. Cutaneous — the skin; thick, waterproof, dry.

21Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

The integumentary system's five functions

Back

Protection (barrier, UV, macrophages) · preventing water loss (keratin) · temperature regulation (sweat, blood flow) · vitamin D production · sensation.

22Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

The three layers, and which is not skin

Back

Epidermis — thin, outer, epithelial, avascular. Dermis — thicker, connective tissue, holds the vessels, nerves, glands and follicles. Hypodermis — anchors the skin and holds half the body's fat; not usually considered part of the skin.

23Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why do epidermal cells die as they move outward?

Back

The epidermis has no blood vessels. Pushed up from the dividing deepest layer, they lose nourishment from the dermis, flatten, fill with keratin and die. 30,000–40,000 shed per minute; two weeks to a month from formation to shedding.

24Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Keratin

Back

The tough, water-resistant fibrous protein that replaces the cytoplasm of epidermal cells. It is what prevents excessive water loss. Nails are the same protein.

25Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why does a transdermal patch work?

Back

The epidermis resists water, but its cells have lipid membranes — so a lipid-soluble drug can cross them, diffuse into the connective tissue and reach the blood. Hormones, nicotine, motion-sickness drugs.

26Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook

Why are tattoos permanent, and why do they hurt?

Back

The ink is injected into the dermis, which does not wear away — unlike the constantly shed epidermis. It hurts because the dermis is laced with nerves and sensory receptors.

27Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook

What is a blister?

Back

Tissue fluid accumulating between epidermis and dermis, separating the layers. That fluid is normally how nutrients reach the avascular epidermis from dermal vessels.

28Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

What determines skin colour?

Back

Pigment and blood flow. All people have about the same number of melanocytes — what differs is the form of melanin (yellow-to-red or black-to-brown) and the size and number of granules. Circulation and oxygenation add the pink, the blush and the blue.

29Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Melanocytes

Back

Spiderlike pigment cells at the base of the epidermis. They make melanin, which is taken up by surrounding epidermal cells and absorbs UV before it damages deeper cells.

30Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why is a tan protective, and what is the catch?

Back

UV drives melanocytes to make more melanin, which absorbs UV. But the buildup is not instantaneous — and that gap is when the damage happens.

31Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook

The three skin cancers

Back

Basal cell — commonest; from the deepest epidermal layer. Squamous cell — second; from newly flattening cells. Melanoma — least common, most dangerous; from melanocytes, and it metastasises. 90% survival before spread, ~14% after.

32Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook

ABCD

Back

Asymmetry · Border (diffuse, unclear) · Colour (mottled brown, black, red, white, blue) · Diameter (over 5 mm is threatening).

33Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Oil (sebaceous) glands

Back

Everywhere except palms and soles. Secrete sebum — fats, cholesterol, proteins, salts — onto the hair follicle, lubricating hair and skin and inhibiting some bacteria. A blocked duct gives acne.

34Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook

Whitehead, blackhead, pimple

Back

Whitehead — a follicle obstructed by sebum and dead cells. Blackhead — the same, with melanin mixed in; not dirt. Pimple — an obstructed follicle that has ruptured into the surrounding epidermis.

35Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Sweat glands vs wax glands

Back

Sweat — water plus salts, lactic acid, vitamin C and wastes such as urea; principal function is temperature regulation by evaporation. Wax — modified sweat glands in the external ear canal, trapping particles.

36Ch. 4flashcard4.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Arrector pili

Back

A tiny smooth muscle in the dermis attached to a hair follicle. Contraction raises the hair — a goose bump — associated with fear and cold. In the cold it is piloerection, trapping insulating air.

37Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Homeostasis

Back

Maintaining a relatively stable internal environment despite external change. It is dynamic, not static — mechanisms dampen fluctuations around a set point rather than holding anything constant.

38Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Negative vs positive feedback

Back

Negative — the response opposes the direction of change and shuts off on reaching the normal value. Positive — the change promotes further change in the same direction; it does not promote homeostasis.

39Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

The three components of a homeostatic mechanism

Back

Receptor — detects the change. Control center — holds the set point, integrates input, selects the response; usually the brain. Effector — usually a muscle or gland; carries it out.

40Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

The temperature loop, mapped

Back

Receptors — skin thermoreceptors and deep blood-temperature receptors. Control center — the hypothalamus, set point about 37 °C (98.6 °F). Effectors — sweat glands, dermal blood vessels, arrector pili, skeletal muscles.

41Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Too hot — what the body does

Back

Sweat glands increase output · dermal vessels dilate (the flushed look) · arrector pili relax · behavioural responses — shade, removing layers.

42Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Too cold — what the body does

Back

Sweating decreases · dermal vessels constrict (core over extremities) · arrector pili contract — piloerection · metabolic rate rises · shivering · behavioural responses.

43Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Hyperthermia — the numbers

Back

Abnormally high body temperature, heat stroke; confusion and dizziness. At about 42 °C (107 °F) the heartbeat becomes irregular, blood oxygen drops and the liver fails. Few survive 43 °C (110 °F).

44Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Hypothermia — the numbers

Back

35 °C (95 °F) or below. Giddiness and confusion first; unconsciousness at 33 °C (91.4 °F); at 30 °C (86 °F) vessels are fully constricted and regulation shuts down.

45Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook

Why are fingers and toes the first to get frostbite?

Back

The cold response constricts dermal vessels and shunts blood to the core — protective for the organs, but it leaves the extremities with the least blood flow exactly when the cold is worst.

46Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook

The house thermostat analogy

Back

The thermostat is both receptor and control center; the furnace is the effector. Temperature oscillates around the set point rather than sitting on it — which is the point of "dynamic".

47Ch. 4flashcard4.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Homeostasis when it fails — the chapter's example

Back

Diabetes. Normally rising blood glucose after a meal makes the pancreas release insulin, lowering it. In diabetes the pancreas makes too little, or cells cannot use it — and high glucose damages eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels.

Ch. 3 · Respiration — Cellular Respiration

Week 7 · study page · 24 multiple choice · 4 short answer · 26 flashcards · 1 diagrams, 10 labels · His first named topic. The four-phase grid on the Week 7 board tab is the thing to know cold — it is simultaneously his 10-point fill-in-the-blank, the four Activity 1 tables and the graded lab summary table.

1Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which phase of cellular respiration happens outside the mitochondrion?

Answer: c

Only glycolysis is in the cytoplasm; the other three phases are in the mitochondrion — the transition reaction and the cycle in the matrix, the chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Location is directly testable and it is one of the study guide's six objectives. Fermentation is also entirely cytoplasmic, which is why the end-of-chapter question offering "fermentation occurs in mitochondria" is the false statement.

2Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

How much ATP does glycolysis net per glucose?

Answer: a

The first steps spend 2 ATP preparing glucose to be split — the energy investment phase — and later steps make 4, for a net of 2. The distractors are the other real numbers in the section: 4 is the gross, 32 is the electron transport chain's yield, and 36 is the total. Getting asked for "net" and answering the gross is the classic slip.

3Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

What happens to glucose during glycolysis?

Answer: b

Glyco = sugar, lysis = splitting: the 6-carbon glucose is split into two 3-carbon pyruvates, with 2 NADH and a net 2 ATP. No carbon is lost as CO2 in glycolysis — the carbons are all still there, in the two pyruvates, which is why option a is wrong. Option c is the transition reaction, the step that comes next.

4Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

The transition reaction produces which set of products per glucose?

Answer: a

One carbon is stripped from each pyruvate as CO2, and the remaining 2-carbon acetyl group binds coenzyme A, giving 2 acetyl CoA, 2 NADH and 2 CO2 for one glucose. The transition reaction makes no ATP at all — that rules out c. Option d is the citric acid cycle's carrier yield, and option b is glycolysis.

5Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Per glucose, what does the citric acid cycle yield?

Answer: b

Per turn the cycle gives 1 ATP, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 2 CO2; two acetyl CoA enter per glucose, so double everything. This is where every FADH2 in the whole pathway comes from. Table 3.4 omits the CO2 from its Main Products column even though the text says the cycle releases it — Whalen gave the counts explicitly, so use them.

6Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which two phases release the CO2 you breathe out?

Answer: c

The transition reaction gives 2 CO2 and the citric acid cycle gives 4, for six carbons out — exactly the six that came in as glucose. Glycolysis loses no carbon (they all leave in the two pyruvates) and the electron transport chain makes water, not CO2. The book asks this as a Stop and Think question, so it is on the chapter's own list.

7Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

What is oxygen's role in cellular respiration?

Answer: b

Oxygen takes the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with two hydrogen ions to form water. It is one of the study guide's six objectives. Option c is the job of NADH and FADH2, the electron carriers. The consequence of removing oxygen is the next question: electrons back up in the carriers and the whole thing stalls.

8Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Oxygen becomes unavailable. What happens to the citric acid cycle?

Answer: c

The cycle does not use oxygen directly, which makes option b tempting — but it depends on the chain to unload NADH and FADH2 and regenerate the empty carriers. With no oxygen the electrons back up, the carriers stay loaded, and the cycle backs up behind them. The cell falls back on fermentation, which regenerates NAD+ in the cytoplasm instead.

9Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

How much of respiration's ATP comes from the electron transport chain?

Answer: c

2 from glycolysis + 2 from the cycle + 32 from the chain = 36 per glucose. The chain is where almost all of it is, which is why the deck spends four slides on it — double any other phase. Whalen was unequivocal that the chain's number is 32, not 34, and said he wanted the class to have the right figure for the exam.

10Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

Why does a cell break glucose down in many small steps rather than all at once?

Answer: b

The book's own argument: burning glucose with oxygen in a beaker happens in one step and loses all the energy as heat. Going step by step lets the cell capture much of that energy as the high-energy bonds of ATP. Option d is a real-sounding chemical claim the chapter never makes, and option a is false — enzymes do act on glucose, in the first steps of glycolysis.

11Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

What distinguishes a catabolic from an anabolic pathway?

Answer: c

Catabolic pathways break complex molecules into simpler ones and release energy — cellular respiration and fermentation are both catabolic. Anabolic pathways build up and consume energy. Option a is the trap: fermentation is catabolic and needs no oxygen, so oxygen cannot be the dividing line. Both kinds are enzyme-driven.

12Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which molecule carries the acetyl group into the citric acid cycle?

Answer: c

CoA carries carbon; NAD+ and FAD carry electrons. That division is the whole point of the transition reaction, and Whalen asked the room who drove the acetyl group, got "NAD" back, and corrected it on the spot. Pyruvate is what arrives, not what carries — it loses a carbon and the remaining acetyl group binds CoA.

13Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Fermentation's real purpose in a muscle cell is what?

Answer: b

Fermentation nets only 2 ATP against respiration's 36, so it is not about yield. Its job is to pass electrons from NADH onto pyruvate, regenerating NAD+ — without which glycolysis runs out of empty carriers and stops. Option c is backwards: fermentation produces the lactic acid. Option d is a contradiction — the whole point is that oxygen is absent.

14Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

In fermentation, what is the final electron acceptor?

Answer: d

Pyruvate, or a derivative of it — which is exactly what makes fermentation anaerobic. In respiration the acceptor is oxygen, which becomes water. NAD+ is not an acceptor at the end of the line; it is the carrier that gets regenerated when pyruvate takes the electrons.

15Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Where does lactic acid go after strenuous exercise?

Answer: c

Lactic acid enters the blood and travels to the liver, which converts it back to pyruvate — which is why the soreness fades. Whalen gave the same route. Option a is tempting because mitochondria are where respiration resumes, but the chapter is specific about the liver being the site of the conversion.

16Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

Glucose and oxygen both have to get into the cell. How does each cross the membrane?

Answer: b

Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it crosses by simple diffusion; glucose needs a carrier protein, so it enters by facilitated diffusion. Neither costs ATP, which rules out option d. It is a small fact and an easy point — the kind the chapter states once and the exam picks up because it links respiration back to membrane transport.

17Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which statement about the inner mitochondrial membrane is correct?

Answer: b

The folding multiplies the surface area, leaving room for thousands of sets of electron carriers — more chain, more ATP. Option c is wrong twice over: glycolysis is in the cytoplasm and the transition reaction is in the matrix. Option d is wrong because the mitochondrion has two membranes, which is what makes an intermembrane space possible.

18Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which pairing of phase and location is wrong?

Answer: c

The citric acid cycle is in the matrix, the fluid inside the inner membrane; only the electron transport chain is embedded in the membrane itself. The distinction matters because the chain's location is what lets it pump H+ into the intermembrane space. The other three pairings are right as written.

19Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which phase produces no ATP directly?

Answer: b

The transition reaction makes 2 acetyl CoA, 2 NADH and 2 CO2 — and no ATP. Glycolysis makes 2 net and the cycle makes 2, both by substrate-level phosphorylation. The electron transport chain is the tempting answer because it makes no ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation either — but it makes 32 through ATP synthase, so "no ATP" is wrong for it.

20Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

Both cellular respiration and fermentation share which phase?

Answer: a

Both begin with glycolysis in the cytoplasm — 2 pyruvate, 2 NADH, net 2 ATP. They diverge at what happens to the pyruvate: into the mitochondrion for the transition reaction if oxygen is available, or reduced to lactic acid in the cytoplasm if it is not. This is a true statement in the book's own "choose the incorrect statement" question.

21Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

How much more ATP does respiration yield than fermentation, per glucose?

Answer: c

36 against 2 is eighteenfold, which is why the chapter calls fermentation very inefficient. Option d is the trap for anyone who remembers 36 and forgets that fermentation still nets 2. The reason fermentation survives at all is speed and independence from oxygen, not yield.

22Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

Mitochondrial diseases are inherited in an unusual pattern. Which statement is right?

Answer: a

Nuclear DNA comes from both parents; mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother, so every child of an affected woman inherits the mutation and only her daughters pass it on. Option d is half right and therefore the good distractor: some mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported, but others are encoded by mitochondrial DNA itself.

23Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook

Two siblings inherit the same mitochondrial mutation but differ sharply in severity. Why?

Answer: b

A cell holds hundreds of mitochondria, some normal and some defective, and the proportion sets the severity. Eggs differ in that proportion, so siblings with the same inherited mutation can be affected very differently. The worst damage lands on the high-energy organs — brain, heart, kidneys, skeletal muscle — whichever sibling it strikes.

24Ch. 3 · Respiration3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which activity would be running mostly on lactic acid fermentation?

Answer: c

Fermentation takes over when oxygen delivery cannot keep up, which is strenuous, short, burst effort. At rest and at low intensity the cardiovascular system supplies plenty of oxygen and the cell runs aerobically, which is both options a, b and d. The lactic acid that builds up during the sprint is what goes to the liver afterwards.

1Ch. 3 · Respirationshort answer3.7
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Name the four phases of aerobic respiration, say where each happens, and give the energy output of each.

Model answer

Glycolysis — cytoplasm. Glucose (6C) is split into 2 pyruvate (3C each). Net 2 ATP (4 made, 2 spent) and 2 NADH. No oxygen needed. Transition reaction — mitochondrial matrix. One carbon is removed from each pyruvate as CO2; the remaining 2-carbon acetyl group binds coenzyme A. Products: 2 acetyl CoA, 2 NADH, 2 CO2 — and no ATP. Citric acid cycle (Krebs / TCA) — mitochondrial matrix. Acetyl CoA joins a 4-carbon compound to form citrate; two turns per glucose. Products: 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 4 CO2. Electron transport chain — inner mitochondrial membrane. NADH and FADH2 unload their electrons onto carrier proteins; the energy released drives ATP synthesis, and oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water. Products: 32 ATP and H2O. Total: 2 + 2 + 32 = 36 ATP per glucose.

This is the study guide's objective three and four in one answer, and Whalen called it a 10-point fill-in-the-blank story. Four phases, four locations, the ATP at each, and the carriers — then the total. Losing the "net" on glycolysis or putting the cycle on the membrane are the marks most often dropped.

2Ch. 3 · Respirationshort answer3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Explain what happens in a muscle cell when oxygen runs short, and why.

Model answer

The electron transport chain stops, because oxygen is its final electron acceptor. Electrons then back up in the carrier proteins, so NADH and FADH2 cannot unload — and because the citric acid cycle depends on empty carriers, it backs up behind the chain and halts too. The transition reaction stops with it. What is left is glycolysis, which needs no oxygen — but glycolysis also needs a supply of empty NAD+, and there is now nowhere for its NADH to unload. Fermentation solves that: the electrons on NADH are passed to pyruvate, reducing it to lactic acid and regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running. The yield is only 2 ATP per glucose against 36 — very inefficient, but it keeps ATP flowing. The lactic acid that accumulates partly accounts for post-exercise muscle pain; it later enters the blood and is converted back to pyruvate in the liver.

Marks for the chain stopping and why — oxygen as final acceptor — then the backup through the cycle, then fermentation's real purpose (NAD+ regeneration, not ATP), then 2 versus 36, then the liver. Saying "the cell switches to fermentation to make ATP" alone misses the point of the question.

3Ch. 3 · Respirationshort answer3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Trace the six carbons of one glucose molecule through respiration. Where does each end up?

Model answer

Glucose has 6 carbons. Glycolysis loses none — it splits the 6-carbon sugar into two 3-carbon pyruvates, so all six are still there. The transition reaction removes one carbon from each pyruvate as CO2 — 2 carbons out, leaving two 2-carbon acetyl groups bound to CoA. The citric acid cycle removes the remaining four: each turn releases 2 CO2, and there are two turns per glucose, so 4 carbons out. Total: 6 CO2, which is exactly the six carbons that came in — and that CO2 is what you breathe out. The electron transport chain releases no carbon at all; its product is water, made when oxygen accepts the electrons and combines with hydrogen ions.

The books balance: 0 + 2 + 4 = 6. Full marks need each phase's contribution and the closing observation that the chain produces water rather than CO2. Note that Table 3.4 omits the cycle's CO2 from its Main Products column even though the section text states it — the counts above are the lecture's and are the complete ones.

4Ch. 3 · Respirationshort answer3.7
  • textbook

What is metabolism, and how do the two kinds of metabolic pathway differ? Give an example of each.

Model answer

Metabolism is all the chemical reactions that take place in a cell. Those reactions are organised into metabolic pathways — series of enzyme-driven steps in which the products of one step become the substrates of the next, modifying a starting molecule into a final product. Catabolic pathways break complex molecules into simpler ones and release energy. Cellular respiration is the example: glucose is broken down to CO2 and water, and the energy is captured as ATP. Fermentation is also catabolic. Anabolic pathways build complex molecules from simpler ones and consume energy. Making ATP itself from ADP + phosphate is an anabolic step, as is assembling proteins from amino acids. Note that needing oxygen is not what makes a pathway catabolic — fermentation is anaerobic and catabolic both.

Definition of metabolism, then pathway as enzyme-driven steps with substrates and products, then the two kinds with direction of energy flow and one example each. The oxygen caveat at the end is the discriminating detail.

1Ch. 3 · Respirationlabel the diagramWhere the four phases happen

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Cytoplasm

    The location of glycolysis — and of fermentation, entirely. Everything else is inside the mitochondrion.

  2. 2name it

    Glycolysis

    Glucose (6C) split into 2 pyruvate (3C). Net 2 ATP (4 made, 2 spent) and 2 NADH. No oxygen needed, and no CO2 released.

  3. 3name it

    Outer mitochondrial membrane

    The smooth boundary of the organelle.

  4. 4name it

    Intermembrane space

    Where H+ is pumped, building the gradient that drives ATP synthase. The steeper the gradient, the faster the ATP.

  5. 5name it

    Inner mitochondrial membrane

    Highly folded, which multiplies the surface area — room for thousands of sets of electron carriers. The electron transport chain is embedded here.

  6. 6name it

    Transition reaction

    In the matrix. One carbon off each pyruvate as CO2; the rest binds coenzyme A. 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 NADH, 2 CO2 — and no ATP at all.

  7. 7name it

    Citric acid cycle

    Also in the matrix, and also called the Krebs or TCA cycle. Two turns per glucose: 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 4 CO2.

  8. 8name it

    Matrix

    The fluid inside the inner membrane. Both the transition reaction and the cycle happen here — not on the membrane.

  9. 9name it

    Electron transport chain

    32 ATP and water. NADH unloads at complex I, FADH2 at complex II — which has no H+ pump, and is why FADH2 is worth less.

  10. 10name it

    Oxygen

    The final electron acceptor. It takes the last electron and combines with hydrogen ions to form water. Remove it and the electrons back up, the carriers stay loaded, and the cycle stalls behind them.

1Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Metabolism

Back

All the chemical reactions that take place in a cell, organised into metabolic pathways — series of enzyme-driven steps where each step's products are the next step's substrates.

2Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Catabolic vs anabolic pathway

Back

Catabolic — breaks complex molecules down, releases energy (respiration, fermentation). Anabolic — builds complex from simple, consumes energy.

3Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Cellular respiration — the one-line definition

Back

The oxygen-requiring breakdown of glucose. Final products: carbon dioxide, water and energy as ATP.

4Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

The four phases and where each happens

Back

Glycolysis — cytoplasm. Transition reaction — mitochondrial matrix. Citric acid cycle — matrix. Electron transport chain — inner mitochondrial membrane.

5Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Glycolysis — in and out

Back

In: 1 glucose (6C) + 2 ATP. Out: 2 pyruvate (3C), net 2 ATP, 2 NADH. No oxygen needed, no CO2 released.

6Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why does glycolysis spend ATP before it makes any?

Back

The first steps add phosphates to glucose — the energy investment phase — which makes it unstable and reactive enough to split into two 3-carbon molecules.

7Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Transition reaction — in and out

Back

In: 2 pyruvate + 2 CoA. Out: 2 acetyl CoA, 2 NADH, 2 CO2. No ATP.

8Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Citric acid cycle — per turn, and per glucose

Back

Per turn: 1 ATP · 3 NADH · 1 FADH2 · 2 CO2. Per glucose (two turns): 2 ATP · 6 NADH · 2 FADH2 · 4 CO2.

9Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Three names for one cycle

Back

Citric acid cycle · Krebs cycle · TCA cycle. Named for its first product, citrate; named for Hans Krebs.

10Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Electron transport chain — in and out

Back

In: 10 NADH + 2 FADH2 + O2. Out: 32 ATP + H2O. Carrier proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is highly folded to fit thousands of sets.

11Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

The ATP tally

Back

2 (glycolysis) + 2 (citric acid cycle) + 32 (electron transport chain) = 36 per glucose. Fermentation: 2.

12Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • lecture

32 or 34 for the chain?

Back

32. The arithmetic 10 NADH × 3 + 2 FADH2 × 2 gives 34, and Whalen noticed — then settled on 32 for the exam.

13Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Where does the CO2 come from?

Back

Transition reaction — 2. Citric acid cycle — 4. Six carbons in as glucose, six out as CO2. Glycolysis and the chain release none.

14Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

What does oxygen do?

Back

It is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain, combining with two hydrogen ions to form water. Without it, electrons back up and everything upstream stalls.

15Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • lecture

Who carries carbon, and who carries electrons?

Back

CoA carries carbon. NAD+ and FAD carry electrons as NADH and FADH2.

16Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Pyruvate

Back

The 3-carbon end product of glycolysis. With oxygen it enters the mitochondrion for the transition reaction; without oxygen it is reduced to lactic acid in the cytoplasm.

17Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Acetyl CoA

Back

A 2-carbon acetyl group bound to coenzyme A — the high-energy fuel that enters the citric acid cycle.

18Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Coenzyme

Back

An organic molecule that helps an enzyme convert substrate into product — NAD+, FAD and coenzyme A are all coenzymes.

19Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Fermentation — what it is and what it yields

Back

Breaking glucose down without oxygen, entirely in the cytoplasm. Net 2 ATP per glucose. Final electron acceptor: pyruvate or a derivative.

20Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

What is fermentation actually for?

Back

Regenerating NAD+. Passing electrons from NADH onto pyruvate frees the carrier so glycolysis can keep running — the 2 ATP is a by-product of keeping the line open.

21Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Lactic acid — where it comes from and where it goes

Back

Made in muscle by lactic acid fermentation when oxygen runs short; partly responsible for post-exercise pain. It enters the blood and the liver converts it back to pyruvate.

22Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

How do glucose and oxygen enter a cell?

Back

Oxygen — simple diffusion. Glucose — facilitated diffusion, through a carrier protein. Neither costs ATP.

23Ch. 3 · RespirationflashcardLab 6 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Substrate-level vs oxidative phosphorylation

Back

Substrate-level — an enzyme moves a phosphate already on another molecule straight onto ADP; glycolysis and the cycle. Oxidative — the H+ gradient drives ATP synthase; the chain only.

24Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Why is respiration stepwise rather than one reaction?

Back

Burning glucose in one step — as in a beaker — loses all the energy as heat. Many small steps let the cell capture it as ATP.

25Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Mitochondrial diseases — inheritance

Back

Mitochondrial DNA passes only from the mother, so every child of an affected woman inherits it and only daughters pass it on. Some mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported.

26Ch. 3 · Respirationflashcard3.7
  • textbook

Mitochondrial diseases — why severity varies

Back

A cell holds hundreds of mitochondria, some normal and some defective, and the proportion sets severity. Eggs differ, so siblings with the same mutation can differ sharply. Worst hit: brain, heart, kidneys, skeletal muscle.

Ch. 15 — Digestive System & Nutrition

Week 7 · study page · 38 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 56 flashcards · 2 diagrams, 25 labels

1Ch. 1515.1
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Reading from the lumen outward, what is the order of the four layers of the GI tract?

Answer: c

Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa — inside out. Option d is the same list read the wrong way, and option a swaps the middle two. Within the muscularis, the same trap runs again: circular is inner, longitudinal is outer. The study guide gives "the structure and functions of the 4 layers" as its own objective, so this is guaranteed material.

2Ch. 1515.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which layer of the GI tract wall carries the blood vessels, lymph vessels and nerves?

Answer: b

The submucosa is connective tissue holding the vessels and nerves; its blood supply maintains the cells and in some regions picks up the products of digestion, and its nerves coordinate the muscularis's contractions. The mucosa is the moist, mucus-secreting absorptive lining — its own lamina propria carries the small vessels, which is why the lab distinguishes the two layers by vessel size.

3Ch. 1515.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Peristalsis and segmental contractions do different jobs. Which description is right?

Answer: b

Peristalsis propels — circular muscle contracts behind the bolus while longitudinal muscle ahead shortens the tube to receive it. Segmental contractions are local, random, and especially common in the small intestine; they mix chyme with digestive juices and move the contents over the intestinal wall, which helps absorption. That absorption role is the half most answers miss.

4Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Why can you swallow while standing on your head?

Answer: b

The muscular wave does the work, so gravity is not required — you could swallow upside down or in space. Option d is the trap the book itself sets: emulsification is what bile salts do to fat, not a muscle contraction. The epiglottis covers the glottis to keep food out of the airway, not to seal the esophagus.

5Ch. 1515.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which compartment is the exception to the two-layer muscularis, and why?

Answer: c

The stomach has three smooth-muscle layers running in different directions — the extra one is oblique, innermost — because it has to twist, knead and compress food into chyme, not just move it along. Whalen made the same point: only the stomach churns. It is the one exception the chapter flags in 15.1 and then delivers in 15.2.

6Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What does salivary amylase do, and where does it stop working?

Answer: a

Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth — salivary amylase breaks polysaccharides into shorter chains, which is why bread chewed for a while tastes sweet. It keeps working inside the swallowed bolus until the stomach's acid denatures it. The rest of saliva is water to moisten and mucus to bind the particles into a bolus.

7Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which pairing of salivary gland and location is right?

Answer: b

Three pairs: parotid in front of the ears, submandibular below the jaw, sublingual under the tongue — the names say it, which is the point. The lab groups them differently but compatibly: sublingual is inside the oral cavity; parotid and submandibular are adjacent to it.

8Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Tooth decay reaches the pulp. Which sequence did it take?

Answer: a

Enamel is the outermost, nonliving, calcium-hardened covering of the crown; under it is the hard, bonelike dentin; at the centre is the pulp, with the blood vessels and nerves. Cementum covers the root, not the crown, so it is not on the path. Mouth bacteria digest trapped sugar and make the acid that erodes the enamel into a cavity; plaque holds that acid against the tooth.

9Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Gingivitis and periodontitis differ how?

Answer: a

Gingivitis is plaque at the gum line inflaming the gums and leaving pockets that trap yet more plaque. Periodontitis is the later stage, where bacteria attack the bone and soft tissue around the tooth and loosen it — it is the major cause of adult tooth loss, and gum disease affects two of three middle-aged Americans. Both are bacterial, which rules out option d.

10Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

During swallowing, what keeps food out of the nasal cavity?

Answer: c

Two structures move and they guard two different routes. The soft palate — muscle only, no bone — blocks the nasal cavity, while the larynx rises and the epiglottis covers the glottis to keep food out of the airway. The hard palate is bone-reinforced and does not move. Swallowing has a voluntary phase (tongue pushes the bolus back) and then an involuntary reflex once food is in the pharynx.

11Ch. 1515.2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which cell of a gastric gland makes hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?

Answer: b

The lab names all four. Parietal cells → HCl and intrinsic factor. Chief cells → pepsinogen and gastric lipase. G cells → gastrin, a hormone. Mucous cells → mucus. The chapter describes the same secretions without naming the cell types, so this is the lab's vocabulary — and intrinsic factor is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the small intestine, which is why one cell doing both matters.

12Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What activates pepsinogen into pepsin?

Answer: a

HCl converts pepsinogen to pepsin, and pepsin then activates more pepsinogen — a positive feedback. Pepsin works best at about pH 2. Option c is the parallel in the small intestine, where enterokinase activates trypsinogen into trypsin — a good distractor precisely because the pattern is the same. Pepsin plus HCl is gastric juice.

13Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Why does the stomach not digest itself?

Answer: c

Four defences, and option c names two of them: pepsin is secreted as inactive pepsinogen, and the lining is repaired at half a million cells a minute. The other two are the thick alkaline mucus coat and neural and hormonal reflexes that hold back gastric juice unless food is present — which is the whole reason section 15.3 exists.

14Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

What is absorbed in the stomach?

Answer: b

Little absorption occurs in the stomach. The named exceptions are alcohol — which is why it acts fast on an empty stomach — and aspirin, which can cause bleeding and is avoided with ulcers. Bile never reaches the stomach; it is squirted into the duodenum. Water recovery is the large intestine's job.

15Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Heartburn happens when what fails?

Answer: b

Stomach contents overwhelm the sphincter at the lower end of the esophagus — from a weak sphincter, or from pressure (a large meal, pregnancy, lying down, constipation). The esophagus has no alkaline mucus coat to protect it. Chronic heartburn — at least weekly — raises esophageal cancer risk about eightfold, which is why it is not just discomfort.

16Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

In which region of the small intestine does most digestion and absorption occur?

Answer: b

The duodenum receives the chyme in squirts along with pancreatic juice and bile, but the chapter puts most digestion and absorption in the jejunum and ileum — the lab says most absorption is in the jejunum specifically, and B12 in the ileum. The cecum is the start of the large intestine, not the small.

17Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Which is the correct account of what bile does?

Answer: c

Bile is not an enzyme and does not chemically digest anything. Its bile salts emulsify fat — breaking globules into small droplets so there is more surface for lipase to work on, which is mechanical digestion. It is made by the liver, stored and concentrated by the gallbladder, and acts in the small intestine. Option d is the pancreas's bicarbonate.

18Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which three features multiply the small intestine's absorptive surface?

Answer: b

Circular folds (accordion pleats that also spin the chyme for better contact), villi (1 mm projections, a tenfold increase), and microvilli (a further twentyfold, forming the brush border). Together: 300–600 m2, bigger than a tennis court. Rugae are the stomach's folds, not the intestine's, and lacteals are lymph vessels inside a villus, not surface features.

19Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Amino acids and fatty acids leave a villus by different routes. Which is right?

Answer: b

Monosaccharides, amino acids, water, ions, vitamins and minerals cross into the capillary and go straight to the liver by the hepatic portal vein. Fat takes the other route because a chylomicron is too large for a capillary — it enters the more porous lacteal, then the lymphatic system, then the bloodstream. Option d is that pair swapped, which is the standard error.

20Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Why is lipid absorption different from every other nutrient's?

Answer: c

Two reasons, and the lab asks for both: the chylomicron's protein coat makes it water-soluble, and it is too large to enter a capillary, so it goes into the lacteal. Inside the villus cell the fatty acids and glycerol are reassembled into triglycerides, mixed with cholesterol and phospholipids, and coated — then leave by exocytosis. Option d misdescribes emulsification as digestion.

21Ch. 1515.2
