  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pancreatic secretion raises the pH of chyme entering the duodenum?

Answer: b

The pancreas has two exocrine outputs: acinar cells make the enzymes (lipase, amylase, nucleases, proteases) and ductal cells make the bicarbonate, which neutralises the acidic chyme so those enzymes can work — and protects the duodenum. The enzymes want about pH 7.5, which is exactly what the bicarbonate delivers. Bile comes from the liver, not the pancreas.

22Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which best describes the hepatic portal system?

Answer: b

A portal system links two capillary beds — here, the small intestine's to the liver's — so all the nutrient-laden blood leaving the gut reaches the liver before the rest of the body. Hepatic veins are what return that blood to circulation, which is option c. The exception is lipids, which bypass the portal route by going into lymph.

23Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Which is not one of the liver's non-digestive functions?

Answer: c

Storing and concentrating bile is the gallbladder's job, not the liver's — the liver makes the bile. The others are all genuine liver functions, along with packaging lipids into lipoproteins and removing toxins such as lead, mercury and pesticides. The chapter credits the liver with about 500 functions.

24Ch. 1515.3
  • textbook

Match hormone to target: which is correct?

Answer: b

CCK hits two targets — pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction. Secretin → pancreas, for sodium bicarbonate. Gastrin → stomach, for gastric juice; its origin and target are both the stomach, though it still travels by blood. VIP → small intestine, for intestinal juices. Whalen taught CCK and nothing else of section 15.3, so the others are textbook-only.

25Ch. 1515.3
  • textbook

Why is saliva under nervous rather than hormonal control?

Answer: b

Nerves act in a fraction of the time a bloodborne hormone needs, and food is in the mouth only briefly. Salivation starts at the thought, sight or smell of food; the main trigger is food in the mouth — flavour and pressure — and flow continues afterwards to rinse. Option c is false: saliva carries amylase.

26Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

The colon absorbs what, and how much?

Answer: b

Material entering the colon is still liquid; it absorbs 90% of the remaining water plus sodium and potassium ions, which sets the consistency of the feces. Its bacteria — about 50 species including E. coli — also make vitamin K and some B vitamins, absorbed there. Whalen's version was water, dissolved ions and "maybe some fat-soluble vitamins".

27Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

A patient has bloating and gas after drinking milk. What is the mechanism?

Answer: a

No lactase means the lactose is never broken into glucose and galactose, so it passes undigested to the colon, where bacteria ferment it into CO2 and methane — the gas and bloating. It is not dangerous and is managed with lactase tablets or avoiding dairy. Lactase is one of the three brush-border enzymes made and used in the small intestine.

28Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

A 1-year-old has severe diarrhea. What is the immediate concern?

Answer: a

Diarrhea means material moves through too fast for water to be reabsorbed. The chapter names dehydration, especially in young children, and calls diarrhea a major cause of death worldwide. Constipation is the mirror image — too slow, too much water absorbed, hard stools — and its straining can produce hemorrhoids and diverticula.

29Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Diverticulosis and diverticulitis differ how?

Answer: c

Diverticula are small pouches pushed out through weak spots in the wall, often from straining. -osis is having them with no symptoms, common after 50. -itis is when they become infected and inflamed — cramping pain, bowel changes, fever, rectal bleeding — treated with more fibre, antispasmodics or surgery. The suffix is the whole distinction.

30Ch. 1515.2
  • textbook

Why is colonoscopy preferred over testing stool for blood?

Answer: b

Colorectal cancer starts as a noncancerous polyp that can take up to 10 years to turn cancerous — plenty of time to catch it, if you can see it. Blood in the stool may be a sign but many polyps do not bleed, so direct viewing wins; and polyps can be removed and biopsied during the procedure. Sigmoidoscopy sees the first third; colonoscopy sees the whole colon.

31Ch. 1515.5
  • textbook

Which fat raises LDL and lowers HDL at the same time?

Answer: c

Trans fats are made by adding hydrogen to oils to stabilise or solidify them, and they do both bad things at once. Saturated fat is the other bad one — it raises LDL by boosting liver production and slowing clearance. The good fats are monounsaturated (olive, canola, peanut, nuts) and polyunsaturated including omega-3 and omega-6.

32Ch. 1515.5
  • textbook

Which statement about blood cholesterol is correct?

Answer: b

Blood cholesterol comes mostly from the liver, and dietary saturated fat raises it more than dietary cholesterol does — which is why the 2015 guidance stopped calling eggs "bad". Options c and d are LDL and HDL swapped: LDL delivers and deposits in artery walls; HDL carries it to the liver for elimination. Total cholesterol to HDL should be no more than 4:1.

33Ch. 1515.5
  • textbook

What does the glycemic index measure?

Answer: c

The glycemic response is how quickly and how much a food raises blood sugar; the glycemic index ranks it 0 to 100, with glucose = 100. High: sugar, white bread, potatoes, white rice. Low: whole fruit, whole grains, brown rice, barley — usually the high-fibre ones. A high-glycemic food spikes insulin, which converts the excess to fat, and hunger returns sooner.

34Ch. 1515.5
  • textbook

Why must a vegetarian pay attention to complementary proteins?

Answer: b

The body makes 11 of the 20 amino acids; 9 are essential and must be eaten. Complete proteins — usually animal — have ample amounts of all nine; incomplete proteins — usually plant — are low in one or more. Combining incomplete plant proteins so they cover each other's gaps is what complementary means. The book's image is the NO PARKING sign: one R caps the whole run at one sign.

35Ch. 1515.5
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A diet drug blocks fat absorption. Which deficiency would you predict?

Answer: b

Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed along with dietary lipids — block the lipids and they go too. B and C are water-soluble and cross by simple diffusion, so they are unaffected; there are 9 water-soluble and 4 fat-soluble vitamins in total. The book sets this as a Stop and Think, so the connection is one it expects you to make.

36Ch. 1515.5
  • textbook

How many calories per gram do carbohydrate, protein and fat supply?

Answer: a

Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 — fat is more than twice as energy-dense, which is the whole reason a small amount of it dominates a calorie count. Note that the 9 kcal/g figure appears only in the chapter's summary, not in the section text, so it is easy to miss on a read-through. A "calorie" in popular usage, and in this book, means a kilocalorie.

37Ch. 1515.7
  • textbook

What is basal metabolic rate, and how much of your energy use is it?

Answer: c

BMR is the minimum to keep an awake, resting body alive and is 60–75% of energy needs — physical activity is second. Men usually run 10–20% higher than a same-sized woman because muscle uses more energy than fat. Both muscle mass and metabolic rate fall with age, which is why weight creeps up after 35 without a change in habits.

38Ch. 1515.8
  • textbook

What most often kills in anorexia nervosa?

Answer: b

Heart problems are the most common cause of death in anorexia — bradycardia and hypotension — because once the fat is gone the body breaks down skeletal and heart muscle protein for energy. Up to 20% die untreated; 2–3% even with treatment. Hypoglycemia can kill in either disorder, because the brain runs on glucose. Option d belongs to bulimia's injury list, not its usual cause of death.

1Ch. 15short answer15.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Name the four layers of the GI tract wall from the lumen outward, and give the job of each.

Model answer

Mucosa — the innermost, moist, mucus-secreting layer. The mucus lubricates the lumen and protects the lining from rough food and from digestive enzymes; in places the mucosa also secretes enzymes, and where it is highly folded it increases the absorptive surface. The lab divides it further into epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae. Submucosa — connective tissue carrying blood vessels, lymph vessels and nerves. The blood maintains the cells and in places picks up the products of digestion; the nerves coordinate the muscularis. Muscularis — smooth muscle in two layers, inner circular (constricts) and outer longitudinal (shortens the tube). Together they churn, mix and propel — peristalsis to move food along and segmental contractions to mix and push contents against the wall for absorption. The stomach is the exception with three layers, the extra being oblique, because it churns. Serosa — a thin epithelial layer on connective tissue wrapping the tube, secreting a fluid that reduces friction with neighbouring organs. Outside the abdominal cavity it is adventitia — connective tissue only, no epithelium.

Four layers in order with one function each is the base; the stomach exception, and peristalsis versus segmental contraction, are where the extra marks are. The serosa/adventitia distinction is the lab's and is worth a mark on a lab-flavoured paper.

2Ch. 15short answer15.2
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Trace a mouthful of cheeseburger from the mouth to absorption, naming where each macromolecule is digested.

Model answer

Mouth. Teeth tear and grind — mechanical digestion — while salivary amylase begins carbohydrate digestion, breaking the bun's starch into shorter chains. The tongue shapes a bolus. Pharynx and esophagus. No digestion; swallowing then peristalsis moves the bolus down. Stomach. Storage, liquefaction into chyme, and protein digestion begins: HCl from parietal cells activates pepsinogen (from chief cells) into pepsin, which breaks the beef protein into polypeptides. No fat digestion of consequence here. Small intestine. Everything is finished. Pancreatic amylase takes polysaccharides to disaccharides, and the brush-border maltase, sucrase and lactase finish them to monosaccharides. Trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase finish the protein to amino acids. Bile from the liver emulsifies the cheese fat into droplets so pancreatic lipase can reach it, giving fatty acids and glycerol. Absorption. Monosaccharides and amino acids cross into the capillary of a villus and go to the liver by the hepatic portal vein; fats are reassembled into triglycerides, coated as chylomicrons, and enter the lacteal and the lymph. Large intestine. Water and ions recovered; bacteria act on the residue.

One mark per compartment with the right digestion happening in it. The two commonest errors are starting fat digestion in the stomach and sending fat into the capillary. Naming the enzymes and the two absorption routes takes it to full marks.

3Ch. 15short answer15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Explain how the small intestine is built for absorption, and how a fat and a sugar leave it differently.

Model answer

Three surface-area multipliers, one inside the next. Circular folds are accordion pleats of the lining that also set the chyme spinning, improving mixing and contact. Villi are 1 mm fingerlike projections covering the lining — a tenfold increase. Microvilli are microscopic projections on each absorptive cell, forming the brush border — a further twentyfold. Total absorptive surface: 300 to 600 m2, larger than a tennis court. Inside each villus is a capillary network and a lacteal, a lymphatic vessel — so an absorbed molecule crosses only two cell layers. A sugar: a monosaccharide enters the epithelial cell by active transport or facilitated diffusion, crosses into the capillary, and goes by the hepatic portal vein to the liver — as do amino acids, water, ions, vitamins and minerals. A fat: glycerol and fatty acids join bile salts to form micelles; at the cell surface the products diffuse in, are reassembled into triglycerides, mixed with cholesterol and phospholipids and coated with protein to form a chylomicron. The coat makes it water-soluble, but it is too large for a capillary, so it leaves by exocytosis into the more porous lacteal, then the lymphatic system, then the blood.

Three multipliers with their factors, then the two routes with the reason fat is different. Both reasons — too large and protein-coated — earn separately; giving only one is the usual half-answer.

4Ch. 15short answer15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Describe the pancreas, liver and gallbladder — what each contributes to digestion and where it acts.

Model answer

They are accessory organs: not part of the GI tract, but releasing secretions into it. Pancreas — behind and below the stomach. Exocrine: acinar cells secrete the enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases including trypsin and chymotrypsin, nucleases) and ductal cells secrete bicarbonate, which neutralises the acidic chyme so those enzymes can work at about pH 7.5. Pancreatic juice travels the pancreatic duct, which joins the common bile duct just before the duodenum. Endocrine: the islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood — glucose regulation, not digestion. Liver — the largest internal organ, below the diaphragm. Its primary digestive role is making bile, whose bile salts emulsify fat. Non-digestive: controls blood glucose (storing excess as glycogen), packages lipids into lipoproteins, stores iron and vitamins A, D, E, K, B12 and folate, removes toxins, and converts amino-acid breakdown products to urea — about 500 functions in all. All blood leaving the gut reaches it first by the hepatic portal vein. Gallbladder — a muscular pear-shaped sac under the liver that stores, modifies and concentrates bile, and contracts when CCK arrives, squirting bile through the common bile duct into the duodenum.

Three organs, each with what it makes, where it acts, and the duct route. The two most-marked details are that bile is made by the liver and only stored by the gallbladder, and that bile emulsifies rather than digests. The pancreas's exocrine/endocrine split is the lab's addition and earns on a lab paper.

5Ch. 15short answer15.3
  • textbook

Name the four digestive hormones, and for each give its origin, its stimulus and its effect.

Model answer

Gastrin — origin stomach, target stomach. Stimulus: distention of the stomach by food, and partially digested protein in it. Effect: increases gastric juice — HCl and enzymes. It still travels through the bloodstream to reach a target in its own organ. Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) — origin small intestine, target small intestine. Stimulus: acidic chyme in the small intestine. Effect: release of intestinal juices. Secretin — origin small intestine, target pancreas. Stimulus: acidic chyme. Effect: release of sodium bicarbonate to neutralise that chyme. Cholecystokinin (CCK) — origin small intestine, two targets. Stimulus: the arrival of chyme containing lipids (the section text says acidic chyme — the chapter is inconsistent here). Effects: pancreas releases enzymes, and the gallbladder contracts and releases bile. Why the control exists at all: the body is made of the same substances as food, so enzymes released into an empty tract would digest the tract itself.

Four hormones × three facts each. CCK is the one Whalen actually taught, and the one with two targets. Noting the chapter's own inconsistency about CCK's stimulus is worth a mark and is honest — the table says lipids, the text says acid.

6Ch. 15short answer15.5
  • textbook

Compare LDL and HDL, and say what a person should do about each.

Model answer

Both are lipoproteins — cholesterol combined with protein and triglyceride so it can travel in blood. LDL — "bad". It delivers cholesterol to cells but also deposits it in artery walls, which is how atherosclerosis builds. HDL — "good". It carries cholesterol to the liver for elimination. What matters is the ratio, not just the total: total cholesterol to HDL should be no more than 4:1, and HDL above 60 mg/dl is itself protective. Total blood cholesterol is recommended under 200 mg/dl; the U.S. middle-aged average is about 215. What raises LDL: saturated fat (red meat, butter, cheese, whole milk), which boosts liver production and slows clearance, and trans fat (hydrogenated oils, margarine, packaged foods), which raises LDL and lowers HDL at once. What helps: monounsaturated fats (olive, canola, peanut oil, nuts) and polyunsaturated ones — omega-3 (mackerel, trout, herring, tuna, salmon) and omega-6 (linoleic acid, in corn and safflower oil) — which lower total cholesterol and LDL; and dietary fibre, which lowers LDL without lowering HDL. Note that most blood cholesterol comes from the liver, not from dietary cholesterol — saturated fat matters more than the cholesterol on the label.

The direction each lipoprotein carries cholesterol is the core mark. Then the ratio rather than the total, the two bad fats with what each does, the good fats, and the liver point. Saying "eat less cholesterol" alone misses what the chapter actually argues.

1Ch. 15label the diagramThe tube, and the organs that feed it

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Mouth (oral cavity)

    Mechanical digestion begins with the teeth; chemical digestion of carbohydrate begins here with salivary amylase. The tongue shapes a bolus.

  2. 2name it

    Pharynx

    The throat, shared by the respiratory and digestive systems — which is why swallowing is a sequence of closing the wrong doors: the soft palate blocks the nose, the epiglottis covers the glottis.

  3. 3name it

    Esophagus

    A muscular tube. No digestion starts here — but chemical digestion continues, because salivary amylase came down with the bolus. Moved by peristalsis, so gravity is not required.

  4. 4name it

    Stomach

    Stores food and regulates its release · liquefies it into chyme · begins protein digestion. The one compartment with three muscle layers, the extra one oblique.

  5. 5name it

    Duodenum

    The first region of the small intestine, past the pyloric sphincter. Receives chyme in squirts plus bile and pancreatic juice, and where the acid is neutralised by bicarbonate.

  6. 6name it

    Jejunum and ileum

    The rest of the small intestine. Most absorption happens in the jejunum; vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum, with intrinsic factor and specific transporters.

  7. 7name it

    Cecum

    The blind pouch beginning the large intestine, past the ileocecal valve — a one-way valve, because colon contents have no business in the small intestine.

  8. 8name it

    Appendix

    Hangs off the cecum. No digestive function; possibly immune. Blockage then bacterial infection is appendicitis — and rupture spills into the abdominal cavity, "a place that has no out."

  9. 9name it

    Transverse colon

    Between the ascending (up the patient's right) and descending (down the left). The colon absorbs 90% of the remaining water plus sodium and potassium ions.

  10. 10name it

    Rectum and anal canal

    Feces stretch the rectal wall, triggering the defecation reflex. Internal sphincter smooth and involuntary; external sphincter skeletal and voluntary — the muscle type is the whole reason.

  11. 11name it

    Salivary glands

    Three pairs — parotid in front of the ears, submandibular below the jaw, sublingual under the tongue. They carry salivary amylase, denatured once it reaches the stomach's pH.

  12. 12name it

    Liver

    Makes bile — its primary digestive role. Also controls blood glucose, packages lipoproteins, stores iron and vitamins A, D, E, K, B12 and folate, detoxifies, and makes urea. All blood leaving the gut reaches it first, by the hepatic portal vein.

  13. 13name it

    Gallbladder

    Stores, modifies and concentrates the bile, and contracts when CCK signals that lipids have arrived. Remove it and bile trickles continuously instead of arriving as a flush.

  14. 14name it

    Pancreas

    99% exocrine. Acinar cells make the enzymes — amylase, lipase, nucleases and the proteases; ductal cells make the bicarbonate. The islets of Langerhans are the endocrine remainder: insulin and glucagon, into the blood.

  15. 15name it

    Common bile duct

    The hepatic ducts and the cystic duct join to form it. It meets the pancreatic duct and empties into the duodenum — at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, through the sphincter of Oddi. Both names are Bio 20 vocabulary Whalen gave early.

  16. 16name it

    Duodenum, receiving

    Where both ducts arrive. The cystic duct is the only one that runs both ways — bile goes up it into the gallbladder for storage, and back down it on release.

2Ch. 15label the diagramOne villus

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Microvilli

    Microscopic projections on the apical surface of each absorptive cell, forming the brush border. A further twentyfold increase in surface area — and the site of the brush-border enzymes: maltase, sucrase, lactase, enterokinase.

  2. 2name it

    Villus

    A 1 mm fingerlike projection of the lining. A tenfold increase in surface area. With the circular folds beneath and the microvilli above: 300–600 m2, bigger than a tennis court.

  3. 3name it

    Simple columnar epithelium

    The absorptive lining. Two cell layers is all an absorbed molecule crosses — this one, then the wall of a capillary or a lacteal.

  4. 4name it

    Goblet cell

    Produces the mucus that keeps the tube wet and everything moving along.

  5. 5name it

    Lumen

    Where the chyme is. Nothing here is inside you yet.

  6. 6name it

    Capillary network

    Takes monosaccharides, amino acids, water, ions, vitamins and minerals — then straight to the liver by the hepatic portal vein.

  7. 7name it

    Lacteal

    The blind-ended lymphatic capillary at the centre of the villus. It takes the products of fat digestion, because a chylomicron is too large for a capillary.

  8. 8name it

    Lamina propria

    The connective tissue core of the villus, carrying the vessels. It is the middle sublayer of the mucosa.

  9. 9name it

    Circular fold

    The accordion pleat the villi sit on — the first of the three surface multipliers. It also sets the chyme spinning, improving mixing and contact.

1Ch. 15flashcard15.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The four layers of the GI tract, inside out

Back

Mucosa · submucosa · muscularis · serosa. Within the muscularis: circular inner, longitudinal outer.

2Ch. 15flashcardLab 6 Activity 2
  • lab manual

The mucosa's three sublayers

Back

Epithelium · lamina propria · muscularis mucosae. The lamina propria carries the small vessels, glands and lymphatic tissue.

3Ch. 15flashcardLab 6 Activity 2
  • lab manual

Serosa or adventitia — which and when?

Back

Serosa — areolar connective tissue under epithelium; inside the abdominal cavity. Adventitia — connective tissue only; outside it.

4Ch. 15flashcard15.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Peristalsis vs segmental contractions

Back

Peristalsis propels food along the tract. Segmental contractions mix — local, random, mainly in the small intestine — and move contents over the wall to aid absorption.

5Ch. 15flashcardLab 6 Activity 2
  • lab manual

The four basic functions of the digestive system

Back

Ingestion · digestion · absorption · excretion.

6Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The route, in order

Back

Mouth → pharynx → esophagus → stomach → duodenum → jejunum → ileum → ileocecal valve → cecum → ascending → transverse → descending → sigmoid colon → rectum → anus.

7Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which compartment has three muscle layers, and why?

Back

The stomach. The extra oblique layer, innermost, lets it churn — twist, knead and compress — not just propel.

8Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Salivary amylase

Back

From the salivary glands; acts in the mouth; begins carbohydrate digestion, polysaccharides into shorter chains. Denatured by the stomach's low pH.

9Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The three pairs of salivary glands

Back

Parotid — in front of the ears. Submandibular — below the jaw. Sublingual — under the tongue.

10Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Tooth structure, outside in

Back

Enamel (crown, nonliving, calcium-hardened) → dentin (hard, bonelike) → pulp (vessels and nerves). Cementum covers the root; the root canal carries vessels and nerves in.

11Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Gingivitis vs periodontitis

Back

Gingivitis — plaque at the gum line inflames the gums, leaving pockets. Periodontitis — bacteria attack the bone and soft tissue around the tooth and loosen it. Major cause of adult tooth loss.

12Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

What blocks the nose, and what blocks the airway, during a swallow?

Back

Soft palate → blocks the nasal cavity. Larynx rises and the epiglottis covers the glottis → blocks the airway.

13Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

The stomach's three functions

Back

Store food and regulate its release to the small intestine · liquefy it into chyme · begin protein digestion.

14Ch. 15flashcardLab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual

The four cell types of the gastric glands

Back

Parietal → HCl + intrinsic factor. Chief → pepsinogen + gastric lipase. G cells → gastrin. Mucous cells → mucus.

15Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Pepsinogen → pepsin

Back

HCl activates it in the stomach lumen, and pepsin then activates more pepsinogen. Works best at pH 2. Pepsin + HCl = gastric juice.

16Ch. 15flashcardLab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual

Trypsinogen → trypsin

Back

Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) from the duodenal brush border activates it; trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and the other pancreatic proteases. Works best at pH 7.5.

17Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why are proteases secreted inactive?

Back

An active protease inside the gland would digest the gland itself — the pancreas or the stomach lining.

18Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Intrinsic factor

Back

Secreted by the stomach's parietal cells; needed to absorb vitamin B12, which is too large to diffuse and uses specific transporters in the ileum.

19Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Four ways the stomach avoids digesting itself

Back

Thick alkaline mucus coat · pepsin made as inactive pepsinogen · neural and hormonal reflexes hold back gastric juice unless food is present · rapid repair (half a million cells a minute).

20Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

What is absorbed in the stomach?

Back

Very little — alcohol and aspirin. Alcohol acts fast on an empty stomach; aspirin can cause bleeding.

21Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Heartburn

Back

Stomach contents overwhelm the lower esophageal sphincter — weak sphincter, or pressure from a large meal, pregnancy, lying down, constipation. Weekly heartburn ≈ 8× the esophageal cancer risk.

22Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The three regions of the small intestine

Back

Duodenum — receives chyme in squirts, plus pancreatic juice and bile. Jejunum — where most absorption happens. Ileum — the last stretch; B12 is absorbed here.

23Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Bile — what it is, what it does, where it is made and stored

Back

Not an enzyme. Its bile salts emulsify fat into droplets — mechanical digestion — so lipase has surface to work on. Made by the liver, stored and concentrated by the gallbladder, acts in the small intestine.

24Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The three surface-area multipliers, with their factors

Back

Circular folds (also spin the chyme) · villi, 10× · microvilli, a further 20×, forming the brush border. Total 300–600 m2 — bigger than a tennis court.

25Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which nutrients go to the capillary, and which to the lacteal?

Back

Capillary — monosaccharides, amino acids, water, ions, vitamins, minerals; then to the liver by the hepatic portal vein. Lacteal — fats, as chylomicrons; then lymph, then blood.

26Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Chylomicron — and the two reasons fat takes the lymph

Back

Triglyceride reassembled in the villus cell, mixed with cholesterol and phospholipid and coated with protein. The coat makes it water-soluble; it is too large for a capillary — so it enters the lacteal.

27Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Micelle

Back

Fat-digestion products — glycerol and fatty acids — combined with bile salts for transport to the villus surface.

28Ch. 15flashcardLab 6 Activity 3
  • lab manual

The pancreas's two exocrine outputs

Back

Acinar cells → digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, nucleases, proteases). Ductal cells → bicarbonate, which raises the pH of the chyme so those enzymes work and the duodenum is protected.

29Ch. 15flashcardLab 6 Activity 3
  • lab manual

The pancreas's endocrine output

Back

The islets of Langerhans release insulin (lowers blood glucose; beta cells), glucagon (raises it; alpha cells) and somatostatin — into the blood, not the gut.

30Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Hepatic portal system

Back

Vessels linking two capillary beds — the small intestine's to the liver's — so all blood leaving the gut reaches the liver first. Hepatic veins return it to circulation. Lipids are the exception; they go by lymph.

31Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

The liver's non-digestive jobs

Back

Controls blood glucose (glycogen) · packages lipids into lipoproteins · stores iron and vitamins A, D, E, K, B12, folate · removes toxins · converts amino-acid breakdown to urea. About 500 functions.

32Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • lab manual
  • lecture

The duct route from liver to duodenum

Back

Hepatic duct (liver) + cystic duct (gallbladder) → common bile duct → joins the pancreatic duct → duodenum. Whalen added the hepatopancreatic ampulla and sphincter of Oddi as Bio 20 vocabulary.

33Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Cirrhosis vs hepatitis

Back

Cirrhosis — the liver becomes fatty, deteriorates and is replaced by scar tissue; sometimes from prolonged heavy alcohol use. Hepatitis — inflammation, usually viral (A, B, C, D, E, G); damaged cells stop clearing bilirubin, giving jaundice.

34Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Gallstones

Back

A crystal precipitates from cholesterol-rich bile and cholesterol builds up around it. A stone blocking bile flow may mean removing the gallbladder.

35Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

What the large intestine absorbs

Back

90% of the remaining water, plus sodium and potassium ions. Its bacteria make vitamin K and some B vitamins, absorbed there.

36Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

The regions of the large intestine

Back

Cecum (with the appendix off it) → colon: ascending (right), transverse, descending (left), sigmoid → rectum → anal canal.

37Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

The appendix

Back

A slender pouch off the cecum. No digestive function; possibly immune. Appendicitis: blockage then infection — vague pain near the navel, then severe lower right pain with fever; rupture causes peritonitis.

38Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

The defecation reflex

Back

Feces stretch the rectal wall → reflex via the spinal cord → rectal contraction. Internal sphincter relaxes automatically; external sphincter is voluntary.

39Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Diarrhea vs constipation

Back

Diarrhea — too fast, too little water absorbed; risk of dehydration, a major cause of death worldwide. Constipation — too slow, too much water absorbed; straining causes hemorrhoids and diverticula.

40Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

Lactose intolerance — the mechanism

Back

No lactase, so lactose reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it into CO2 and methane — bloating and gas. Not dangerous.

41Ch. 15flashcard15.3
  • textbook

The four digestive hormones and their targets

Back

Gastrin → stomach (gastric juice). VIP → small intestine (intestinal juices). Secretin → pancreas (bicarbonate). CCK → pancreas (enzymes) and gallbladder (bile).

42Ch. 15flashcard15.3
  • textbook

Why is saliva under nervous, not hormonal, control?

Back

Food spends little time in the mouth and nerves are faster than hormones. Triggered by thought, sight, smell — and mainly by food in the mouth.

43Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook

The three brush-border carbohydrases

Back

Maltase, sucrase, lactase — made in the small intestine and acting in the small intestine, the only enzymes whose site of production and site of action are the same.

44Ch. 15flashcard15.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The four pancreatic proteases

Back

Trypsin · chymotrypsin · carboxypeptidase · elastase. Carboxypeptidase is the one that finishes the job — its products are individual amino acids.

45Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

LDL vs HDL

Back

LDL — "bad": delivers cholesterol to cells and deposits it in artery walls. HDL — "good": carries it to the liver for elimination. Total : HDL should be ≤ 4:1; HDL above 60 mg/dl is protective.

46Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

The two bad fats, and what each does

Back

Saturated — raises LDL by boosting liver production and slowing clearance (red meat, butter, cheese, whole milk). Trans — hydrogenated oils; raises LDL and lowers HDL.

47Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

Where does blood cholesterol actually come from?

Back

Mostly the liver, not the diet. Dietary saturated fat raises it more than dietary cholesterol does. Recommended total under 200 mg/dl.

48Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

Glycemic index

Back

A 0–100 ranking of how fast and how far a food raises blood sugar, with glucose = 100. High: sugar, white bread, potatoes, white rice. Low: whole fruit, whole grains, brown rice, barley.

49Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

Dietary fibre — what it does

Back

Indigestible plant carbohydrate. Passes to the large intestine, where bacteria digest some and the rest adds bulk. Lowers LDL but not HDL; absorbs water, softening stools; helps constipation and hemorrhoids.

50Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

Essential amino acids

Back

9 of the 20 — the body makes the other 11. A protein cannot be built if one is missing: the NO PARKING sign — one R means one sign.

51Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

Complete, incomplete and complementary proteins

Back

Complete — ample amounts of all 9 essentials, usually animal. Incomplete — low in one or more, usually plant. Complementary — incomplete plant proteins combined so they cover each other's gaps.

52Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

The 13 vitamins, split

Back

9 water-soluble — C and the B vitamins. 4 fat-soluble — A, D, E, K, absorbed with dietary lipids. Most act as coenzymes; only vitamin D can be made by our own cells.

53Ch. 15flashcard15.5
  • textbook

Calories per gram

Back

Carbohydrate 4 · protein 4 · fat 9.

54Ch. 15flashcard15.7
  • textbook

Basal metabolic rate

Back

The minimum energy to keep an awake, resting body alive — 60–75% of energy use. Men run 10–20% higher than same-sized women; it falls with age along with muscle mass.

55Ch. 15flashcard15.8
  • textbook

Anorexia nervosa

Back

Deliberate self-starvation; body weight 85% or less of expected. Driven by intense fear of fatness and a distorted body image, not lack of appetite. Heart problems are the commonest cause of death; up to 20% die untreated.

56Ch. 15flashcard15.8
  • textbook

Bulimia nervosa

Back

Binge eating — up to 8 hours and 20,000 calories — followed by purging (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, excessive exercise). Effects: esophageal injury, tooth decay, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance.

Ch. 15a — Special Topic — The Obesity Epidemic

Week 7 · study page · 14 multiple choice · 2 short answer · 15 flashcards · He said digestive, not obesity. Ch. 15a is a special-topic section of the digestive chapter and Canvas assigns it with Ch. 15, so it is banked — but if something has to be cut on the last night, cut this.

1Ch. 15a15a.1
  • textbook

A bodybuilder has a BMI of 32. What does that tell you?

Answer: b

BMI is a screen, not a diagnosis, and the chapter says so in both directions in one paragraph: a very muscular person can be above 30 and not obese, and someone inside the healthy range can have too much fat and little muscle. Overweight means heavy for your height; obese means heavy because of excess fat. Option c invents a rule the chapter does not give.

2Ch. 15a15a.1
  • textbook

According to the CDC figures the chapter gives, what share of Americans are overweight and obese?

Answer: c

68% overweight, almost 35% obese — roughly two in three and one in three. Option a is the same two numbers swapped, which is the distractor to watch for. The number of obese people has risen steadily since 1985, though the chapter notes the rate of increase is now slowing.

3Ch. 15a15a.2
  • textbook

How does obesity change blood lipids?

Answer: a

Both moves are the wrong way. Total cholesterol rises while HDL — the carrier that takes cholesterol from cells to the liver for removal — falls. Those values promote lipid deposits in the arteries, which is atherosclerosis; the deposits narrow the artery, raise blood pressure, and may rupture and form a clot.

4Ch. 15a15a.2
  • textbook

What is the difference between a heart attack and a stroke?

Answer: c

Both follow the same mechanism — a deposit ruptures, a clot forms, flow stops and the cells downstream die. The discriminator is location, not process: heart muscle cells in one, brain nerve cells in the other. That is why option a is wrong — the clot route is common to both.

5Ch. 15a15a.2
  • textbook

What makes type 2 diabetes different from type 1?

Answer: b

In type 2, blood glucose is elevated because the cells cannot use insulin — and it is far more common than type 1 and strongly correlated with obesity. High blood glucose eventually damages the small vessels of the eyes, kidneys and heart, and can itself cause atherosclerosis and high blood pressure, so it feeds the cardiovascular risk as well as being its own.

6Ch. 15a15a.2
  • textbook

Why does obesity raise the risk of breast cancer after menopause?

Answer: a

Fat cells produce estrogen, which is the chapter's stated mechanism for both postmenopausal breast cancer and endometrial cancer. The other cancers whose risk it raises — colon and rectum, esophagus, kidney, pancreas — are listed without a mechanism. This is the one sentence in the section a question can be built from directly.

7Ch. 15a15a.3
  • textbook

Leptin rises. What does the hypothalamus do?

Answer: b

Leptin is a satiety signal, not a hunger signal — and its direction is counter-intuitive on first reading. More fat → more leptin → less appetite and a higher metabolic rate. Shed fat and leptin falls, which stimulates appetite and slows metabolism. That is the thermostat holding the fat set point.

8Ch. 15a15a.3
  • textbook

Where is leptin made, and why does that matter?

Answer: c

Fat cells release leptin into the bloodstream, so the amount of leptin reflects how much fat there is — the "fat stat". That is exactly what makes it usable as a set-point signal. The hypothalamus is where the signal is read, by two opposing sets of neurons that both carry leptin receptors and respond in opposite ways.

9Ch. 15a15a.3
  • textbook

A mouse with a defective ob gene and a mouse with a defective db gene both become obese. How do their leptin levels compare?

Answer: b

Opposite causes, same endpoint. The *ob gene carries the instructions to make leptin, so a defect gives meagre leptin regardless of fat stores. The db defect gives defective leptin receptors, so leptin is very high but unreadable. Either way the brain concludes "low fat stores"* and drives weight gain — which is exactly what makes this pair examinable.

10Ch. 15a15a.3
  • textbook

Which definition of epigenetics is correct?

Answer: b

Expression changes; sequence does not. The chapter's own example is the *FTO (fat mass and obesity) gene: the risk of obesity in people carrying a variant of it is dramatically increased by a high-fat diet, and foods high in folate and B vitamins reduce that risk by turning the gene off. It reaches forward: maternal nutrition in pregnancy causes epigenetic changes in fetal gene activity*.

11Ch. 15a15a.4
  • textbook

What are the three components of a successful weight-loss program?

Answer: a

Fewer calories in — without abandoning nutritional guidelines — more energy out, and changed behaviour. The chapter adds that gradual changes are the ones that become permanent, which is the argument against the crash approach the next question covers. Nothing in the section endorses supplements, fasting days or suppressants.

12Ch. 15a15a.4
  • textbook

What share of dieters who lose weight regain all of it?

Answer: c

60% to 90% — the yo-yo effect. The usual reason is that the loss came from drastically cutting calories, which is unhealthy and very hard to sustain; old habits return and so do the pounds. The mechanism that makes each round worse is the subject of the next question.

13Ch. 15a15a.4
  • textbook

Why does repeated crash dieting leave a person worse off than before?

Answer: b

A three-step ratchet. Severe restriction triggers a calorie-sparing defence that cuts resting metabolic rate by as much as 45% — an adaptation to food scarcity. Each diet loses lean tissue as well as fat, especially without exercise, but what is regained is mostly fat. And fat is less metabolically active than lean muscle, so the resting rate ends up lower still.

14Ch. 15a15a.4
  • textbook

The chapter gives three dietary tips. Which reason is correctly paired?

Answer: a

Sugar is calorie-dense and high-glycemic — it elevates blood glucose quickly. Option b reverses the chapter: unused dietary fat is easier for the body to store as body fat than protein or carbohydrate, and it carries more than twice the calories per gram. Option c is wrong because fibre is not digested to monosaccharides at all — it is filling and bulky, which is the actual reason.

1Ch. 15ashort answer15a.3
  • textbook

Explain how leptin regulates body fat, and what happens when the ob or db gene is defective.

Model answer

Leptin is a hormone released into the bloodstream by fat cells, so the amount circulating reflects the body's energy stores — the "fat stat". It is read in the hypothalamus, which holds a hunger circuit of two opposing sets of neurons: one stimulates appetite and food-seeking, the other inhibits it. Both sets carry leptin receptors and respond in opposite ways, releasing their own peptide hormones. The system behaves like a thermostat holding a fat set point: fat gained → leptin rises → appetite falls and metabolic rate rises; fat lost → leptin falls → appetite rises and metabolism slows. A defective ob gene means little or no leptin is made, regardless of how much fat there actually is — the brain reads low leptin as low stores and drives eating. A defective db gene gives defective leptin receptors: leptin is very high, but the brain cannot read it, and again concludes the stores are low. Opposite leptin levels, the same outcome. Weight is not only about this circuit: emotional states — depression, boredom, anxiety, stress — and the power of suggestion from advertising or company also drive eating.

Leptin's source and what it reports, the hypothalamic circuit, the set-point behaviour in both directions, then the two gene defects with their opposite leptin levels and shared endpoint. Getting leptin's direction backwards — treating it as a hunger signal — loses most of the answer.

2Ch. 15ashort answer15a.2
  • textbook

Describe the health risks of obesity and explain how they interact.

Model answer

Cardiovascular disease. Obesity raises total blood cholesterol and lowers HDL, the carrier that removes cholesterol from cells to the liver. Those values promote atherosclerosis — lipid deposits in artery walls — which narrow or clog the artery and raise blood pressure. High blood pressure can kill through heart attack, stroke or kidney disease, and a deposit can rupture and form a clot that stops flow and kills the tissue downstream: heart muscle cells dying is a heart attack; brain nerve cells dying is a stroke. Type 2 diabetes. Strongly correlated with obesity, far more common than type 1, and caused by cells that cannot use insulin, leaving blood glucose elevated. That damages the small vessels of the eyes, kidneys and heart — and it itself causes atherosclerosis and high blood pressure, so it feeds back into the cardiovascular risk. Cancer. Raised risk of colon and rectal, esophageal, kidney and pancreatic cancer, plus postmenopausal breast cancer and endometrial cancer — the stated mechanism for those two being that fat cells produce estrogen. The interaction is the point: diabetes is both its own disease and a driver of the cardiovascular pathway, which is why the chapter draws the three risks as a loop rather than a list.

Three risk categories with mechanisms, then the interaction. The heart-attack-versus-stroke definition and the estrogen mechanism are the two specific facts most likely to be asked. Listing the risks without saying how diabetes feeds atherosclerosis misses what the figure is for.

1Ch. 15aflashcard15a.1
  • textbook

Overweight vs obese

Back

Overweight — weighing more than the ideal for your height. Obese — overweight because of excess fat. A muscular person can be overweight and not obese.

2Ch. 15aflashcard15a.1
  • textbook

BMI — the number and the caveat

Back

Weight evaluated relative to height. Over 30 indicates obesity. But it is a screen, not a diagnosis: a muscular person can exceed 30 and not be obese, and a normal-BMI person can carry too much fat.

3Ch. 15aflashcard15a.1
  • textbook

The CDC numbers

Back

68% of Americans overweight; almost 35% obese. Rising steadily since 1985, with the rate of increase now slowing.

4Ch. 15aflashcard15a.2
  • textbook

Obesity's effect on blood lipids

Back

Raises total cholesterol; lowers HDL. Both wrong-way moves, and both promote atherosclerosis.

5Ch. 15aflashcard15a.2
  • textbook

Heart attack vs stroke

Back

Same mechanism — a ruptured deposit, a clot, flow stops. The difference is which cells die: heart muscle (heart attack) or brain nerve cells (stroke).

6Ch. 15aflashcard15a.2
  • textbook

Type 2 diabetes

Back

Elevated blood glucose because cells cannot use insulin. Far more common than type 1; strongly correlated with obesity. Damages small vessels of the eyes, kidneys and heart, and itself causes atherosclerosis and high blood pressure.

7Ch. 15aflashcard15a.2
  • textbook

Which cancers does obesity raise the risk of?

Back

Colon and rectum, esophagus, kidney, pancreas — plus postmenopausal breast and endometrial, because fat cells produce estrogen.

8Ch. 15aflashcard15a.3
  • textbook

Leptin

Back

A hormone released by fat cells, so its level reports the body's energy stores — the "fat stat". A satiety signal: more fat → more leptin → less appetite and faster metabolism.

9Ch. 15aflashcard15a.3
  • textbook

The hunger circuit

Back

Two opposing sets of hypothalamic neurons — one stimulates appetite, one inhibits it. Both carry leptin receptors and respond oppositely. Works like a thermostat holding a fat set point; responds within seconds.

10Ch. 15aflashcard15a.3
  • textbook

The ob gene

Back

Carries the instructions to make leptin. A defect → very little leptin regardless of fat stores → the brain reads "low fat" and drives eating.

11Ch. 15aflashcard15a.3
  • textbook

The db gene

Back

A defect gives defective leptin receptors. Leptin is very high but unreadable → the brain again reads "low fat" and drives eating. Opposite leptin level to ob, same outcome.

12Ch. 15aflashcard15a.3
  • textbook

Epigenetics

Back

A stable change in gene expression without a change in DNA sequence. The chapter's example: the *FTO gene's obesity risk is raised by a high-fat diet and lowered by folate and B vitamins*, which turn it off.

13Ch. 15aflashcard15a.4
  • textbook

The three components of weight loss

Back

Fewer calories (within nutritional guidelines) · more energy expenditure · behaviour modification. Gradual changes are the ones that stick.

14Ch. 15aflashcard15a.4
  • textbook

The yo-yo effect — and why each round is worse

Back

60–90% of dieters regain everything. Severe restriction triggers a calorie-sparing defence cutting resting metabolic rate by up to 45%; each diet loses lean tissue as well as fat, but what is regained is mostly fat, which is less metabolically active — so the rate ends lower still.

15Ch. 15aflashcard15a.4
  • textbook

The three dietary tips, with their reasons

Back

Avoid sugar — calorie-dense and high-glycemic. Cut saturated fat — more than twice the calories per gram, and unused dietary fat is easier to store as body fat. Increase fibre — low in calories and fat, high in vitamins and minerals, and bulky, so filling.

Ch. 5 — The Skeletal System

Week 8 · study page · 44 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 72 flashcards · 4 diagrams, 49 labels

1Ch. 55.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

A bone sample is treated so that all of its mineral salts are removed but its collagen is left intact. What happens to it?

Answer: b

The matrix has two components with opposite contributions — mineral salts give hardness, collagen gives resilience. Strip the salts and only the elastic protein is left, so the bone bends: the book's own simile is a garden hose. The chalk option is the other half of the same pair and is the tempting wrong answer — that is what happens when the collagen goes. Rickets is the clinical version of the salt-poor case, and it is why children with it become bowlegged.

2Ch. 55.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which structure carries most of the pain when you bruise your shin?

Answer: a

The periosteum is the membrane over compact bone and it carries the nerves, so injury to it is what hurts — the chapter says most fracture and bruise pain comes from there, and Whalen made the same point from years of handball bone bruises. Osteocytes are the tempting answer because they are the living cells, but they are walled into matrix and are not what registers the blow. The same membrane supplies the fibroblasts and osteoblasts that repair the break.

3Ch. 55.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

What makes a structure an osteon rather than a trabecula of spongy bone?

Answer: c

Whalen gave this as the distinguishing test twice, once after the recording restarted: an osteon has a central canal with blood vessels and nerves in it, and many concentric lamellae; a trabecula has no central canal and only a couple of layers. Osteocytes in lacunae is the trap — both structures have those, so the feature cannot separate them. The central canal is also called the Haversian canal.

4Ch. 55.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

An osteocyte sits several rings out from the central canal. How does it get oxygen?

Answer: d

Canaliculi are tiny fluid-filled channels connecting lacuna to lacuna and finally to the central canal, and the osteocytes send projections through them to touch their neighbours. Nutrients and oxygen pass cell to cell inward, waste passes out. The capillary option is tempting because bone is highly vascular, but the vessels stop at the central and perforating canals — nothing runs through solid matrix. Whalen asked the room why the link had to exist and took "nutrient acquisition and waste" as the answer.

5Ch. 55.3
  • lecture

Which lamellae fill the gaps left between neighbouring osteons?

Answer: b

Osteons are round, and round things stack badly, so the gaps between them are filled with interstitial lamellae. Concentric lamellae are the rings that make an osteon an osteon, and circumferential lamellae wrap the whole shaft under the periosteum. There is no such thing as a perforating lamella — perforating describes a canal, Volkmann's, which runs crosswise between central canals.

6Ch. 55.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Red marrow and yellow marrow differ in location as well as in job. Which pairing is right?

Answer: c

Red marrow fills the spaces of spongy bone — the epiphyses of long bones and flat bones like the ribs, pelvis, sternum and skull — and is where blood cells form. Yellow marrow fills the medullary cavity of the shaft and is fat for energy storage. Option a is the same two facts swapped, which is exactly how a question will offer it. Whalen kept the two separate every time he said them.

7Ch. 55.3
  • lecture

Where in a long bone is the epiphyseal growth plate located?

Answer: d

The metaphysis is the region between the epiphysis and the diaphysis, and that is where the plate sits. Whalen flagged this as a question he asks in Bio 20 and named the trap out loud — "the answer is metaphysis, even though epiphysis is like in the name." The plate is named epiphyseal for the end it pushes away, not for where it is.

8Ch. 55.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why is the fetal skeleton first laid down as cartilage rather than as bone?

Answer: a

Mature bone cells cannot divide — an osteocyte is walled into solid matrix — whereas chondrocytes divide and multiply quickly, so a cartilage model can grow as fast as the fetus does. Replacement by bone begins around the third month. Option b sounds plausible and is never claimed; the birth-canal answer belongs to the fontanelles, not to the skeleton as a whole.

9Ch. 55.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

An osteoblast finishes secreting matrix all around itself. What is it now?

Answer: c

Osteoblast and osteocyte are a before and after of one cell, not two cell types: the blast lays down matrix, traps itself in the lacuna it has just built, and becomes the osteocyte that maintains bone integrity. Whalen told it as a story — "it trapped itself in that lacuna." The osteoclast option is the standard confusion: three cells, two letters apart, and the clast is the one that breaks bone down.

10Ch. 55.3
  • textbook

Growth hormone is given to a 45-year-old who wants to be taller. Why will it not work?

Answer: d

Growth hormone works through the growth plates, driving the cartilage cells there to divide. In an adult the sex hormones have already closed those plates — cartilage replaced by bone, the epiphyses fused to the shaft — so there is nothing for it to act on. Bones can still widen; they cannot lengthen. The receptor option is invented, and the liver's actual role is the opposite: it releases the growth factors.

11Ch. 55.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which statement about the sex hormones and the growth spurt is correct?

Answer: b

Rising testosterone and estrogen first drive the growth-plate cartilage into a frenzy of division, then the same hormones slow that division, thin the plates and fuse the bone ends — generally about 18 in females and 21 in males. A question asking why growth stops has the same answer as one asking why it accelerated. Thyroid hormone's job is different: it keeps the growth proportional.

12Ch. 55.4
  • textbook
  • lecture

Put fracture repair in order: bony callus, hematoma, remodeling, cartilage callus.

Answer: a

Bleeding and a clot first, because bone is highly vascular; then fibroblasts from the periosteum invade and lay collagen and cartilage into a soft callus; then osteoblasts convert that into a bony callus; then remodeling trims it. The order matters because two cell types do two steps — swapping the calluses gets the cells wrong too. During repair the bony callus is briefly thicker than the undamaged bone before it is cut back.

13Ch. 55.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where do the osteoblasts that convert a fracture callus into bone actually come from?

Answer: c

They were on site the whole time as osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cells in the periosteum's inner cellular layer, waiting to be called. Whalen added a second front the chapter does not stress: the same stem cells line the trabeculae of spongy bone, so a fracture heals outside-in and inside-out at roughly the same rate. The periosteum also supplies the fibroblasts, which makes it the hardest-working structure in the chapter.

14Ch. 55.4
  • textbook

A fracture is described as nondisplaced and open. What does that tell you?

Answer: a

These are two independent axes, so every fracture is one of each and there are four combinations. Nondisplaced means the ends stayed aligned; open means a broken end punctured the skin. The bone may retreat back under the skin afterwards, and the infection risk stays higher than for a closed break. Questions exploit the assumption that displaced/nondisplaced and open/closed are one scale.

15Ch. 55.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

Blood calcium falls below normal. Which response follows?

Answer: c

PTH is the low-calcium hormone. It stimulates osteoclasts to break matrix down and release calcium to the blood, increases reabsorption of calcium in the kidney, and activates vitamin D into calcitriol so more calcium is absorbed in the GI tract. Option a is the exact opposite response — calcitonin is released when calcium is high — and it is the distractor most students take because the two hormones are learned as a pair.

16Ch. 55.5
  • lecture

Calcitonin acts on the kidney as well as on bone. What does it do there?

Answer: b

Every calcitonin action points the same way — down. It tells osteoclasts to stop, and it blocks reabsorption in the renal tubules, so the calcium in the filtrate is lost in urine instead of being put back. Whalen walked the room through it as a chain of questions: block reabsorption, where does the calcium go, what happens to blood calcium. Option a is PTH's kidney action, which is the mirror image.

17Ch. 55.5
  • lecture

Which of PTH's three actions is the one most often forgotten?

Answer: c

Bone and kidney come to mind easily; the third lever is activation of vitamin D into calcitriol, which then promotes calcium absorption in the GI tract, and Whalen spent longer on it than on the other two. Option d is true but is not an action on calcium — the parathyroid glands sit on the posterior surface of the thyroid, which is a separate fact worth knowing.

18Ch. 55.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

Estrogen protects bone in three ways. Which is not one of them?

Answer: d

Estrogen's three effects all push in the same direction — more bone: absorb more calcium, build more, break down less. The kidney lever belongs to PTH and calcitonin, not to estrogen. Losing all three at once at menopause is the whole mechanism of postmenopausal osteoporosis, and it is why bone loss accelerates for several years after menopause rather than staying steady.

19Ch. 55.5
  • textbook

Which person would you expect to have the densest bones?

Answer: a

Three factors stack for him — age in the mid-thirties, when density peaks; male, with bone mass generally about 30% higher; and weight-bearing exercise with dietary calcium. The swimmer is the trap: she is young, but swimming is not weight-bearing, and bone thickens only along lines of stress. It is the same distinction the chapter draws between cross-country skiing and diving.

20Ch. 55.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

A leg is immobilised in a cast for several weeks. What happens to the bone?

Answer: c

Bone forms in response to stress and is absorbed in its absence — a few weeks without loading can cost nearly a third of a bone's mass, which is the same problem astronauts have in weightlessness. Option b is the subtle wrong answer: remodeling does not stop, it tips toward resorption, which is precisely why the mass is lost. Whalen's version was the savings account you can only draw on after thirty.

21Ch. 55.5
  • textbook

Bisphosphonates such as Fosamax work by which mechanism?

Answer: b

Each osteoporosis drug in the chapter maps onto one mechanism from the remodeling section, which is why they are listed there. Bisphosphonates shut down the breakdown side and leave the building side alone. SERMs such as Evista are the ones that mimic estrogen, and calcitonin is the one that drives deposition. Blocking vitamin D would make osteoporosis worse.

22Ch. 55.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which bone is not part of the axial skeleton?

Answer: d

The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column and chest bones — about 80 of them — and its job is to protect and support the internal organs. The femur is a limb bone, so it is appendicular, along with the two girdles and everything hanging off them. Whalen's split was roughly 80 axial and 126 appendicular, which closes at 206.

23Ch. 55.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

The spinal cord leaves the skull through an opening in which bone?

Answer: b

The occipital bone forms the back of the head and surrounds the foramen magnum, the large opening the spinal cord passes through. The sphenoid is the bow-tie-shaped floor of the cranium; the ethmoid is the cranium's smallest bone and carries the tiny holes the olfactory nerves pass through. Whalen's warning applies here: every hole exists because something goes through it.

24Ch. 55.6
  • textbook

Which pairing of "smallest bone" with its region is correct?

Answer: a

Two superlatives in two different places: the ethmoid is the smallest bone of the cranium, separating the cranial cavity from the nasal cavity; the lacrimal bones are the smallest of the face, at the inner corners of the eyes. The lacrimal duct drains tears into the nasal chambers, which is why the nose runs when you cry.

25Ch. 55.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Fontanelles serve two purposes. Which pair is correct?

Answer: c

The membranous soft spots let the skull be compressed as the baby passes through the birth canal and then accommodate the rapid enlargement of the brain. They are replaced by bone by about age 2. The lightening role belongs to the sinuses, which are air spaces that also act as resonating chambers for the voice — a plausible-sounding swap.

26Ch. 55.6
  • lecture

Which of the four fontanelles carries the alternative name "mastoid"?

Answer: b

The posterolateral fontanelle is also called the mastoid fontanelle, after the mastoid process it sits near, and it is bilateral — one on each side. The anterolateral one is the sphenoidal fontanelle, also bilateral. The anterior and posterior fontanelles are single and carry no second name.

27Ch. 55.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

The vertebral column has 26 bones. Which count is right?

Answer: d

Seven in the neck, twelve in the chest where the ribs attach, five in the lower back — Whalen's mnemonic is breakfast, lunch and dinner: 7, 12, 5. Add the sacrum, fused from five, and the coccyx, fused from four, and you have 26. Every wrong option is the same three numbers in a different order, which is how this gets asked.

28Ch. 55.6
  • textbook

Why does the sacrum fuse into a single bone when the other vertebrae do not?

Answer: b

Fusing five vertebrae gives extra strength where the backbone meets the pelvic girdle, which has to take both the weight of the column above and the powerful movements of the leg below. Option d is true as a consequence but is not the reason — the disks are absent because the segments fused. The coccyx, fused from four, is by contrast regarded as a vestigial tail with no function, though its upper part is well supplied with nerves and hurts badly when injured.

29Ch. 55.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

A disk bulges inward against the spinal cord. What would you expect?

Answer: b

Direction decides the symptom. Inward presses the spinal cord, interfering with the perception of incoming stimuli and with muscle control — numbness and tingling. Outward presses a spinal nerve, and the classic case is the sciatic nerve down the back of the leg, giving the radiating pain of sciatica. Option a is that other case. The disk never actually slips: the fibrocartilage teases apart and the nucleus pulposus pushes out.

30Ch. 55.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ribs 8, 9 and 10 are called false ribs. Why?

Answer: c

The distinguishing fact is whose cartilage, not whether there is cartilage. Ribs 1–7 are true ribs, each with its own costal cartilage running straight to the sternum; 8–10 hijack rib 7's cartilage to reach the sternal body; 11 and 12 are floating, with no anterior attachment at all. All twelve pairs attach at the back to the thoracic vertebrae, which rules out option b for every rib.

31Ch. 55.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

In standard anatomical position, how do the radius and ulna sit?

Answer: a

Radius lateral, ulna medial — and Whalen said the qualifier out loud both times he gave it, because rotating the forearm changes the relationship. That rotation is pronation and supination, which is why the position has to be specified. The ulna is also the one that forms the elbow, extending past its junction with the humerus.

32Ch. 55.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

How many phalanges does the pollex have, and how many does a finger have?

Answer: a

Every other digit has proximal, intermediate and distal phalanges; the pollex — the proper name for the thumb, digit 1 — has no intermediate, so two. Whalen used the proper terms deliberately and asked the room for both pollex and hallux, the big toe. Fingers and toes both use the word phalanges, which is the other half of this question.

33Ch. 55.7
  • textbook

Carpal tunnel syndrome produces numbness and tingling in the hand. What is actually compressed?

Answer: b

Both tissues are in the tunnel, and the order of events is what the question tests: repetitive motion inflames the tendons, and the swollen tendons press on the nerve. The nerve is what produces the numbness, tingling and pain, and it also controls some hand muscles. Option a reverses cause and victim, which is the standard misread.

34Ch. 55.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where do the ilium, ischium and pubis meet?

Answer: c

The three bones of the os coxae (the innominate) converge at the acetabulum, the socket that accepts the head of the femur — Whalen's mnemonic was that it is not far from your ass. They do not fully fuse into one bone until the mid to late twenties, so most of the class still has three. The pubic symphysis is where the two os coxae meet each other in front, across a pad of fibrocartilage.

35Ch. 55.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which three superlatives belong to the femur?

Answer: b

Largest, longest and heaviest — Whalen listed all three together, which is how a question will ask it, and the chapter adds that the femur accounts for roughly 25% of your height. Its head sits in the acetabulum and it meets the tibia at the knee, with the smaller fibula running down the side and the patella covering the junction.

36Ch. 55.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which joint type has no joint cavity?

Answer: d

Fibrous joints are held together by fibrous connective tissue with no cavity, and most permit no movement — the sutures of the adult skull are the example. Hinge and ball-and-socket are both kinds of synovial joint, and every synovial joint has a cavity filled with synovial fluid. The chapter adds a detail worth having: sutures do move a little, which absorbs shock when you hit your head, and they close completely in old age.

37Ch. 55.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which list is made only of cartilaginous joints?

Answer: c

Cartilaginous joints allow little or no movement and the chapter names exactly these three sites. Option a and option d are all synovial; option b mixes a fibrous joint with two synovial ones. A detail that pays out: in pregnancy hormones loosen the cartilage of the pubic symphysis so the pelvis can widen.

38Ch. 55.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

What type of cartilage covers the articulating surface of a synovial joint?

Answer: a

Hyaline — the weakest and the most abundant cartilage in the body, and Whalen asked for it twice in one lecture, once as the cap on the epiphysis and once as the surface of a synovial joint. Fibrocartilage is the tempting answer because it is the toughest, but it is the intervertebral disks and the pubic symphysis, not the joint surface. Its job here is to reduce friction so the bones slide without grating.

39Ch. 55.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

A ligament and a tendon differ in what they connect. Which is right?

Answer: a

Ligament holds bone to bone at a joint, supporting it and directing the movement, and Whalen named the tissue specifically — dense regular fibrous connective tissue, which ties straight back to the Ch. 4 tissue tab. Tendon attaches muscle to bone. Both have few blood vessels and therefore heal slowly, which is why a sprain lingers.

40Ch. 55.8
  • textbook

You sprain an ankle. What should you apply first, and why?

Answer: b

Ice first, then heat, and the chapter gives a physiological reason for each. Ice constricts blood vessels and reduces bleeding, which usually stops by the next day; heat afterwards dilates them so blood can deliver nutrients, oxygen and anti-inflammatory chemicals. Option a is the right reason attached to the wrong stage. Option d is a real effect but not the stated rationale.

41Ch. 55.8
  • textbook

Which statement distinguishes osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis?

Answer: c

That single distinction drives everything else. Osteoarthritis is degeneration of the joint surfaces from wear, so it strikes weight-bearing joints — hip, knee, spine — and can be discouraged by controlling weight and exercising. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune attack on the synovial membranes; it is permanent, and sometimes the only effective treatment is joint replacement.

42Ch. 55.8
  • textbook

A bursa is inflamed by repeated pressure. Which description fits?

Answer: a

Bursitis is intense pain, worse when the joint moves and not relieved by resting in any position, and the chapter calls it not serious — usually subsiding in a week or two, though a physician may drain the fluid. Option d is the specific thing the chapter denies. A bursa is a fluid-filled sac lined with synovial membrane, found where skin rubs over bone and between tendons, muscles or ligaments and bone.

43Ch. 55.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Circumduction is which combination of movements?

Answer: c

Run those four in sequence and the limb traces a circle — Whalen's line was that all circles have a circumference, so circumduction is just circular motion. It needs a joint that moves in all planes, so it belongs to ball-and-socket joints such as the shoulder and hip, not to a hinge. Rotation is different: movement of a body part around its own axis.

44Ch. 55.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pair of movements is correctly defined?

Answer: c

Abduction takes a limb away from the midline; adduction adds it back. Option a is the same pair reversed, which is the single most common slip. Flexion decreases the angle between two articulating bones and extension increases it — option b is that pair reversed too. And supination is the palm-up rotation: Whalen's device was that you can hold soup when you supinate.

1Ch. 5short answer5.3
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Describe the structure of an osteon, naming every component and saying what each one does.

Model answer

An osteon is the functional unit of compact bone. At its core is the central canal, also called the Haversian canal, carrying blood vessels and nerves. Around it are rings of bone matrix called concentric lamellae. Between the rings, each in a small cavity called a lacuna, sit the osteocytes — mature bone cells, each of them an osteoblast that walled itself in while laying down matrix. Canaliculi, tiny fluid-filled channels, connect lacuna to lacuna and finally to the central canal, so nutrients and oxygen reach cells deep in the matrix and waste is carried out. Perforating (Volkmann's) canals run crosswise, connecting the vessels of neighbouring central canals. Between adjacent osteons sit interstitial lamellae filling the gaps; circumferential lamellae wrap the whole shaft.

One mark each for central canal (with vessels and nerves), concentric lamellae, lacuna, osteocyte, canaliculi and their function. Naming the Haversian and Volkmann alternatives, and distinguishing the three lamella types, is where the extra marks are — Whalen gave both name pairs deliberately.

2Ch. 5short answer5.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Blood calcium has dropped. Trace what happens, naming the hormone and all three of its actions.

Model answer

The parathyroid glands, on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, release parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH does three things, all of which raise blood calcium. One — bone: it stimulates osteoclasts, which break down bone matrix and release calcium salts from the hydroxyapatite crystals into the blood. Two — kidney: it increases reabsorption of calcium from the filtrate back into the blood, so less is lost in urine. Three — gut: it increases the activation of vitamin D into calcitriol, and calcitriol promotes the absorption of dietary calcium in the GI tract. When calcium is instead too high, calcitonin from the thyroid does the reverse: it inhibits osteoclasts and inhibits renal reabsorption, so calcium is lost in the urine.

Name the hormone and gland, then all three levers — bone, kidney, gut — with the direction of each. The vitamin D → calcitriol step is the one most answers drop and the one Whalen spent longest on. A full-mark answer closes with calcitonin as the antagonist.

3Ch. 5short answer5.4
  • textbook
  • lecture

Explain how a fracture heals, naming each stage and the cell responsible.

Model answer

One — hematoma. Bone is highly vascular, so the break bleeds and a blood clot forms at the site. Two — fibrocartilage callus. Within a few days fibroblasts grow inward from the periosteum, invade the clot and secrete collagen fibres, forming a soft callus that links the broken surfaces; some then turn into cartilage-producing cells and add cartilage to it. Three — bony callus. New blood vessels infiltrate and osteoblasts, also from the periosteum, convert that cartilage into bone. At this stage the callus is thicker than the surrounding bone and protrudes. Four — remodeling. The excess is broken down and the bone returns to close to its original shape. The osteoblasts were present the whole time as osteoprogenitor cells in the periosteum's inner cellular layer, and matching stem cells line the trabeculae of spongy bone, so the bone heals from the outside in and the inside out at about the same rate.

Four stages in order, with fibroblast on the soft callus and osteoblast on the bony callus. Swapping those two cells is the common error. The periosteum's inner cellular layer as the source of both cell types is the detail that separates a full answer.

4Ch. 5short answer5.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why is osteoporosis more common in women than in men? Give at least three reasons.

Model answer

One — lower peak bone mass. Men's bone mass is generally about 30% higher, so women start from less. Two — the loss of estrogen at menopause. Estrogen does three things for bone: it promotes calcium absorption from the digestive system, it stimulates bone formation, and it impairs osteoclasts' ability to break bone down. All three disappear together when estrogen falls, so breakdown begins to outpace deposition. Three — the rate of loss accelerates for several years after menopause rather than staying steady. Beyond that, peak bone density is reached in the mid-thirties and only declines afterwards, so a smaller peak matters permanently. Other stated risk factors that can compound it: being short, low body fat (fat cells produce estrogen), heavy drinking and smoking (both interfere with estrogen), too little dietary calcium or vitamin D, caffeine, and a sedentary life.

Three reasons, and the strongest answer is built round estrogen's three effects rather than round "women have less bone". Naming the mid-thirties peak, and any two of the listed risk factors with their mechanism, earns the rest.

5Ch. 5short answer5.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Classify joints structurally, giving an example and the amount of movement each allows.

Model answer

Fibrous — held together by fibrous connective tissue, no joint cavity, and mostly immovable. The sutures between adult skull bones are the example; they in fact move very slightly, which absorbs shock to the head, and they close completely in old age. Cartilaginous — bones held by rigid cartilage, allowing little or no movement. Examples: between adjacent vertebrae, where the ribs attach to the sternum, and the pubic symphysis. Synovial — freely movable, and most joints in the body. Each has a joint cavity lined by a synovial membrane secreting synovial fluid to lubricate and cushion; a thin layer of hyaline (articular) cartilage on the moving surfaces to reduce friction; a two-layer capsule; and ligaments outside it holding bone to bone and directing movement. Hinge joints such as the elbow and knee move in one plane; ball-and-socket joints such as the shoulder and hip move in all planes, including rotation.

Three classes, each with movement and an example, is the base. Full marks need the synovial anatomy — cavity, membrane, fluid, hyaline cartilage, capsule, ligaments — and the hinge-versus-ball-and-socket contrast. Saying the articular cartilage is hyaline is worth a mark on its own; Whalen asked it twice.

6Ch. 5short answer5.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

A lab partner says the bone matrix is alive because bone is living tissue. Correct them, and explain what the matrix is made of.

Model answer

Bone is living tissue, but the matrix is not — Whalen answered this exact question in class: "Matrix by definition is non-living. Osteocytes are living." The living part of bone is its cells: osteoblasts that build matrix, osteocytes that maintain it from inside their lacunae, osteoclasts that break it down, and the osteoprogenitor cells in the periosteum. The matrix itself is a nonliving composite of two things. Mineral salts — primarily calcium and phosphorus, as the crystal hydroxyapatite (tricalcium phosphate combined with calcium hydroxide) — give it hardness; think of them as cinder blocks. Collagen, a strong elastic protein, is the framework they are laid down on, and it gives bone its resilience. Remove the salts and the bone becomes rubbery like a hose; remove the collagen and it becomes brittle like chalk.

The correction itself is the first mark: living cells, nonliving matrix. Then the two components with what each contributes, and the two failure modes. Naming hydroxyapatite is the extra. Note the wobble to avoid: the transcript has Whalen saying "calcium and magnesium salts" twice, but the chemistry he walked through is calcium and phosphorus.

1Ch. 5label the diagramA long bone in longitudinal section

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Articular cartilage

    Hyaline. Caps the joint surface and reduces friction where one bone glides on another. Not the same structure as the growth plate.

  2. 2name it

    Proximal epiphysis

    The enlarged end. Mostly spongy bone under a thin compact shell.

  3. 3name it

    Epiphyseal (growth) plate

    Cartilage. Its cells divide and push the end away from the shaft; it fuses at about 18 in females and 21 in males.

  4. 4name it

    Metaphysis

    The region between epiphysis and diaphysis — and therefore where the growth plate is. Whalen flagged this as a question he sets.

  5. 5name it

    Compact bone
