    Very dense, few internal spaces, packed with osteons. Forms most of the shaft wall and the outer shell everywhere.

  6. 6name it

    Medullary cavity

    The space inside the shaft.

  7. 7name it

    Yellow marrow

    Fat, for energy storage. Fills the medullary cavity in an adult.

  8. 8name it

    Periosteum

    The membrane over compact bone — blood vessels, nerves, and the cells for growth and repair. Most fracture pain is here.

  9. 9name it

    Diaphysis

    The shaft.

  10. 10name it

    Spongy bone

    A latticework of trabeculae bracing the bone from within. Strength without weight.

  11. 11name it

    Red marrow

    In the spaces of spongy bone. Where blood cells are formed, from hematopoietic stem cells.

  12. 12name it

    Distal epiphysis

    The other enlarged end. Same construction as the proximal one.

2Ch. 5label the diagramThe osteon, in cross-section

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Central canal

    Also the Haversian canal. Carries the blood vessels and nerves. Its presence is what makes this an osteon and not a trabecula.

  2. 2name it

    Concentric lamellae

    Rings of matrix around the central canal. Lamella is the matrix; the matrix is non-living.

  3. 3name it

    Lacuna

    The small cavity in hardened matrix — the space the osteoblast left when it walled itself in.

  4. 4name it

    Osteocyte

    The mature bone cell living in that lacuna. An osteoblast that trapped itself and changed job to maintaining the bone.

  5. 5name it

    Canaliculi

    Tiny fluid-filled channels linking lacuna to lacuna and out to the central canal. Nutrients and oxygen in, waste out, cell to cell.

  6. 6name it

    Interstitial lamellae

    Filler in the gaps between neighbouring osteons. Osteons are round, and round things stack badly.

  7. 7name it

    Circumferential lamellae

    Wrap the whole circumference of the bone, under the periosteum.

  8. 8name it

    Perforating canal

    Also Volkmann's canal. Runs crosswise, connecting the vessels of one central canal to the next.

  9. 9name it

    Osteon

    The structural and functional unit of compact bone. Whalen's image: the cut end of a tree trunk.

3Ch. 5label the diagramThe axial skeleton

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Cranium

    Eight bones — frontal, two parietal, occipital, two temporal, sphenoid, ethmoid. All eight touch the brain.

  2. 2name it

    Facial bones

    Fourteen, including the maxillae, zygomatics, nasals, lacrimals, palatines and vomer. The orbit and the nasal aperture are drawn inside this region.

  3. 3name it

    Mandible

    The lower jaw — the only movable bone of the skull, meeting the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint.

  4. 4name it

    Cervical vertebrae

    Seven. The neck, and the smallest bodies. Breakfast, lunch and dinner — 7, 12, 5.

  5. 5name it

    Intervertebral disc

    Fibrocartilage, the toughest cartilage type. Sits between adjacent vertebral bodies, and compresses over the years, which is part of why people get shorter.

  6. 6name it

    Thoracic vertebrae

    Twelve. The chest — every rib pair attaches here at the back, floating ribs included.

  7. 7name it

    Lumbar vertebrae

    Five, and the largest bodies, because they carry everything above them. L5–S1 is where back problems concentrate.

  8. 8name it

    Sacrum

    One bone, fused from five. It fuses for strength where the column meets the pelvic girdle.

  9. 9name it

    Coccyx

    One bone, fused from four — texts say three to five. A vestigial tail with no function, though its upper part is nerve-supplied and extremely painful when injured.

  10. 10name it

    Sternum

    The breastbone — manubrium, body and xiphoid process. Ribs 1–7 reach it by their own costal cartilage.

  11. 11name it

    True ribs

    1–7. Each has its own costal cartilage running directly to the sternum.

  12. 12name it

    False ribs

    8–10. They have cartilage, but not their own route — theirs joins rib 7's cartilage, which is what the converging lines show.

  13. 13name it

    Floating ribs

    11–12. No anterior attachment at all — they end free. Still attached at the back to the thoracic vertebrae, like every other pair.

4Ch. 5label the diagramThe appendicular skeleton

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Clavicle

    The collarbone. A relatively rigid bridge between the scapula and the sternum. More curved in males — one of the two ways to sex a skeleton.

  2. 2name it

    Scapula

    The shoulder blade — roughly triangular, with a socket at one corner taking the humerus. Scapula plus clavicle is the pectoral girdle.

  3. 3name it

    Humerus

    The single bone of the upper arm.

  4. 4name it

    Radius

    Lateral in standard anatomical position, and broader at the wrist. Rotate the forearm and the relationship changes — that rotation is pronation and supination, which is why the position has to be specified.

  5. 5name it

    Ulna

    Medial in anatomical position, and broader at the elbow. Its extension past the junction with the humerus is what forms the elbow.

  6. 6name it

    Carpals

    Eight, in two rows: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.

  7. 7name it

    Metacarpals

    Five. Metacarpal 1 belongs to the pollex — the thumb, drawn set apart from the other four.

  8. 8name it

    Phalanges

    Proximal, intermediate and distal — except the pollex, which has no intermediate and so carries two rather than three. Toes use the same word.

  9. 9name it

    Os coxae

    The hip bone, also called the innominate. Ilium above, ischium below, pubis in front — three bones that do not fuse into one until the mid-to-late twenties. The two of them plus the sacrum make the pelvis, joined in front at the pubic symphysis.

  10. 10name it

    Acetabulum

    The socket where ilium, ischium and pubis meet. It accepts the head of the femur — drawn empty on this side and occupied on the other.

  11. 11name it

    Femur

    Largest, longest and heaviest bone in the body — about 25% of your height.

  12. 12name it

    Patella

    The kneecap. Covers the junction of the femur with the tibia.

  13. 13name it

    Tibia

    The larger, weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. Its anterior crest is the shin. Big tib, told a little fib.

  14. 14name it

    Fibula

    The smaller one, running down the lateral side. It does not bear weight.

  15. 15name it

    Tarsals

    Seven — talus, calcaneus, navicular, the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms, and the cuboid. Distal to them the five metatarsals, of which M1 is the hallux.

1Ch. 5flashcard5.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

The six functions of the skeleton

Back

Support · movement · protection · mineral storage (calcium and phosphorus) · fat storage (yellow marrow) · blood cell production (red marrow).

2Ch. 5flashcard5.2
  • textbook

Compact bone

Back

Dense bone with few internal spaces; forms most of the shaft (diaphysis) of a long bone. Covered by the periosteum except at joint surfaces.

3Ch. 5flashcard5.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Spongy bone

Back

A latticework of beams and plates — trabeculae — bracing the bone from within. In flat bones and the ends of long bones; its spaces hold red marrow.

4Ch. 5flashcard5.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Periosteum — the two layers and what each holds

Back

Outer fibrous layer; inner cellular layer holding osteogenic (osteoprogenitor) cells. Carries blood vessels and nerves; nourishes the bone; the source of fracture pain.

5Ch. 5flashcard5.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Red marrow — where, and what for

Back

In the spongy bone of the epiphyses and of flat bones (ribs, pelvis, sternum, skull). Blood cell formation, from hematopoietic stem cells.

6Ch. 5flashcard5.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Yellow marrow — where, and what for

Back

In the medullary cavity of the shaft. Fat, for energy storage.

7Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Osteon

Back

The structural and functional unit of compact bone — concentric lamellae around a central canal, with osteocytes in lacunae between the rings.

8Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • lecture

Central canal — the other name for it

Back

The Haversian canal. The void at the centre of an osteon, carrying blood vessels and nerves.

9Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • lecture

Perforating canal — the other name for it

Back

Volkmann's canal. Runs crosswise, connecting the blood vessels of neighbouring central canals.

10Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Lacuna

Back

The small cavity in hardened matrix where an osteocyte lives — the space the osteoblast left when it walled itself in.

11Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Canaliculi

Back

Tiny fluid-filled channels linking lacuna to lacuna and to the central canal, carrying nutrients and oxygen in and waste out.

12Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • lecture

The three kinds of lamellae

Back

Concentric — rings around a central canal, what makes an osteon. Circumferential — around the whole shaft. Interstitial — filling the gaps between osteons.

13Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Osteoblast · osteocyte · osteoclast

Back

Blast builds matrix. Cyte is the blast walled into its own lacuna, maintaining the bone. Clast crushes — breaks matrix down and releases calcium.

14Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

What makes bone hard, and what makes it resilient

Back

Mineral salts — calcium and phosphorus, as hydroxyapatite — hardness. Collagen — resilience. No salts → rubbery like a hose. No collagen → brittle like chalk.

15Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • lecture

Hydroxyapatite

Back

The calcium salt crystal of bone matrix — tricalcium phosphate plus calcium hydroxide — deposited on a framework of collagen.

16Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Diaphysis · metaphysis · epiphysis

Back

Diaphysis — the shaft, compact bone round the medullary cavity. Metaphysis — between the two, and where the growth plate is. Epiphysis — the end, spongy bone with articular cartilage on it.

17Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • lecture

Where is the epiphyseal growth plate?

Back

In the metaphysis — not the epiphysis, despite the name. Whalen flagged this as an exam question he sets.

18Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Hyaline cartilage — the two superlatives

Back

The weakest and the most abundant cartilage in the body. It is the articular cartilage on joint surfaces.

19Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fibrocartilage — where it is

Back

The toughest cartilage. Intervertebral disks and the pubic symphysis.

20Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why is the fetal skeleton cartilage first?

Back

Chondrocytes divide; mature bone cells cannot — they are walled into solid matrix. So the model can grow as fast as the fetus. Replacement by bone starts about month 3.

21Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Growth hormone vs thyroid hormone vs sex hormones, on bone

Back

Growth hormone — drives childhood growth (via liver growth factors). Thyroid hormone — keeps growth proportional. Sex hormones — start the pubertal spurt and then close the plates.

22Ch. 5flashcard5.3
  • textbook

When do the growth plates close?

Back

About age 18 in females, 21 in males. After that a bone can still widen but can no longer lengthen.

23Ch. 5flashcard5.4
  • textbook
  • lecture

The four stages of fracture repair

Back

Hematoma → fibrocartilage callus (fibroblasts) → bony callus (osteoblasts) → remodeling.

24Ch. 5flashcard5.4
  • textbook

Displaced vs nondisplaced; open vs closed

Back

Displaced — ends not aligned, must be realigned. Open — a bone end broke the skin, higher infection risk. Two independent axes, so four combinations.

25Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Parathyroid hormone — source and three actions

Back

From the parathyroid glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid. Raises blood calcium: stimulates osteoclasts · increases kidney reabsorption · activates vitamin D into calcitriol for gut absorption.

26Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Calcitonin — source and actions

Back

From the thyroid gland. Lowers blood calcium: inhibits osteoclasts and inhibits kidney reabsorption, so calcium leaves in the urine. The textbook notes its role in remodeling is not clear and that it is released in children.

27Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • lecture

Calcitriol

Back

Activated vitamin D. PTH drives its activation; it promotes calcium absorption in the GI tract. Vitamin D itself is made in skin exposed to sun, but must be activated to work.

28Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

Estrogen's three effects on bone

Back

Promotes calcium absorption from the gut · stimulates bone formation · impairs osteoclasts. All three are lost at menopause, which is why osteoporosis is commoner in women.

29Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • textbook

Osteoporosis

Back

Breakdown outpacing deposition — progressive loss of bone density; thin, brittle, fracture-prone bone. About 40 million Americans, mostly elderly white women.

30Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

When is bone density at its peak?

Back

The mid-thirties — bone is formed faster than it is broken down until about 35, and density is lost after that. Whalen's version: the savings account you can only add to until thirty.

31Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • textbook

The three osteoporosis drug mechanisms

Back

Bisphosphonates (Fosamax, Actonel, Boniva) — inhibit osteoclasts, not osteoblasts. SERMs (Evista) — mimic estrogen. Calcitonin — increases deposition.

32Ch. 5flashcard5.5
  • textbook

What does disuse cost a bone?

Back

Nearly a third of its mass in a few weeks — a limb in a cast, or an astronaut in weightlessness. Bone forms along lines of stress and is absorbed without them.

33Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Axial vs appendicular — the split and the counts

Back

Axial ≈ 80 — skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs; protects and supports the organs. Appendicular ≈ 126 — the two girdles and the limbs. 206 total.

34Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

The eight cranial bones

Back

Frontal (1) · parietal (2) · occipital (1) · temporal (2) · sphenoid (1) · ethmoid (1). All eight touch the brain.

35Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook

Foramen magnum

Back

The opening in the occipital bone through which the spinal cord passes.

36Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook

Sinuses — what they are for

Back

Air spaces in several skull bones. They lighten the head and act as resonating chambers for the voice.

37Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook

The two "smallest bone" answers

Back

Ethmoid — smallest of the cranium; separates cranial from nasal cavity, olfactory nerves pass through it. Lacrimal — smallest of the face; drains tears into the nose.

38Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Zygomatic arch

Back

The arch formed where the zygomatic bone (cheekbone) meets an extension from the temporal bone.

39Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook

Cleft palate — what has failed

Back

The maxillae failed to fuse at the midline below the nasal septum, so the mouth and nasal cavities are not fully separated. The hard palate is maxillae in front, palatine bones behind.

40Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook

TMJ syndrome

Back

Stress on the temporomandibular joint — where the mandible meets the temporal bone — from clenching or grinding. Causes headaches, toothaches, even earaches.

41Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

The four fontanelles

Back

Anterior · posterior · anterolateral = sphenoidal (bilateral) · posterolateral = mastoid (bilateral). Replaced by bone by about age 2.

42Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why do fontanelles exist?

Back

So the skull can be compressed during birth, and to allow the rapid enlargement of the brain in infancy.

43Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

The vertebral column, by the numbers

Back

26 bones: 7 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 1 sacrum (5 fused) · 1 coccyx (4 fused). Whalen's mnemonic: breakfast, lunch, dinner — 7, 12, 5.

44Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • lecture

Intervertebral foramen

Back

The hole between two stacked vertebrae where a spinal nerve exits. It does not exist on a single vertebra. Foramen just means hole.

45Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why "slipped disk" is the wrong name

Back

The disk does not move — it bulges. Inward → presses the spinal cord → lost muscle control and sensation. Outward → presses a spinal nerve → pain, classically sciatica.

46Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • lecture

Nucleus pulposus

Back

The soft centre of an intervertebral disk. In a herniation the surrounding fibrocartilage teases apart and this pushes out against a nerve or the cord.

47Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Scoliosis — the facts given

Back

Abnormal lateral curvature of the spine. Commonest form has no known cause; over 1.5 million adolescents, primarily female; progresses through the adolescent growth spurt. Brace or surgery.

48Ch. 5flashcard5.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

True, false and floating ribs

Back

1–7 true — own costal cartilage to the sternum. 8–10 false — reach it via rib 7's cartilage. 11–12 floating — no anterior attachment. All 12 pairs attach behind to the thoracic vertebrae.

49Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Pectoral girdle

Back

Clavicle + scapula. Connects the arm to the rib cage. The clavicles are more curved in males — one way to sex a skeleton.

50Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Radius and ulna — which is which

Back

Radius lateral, ulna medial, in standard anatomical position. The ulna forms the elbow, extending past its junction with the humerus.

51Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture

The eight carpals

Back

Scaphoid · lunate · triquetrum · pisiform · trapezium · trapezoid · capitate · hamate.

52Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture

Pollex and hallux

Back

Pollex — the thumb, digit 1 of the hand; has only two phalanges (no intermediate). Hallux — the big toe, metatarsal 1.

53Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • textbook

Carpal tunnel syndrome — the actual mechanism

Back

Repetitive motion inflames the tendons in the tunnel; the swollen tendons press on the nerve. The nerve is what produces the numbness, tingling and pain.

54Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Os coxae — the three bones and when they fuse

Back

Ilium (upper) · ischium (lower) · pubis (anterior), also called the innominate. They do not fuse until the mid-to-late twenties.

55Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Acetabulum

Back

The socket where ilium, ischium and pubis meet, receiving the head of the femur.

56Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Pubic symphysis

Back

The fibrocartilage pad joining the two os coxae in front. A cartilaginous joint — and in pregnancy hormones loosen it so the pelvis can widen.

57Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

The femur's three superlatives

Back

Largest, longest and heaviest bone in the body. About 25% of your height.

58Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Tibia vs fibula

Back

Tibia — the larger, weight-bearing bone; its anterior tibial crest is the shin. Fibula — the smaller one down the side. Big tib, told a little fib.

59Ch. 5flashcard5.7
  • lecture

The seven tarsals

Back

Talus · calcaneus · navicular · medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms · cuboid.

60Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

The three structural classes of joint

Back

Fibrous — no cavity, mostly immovable (skull sutures). Cartilaginous — little movement (between vertebrae, ribs to sternum, pubic symphysis). Synovial — freely movable, most joints in the body.

61Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

What every synovial joint has

Back

A joint cavity with synovial fluid from the synovial membrane; a two-layer capsule; hyaline (articular) cartilage on the moving surfaces; ligaments outside reinforcing it.

62Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Ligament vs tendon

Back

Ligament: bone to bone, at a joint — dense regular fibrous connective tissue. Tendon: muscle to bone. Both are poorly vascularised and heal slowly.

63Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Hinge vs ball-and-socket

Back

Hinge — one plane only; elbow, knee. Ball-and-socket — all planes plus rotation; shoulder, hip.

64Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Flexion and extension

Back

Flexion decreases the angle between two articulating bones. Extension increases it.

65Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Abduction and adduction

Back

Abduction — away from the midline. Adduction — toward it (it adds the limb back).

66Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Circumduction

Back

Flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence — the limb traces a circle. Needs a ball-and-socket joint.

67Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • lecture

Supination and pronation

Back

Supination turns the palm up — you can hold soup. Pronation turns it down. Forearm rotation, so the radius crosses the ulna.

68Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook

Sprain

Back

Damage to a ligament, from overstretching to a tear. Ligaments carry many pain receptors sensitive to stretching and swelling, so it can hurt more than it is serious.

69Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook

Ice or heat first, and why

Back

Ice first — constricts vessels and reduces bleeding. Then heat — dilates vessels to bring in nutrients, oxygen and anti-inflammatory chemicals.

70Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook

Bursa and bursitis

Back

A fluid-filled sac lined with synovial membrane giving a gliding surface where skin, tendon, muscle or ligament rubs on bone. Inflamed → bursitis: intense pain, worse on movement, not relieved by rest in any position; usually settles in a week or two.

71Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook

Osteoarthritis vs rheumatoid arthritis

Back

Osteoarthritis — wear and tear on joint surfaces; weight-bearing joints (hip, knee, spine). Rheumatoid — autoimmune attack on the synovial membranes; permanent, may need joint replacement.

72Ch. 5flashcard5.8
  • textbook

ACL — what it does and how it tears

Back

With the knee bent it acts as a restraining wire against front-to-back twisting between femur and tibia. An external blow to a bent knee stretches it; past its strength, it tears.

Ch. 6 — The Muscular System

Week 8 · study page · 43 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 51 flashcards · 4 diagrams, 46 labels

1Ch. 66.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which property does not belong to all three muscle types?

Answer: c

All three types are excitable, contractile, extensible and elastic — those four are shared, which is why none of them separates skeletal from cardiac or smooth. The separating property is voluntary control, and only skeletal muscle has it. The lab calls extensibility distensible; it is the same property, not a fifth one.

2Ch. 66.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Skeletal muscle helps move blood and lymph. How?

Answer: b

Contracting skeletal muscle pushes against veins and lymphatic vessels, driving their contents along — which is why moving about helps venous return. Option d is cardiac muscle, found in the walls of the heart and nowhere else; arterial diameter is regulated by smooth muscle. Warming the body is a real skeletal function, but heat is a by-product of ATP production, not a way of moving blood.

3Ch. 66.2
  • textbook

The biceps contracts and the arm flexes. What must the triceps be doing?

Answer: c

A muscle can only pull, never push, so movement in two directions takes two muscles. In an antagonistic pair one contracts while the other relaxes; to straighten the arm again, the biceps relaxes and the triceps contracts. Synergistic muscles are the other arrangement — muscles that must contract at the same time to produce one movement.

4Ch. 66.2
  • textbook

Origin and insertion are told apart by what?

Answer: c

The insertion is on the bone that moves; the origin is on the bone that stays relatively stationary. The distinction is functional, not positional — which is why option a, the intuitive reading, is the one the exam offers. Both ends attach by a tendon, so option b cannot separate them either. The bones themselves act as levers.

5Ch. 66.2
  • textbook

Tendinitis and a muscle pull get different first-line treatment. Which pairing is right?

Answer: a

Tendinitis: rest — "if it hurts, do not use it" — and the reason is anatomical, since tendons are poorly supplied with blood vessels and heal slowly whatever you do. Muscle pull: ice to reduce swelling, and keep the muscle stretched. Option b is the right pair of treatments attached to the wrong injuries, which is how the question is usually set.

6Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Put the nested structure of a muscle in order, largest to smallest.

Answer: b

Muscle → fascicle → fiber → myofibril → myofilament → sarcomere. Nearly every term in the chapter sits at one level of that nest, so getting the order wrong scrambles everything after it. The most common slip is putting fiber above fascicle — a fiber is a single cell, and a fascicle is a bundle of them.

7Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual

In the lab's terms, which connective tissue sheath wraps a single muscle fiber?

Answer: c

Epimysium wraps the whole muscle, perimysium wraps a fascicle, endomysium wraps one fiber — and all three merge at the ends of the muscle to form the tendon. These are the lab's terms; Chapter 6 says only "a membrane of fibrous connective tissue". The sarcolemma is the fiber's own plasma membrane, not a connective tissue sheath.

8Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What actually shortens when a muscle contracts?

Answer: d

The sliding filament model: actin slides along myosin, the overlap increases, and the sarcomere shortens — but neither filament changes length. When many sarcomeres shorten, the whole muscle does. This is the single most-tested misconception in the chapter, and both the lab and the book state it explicitly.

9Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Where is one end of each actin filament anchored?

Answer: a

One end of each actin filament attaches to a Z line, which marks the end of a sarcomere; the myosin filaments lie in the middle, overlapping the actin from both sides. The M line is the central protein the myosin bases attach to — the lab names it, the chapter does not. Actin binds myosin heads transiently during the cycle, but that is not an anchor.

10Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

In the cross-bridge cycle, what does the ATP bound in step 3 actually do?

Answer: b

New ATP binding causes the head to let go of actin. The pull itself — the power stroke — is driven by energy stored from an earlier ATP split, which is what cocked the head in the first place; the head then splits the new ATP in step 4 and re-cocks. Getting this backwards makes rigor mortis inexplicable, because a muscle with no ATP would go limp instead of stiff.

11Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Calcium enters the sarcomere. What does it bind to, and what happens?

Answer: c

At rest the troponin–tropomyosin complex covers the myosin-binding sites on actin. Calcium binds troponin, troponin changes shape, and tropomyosin is shifted off the sites so myosin heads can attach. Option a inverts the two regulatory proteins, which is the standard mix-up — troponin is the calcium receptor, tropomyosin is the cover.

12Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Where is the calcium stored before contraction?

Answer: d

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialised smooth endoplasmic reticulum wrapped round each myofibril "like a sleeve of thick lace", and it is the calcium store. The T tubules are the tempting answer because they are the other membrane system in the cell — but they carry the signal, not the calcium. Sarcoplasmic reticulum on both sides of one T tubule makes a triad.

13Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A thigh muscle cell can be 30 cm long. How does a signal at its surface reach the sarcomeres in the middle?

Answer: b

Transverse tubules are infoldings of the plasma membrane that dive into the cell, carrying the electrochemical message to virtually every sarcomere. That is the whole point of them, and the length of the cell is the exam's usual framing. Option a describes what happens after the signal arrives and only over very short distances — calcium comes out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not in from the surface.

14Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Why does a body stiffen a few hours after death?

Answer: c

Calcium leaks out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum after death and starts contraction; contraction continues while ATP lasts, but no more ATP is made, and it takes an ATP to break a cross-bridge. Stiffness sets in within 3 to 4 hours. Option d is what ends it — actin and myosin do break down, and the muscles relax again after 2 to 3 days.

15Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Put the neuromuscular junction steps in order.

Answer: b

Impulse → acetylcholine released from packets in the neuron tip → it diffuses across the gap and binds receptors on the muscle membrane, creating an electrochemical message → that message runs along the membrane and into the T tubules → the sarcoplasmic reticulum opens and releases calcium. Calcium is always last, because it is the switch, not the signal.

16Ch. 66.3
  • textbook

Curare blocks acetylcholine from binding to its receptor. Why is that fatal?

Answer: b

With no acetylcholine binding there is no membrane message, no T tubule signal, no calcium release and no contraction — flaccid paralysis of every skeletal muscle. The diaphragm is skeletal muscle, so inhalation stops and the victim suffocates. The heart is cardiac muscle, not skeletal, and is not driven by this junction — which rules out option a. Option d is Duchenne muscular dystrophy's mechanism.

17Ch. 66.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Botulinum toxin and curare both cause flaccid paralysis. How do they differ?

Answer: a

Two adjacent steps of the same drawing. Botulinum stops acetylcholine being released from the motor neuron's packets; curare stops it binding to the receptors on the muscle membrane. The downstream failure is identical — no calcium, no contraction — and both kill by paralysing the diaphragm. The lab's Block 11 puts them side by side with Duchenne for exactly this reason.

18Ch. 66.3
  • textbook

Duchenne muscular dystrophy comes from a defective gene for dystrophin. What goes wrong?

Answer: b

Lack of dystrophin lets excess calcium into the muscle cell, and that excess destroys proteins within it, so the cell dies. Dead muscle cells are replaced by fat and connective tissue, and the muscle gets progressively weaker. It is the mirror image of the toxin questions: those are too little signal, this is too much calcium.

19Ch. 66.4
  • textbook

Which muscle would you expect to have the fewest cells per motor unit?

Answer: a

Motor unit size is inversely related to precision. A single motor neuron in a tiny eye muscle may control only three muscle cells; one in a calf muscle may control thousands. The average across the body is about 150. Fine control needs a neuron to command very few cells at a time, which is the same reason fingers have small units.

20Ch. 66.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

You lift a fork, then lift a table, using the same muscles. What changed?

Answer: a

Recruitment — the nervous system raises the strength of contraction by stimulating more motor units. An individual muscle cell is all-or-none: it contracts completely each time it is stimulated. The chapter's second mechanism, summation, changes force per cell by changing the frequency of stimulation, not by the choice between fork and table.

21Ch. 66.4
  • textbook

A relaxed muscle is still firm to the touch. Why?

Answer: b

That is muscle tone: even at rest some motor units are firing, and they rotate, so no unit fatigues and the muscle stays firm and solid. A muscle that lacks tone is limp. Option d would be rigor mortis, and option a is the opposite of what happens at rest — membrane pumps clear calcium out to allow relaxation.

22Ch. 66.4
  • textbook

A second stimulus arrives before the muscle has fully relaxed. What is the result called?

Answer: c

Summation is the second twitch added to the first, giving a stronger contraction, because an increasing number of muscle cells are stimulated. Tetanus is the extreme of the same process — stimuli arriving so fast that there is no relaxation at all, giving a sustained maximal contraction. The question turns on "before it fully relaxed" versus "no time to relax at all".

23Ch. 66.4
  • textbook

In this chapter, tetanus means what?

Answer: b

Tetanus here is a normal physiological state, not the disease — it is what a muscle does whenever you hold anything. Option c is a cramp, possibly caused by low blood levels of calcium, magnesium or potassium and relieved by stretching or gently rubbing. Option d is fatigue, which is what eventually ends tetanus when ATP runs short and lactic acid builds up.

24Ch. 66.5
  • textbook

Which energy source fuels a 100 m sprint from about 6 to 16 seconds in?

Answer: b

Read the clock. Stored ATP lasts about 6 seconds; creatine phosphate covers roughly the next 10; anaerobic pathways take over for strenuous effort lasting 30 or 40 seconds; aerobic supplies everything longer. Diving, weight lifting and sprinting are powered entirely by the ATP and creatine phosphate reserves. A resting muscle stores about six times as much creatine phosphate as ATP.

25Ch. 66.5
  • textbook

Why are anaerobic pathways used for burst activity such as tennis or soccer?

Answer: c

Speed, not yield. Anaerobic pathways make ATP about 2.5 times faster than aerobic ones, which is what a burst needs. They yield far less per glucose, which is option a's error, and they are the pathway that produces lactic acid — the pyruvic acid from glycolysis is converted to it — so option d is backwards.

26Ch. 66.5
  • textbook

What is most of the extra oxygen used for when you keep breathing hard after exercise?

Answer: a

Oxygen debt is mostly about lactic acid, not about catching your breath. The chapter says most of that oxygen generates the ATP needed to convert lactic acid back to glucose. Options b, c and d are all real uses the chapter lists — they are just the smaller share, which is what makes them good distractors.

27Ch. 66.5
  • textbook

Myoglobin and hemoglobin both bind oxygen. Where is each?

Answer: c

Myoglobin is the oxygen-binding pigment inside muscle cells; hemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood. During prolonged activity the chapter names both as oxygen sources. Myoglobin is also what makes slow-twitch cells dark, which ties this straight to the next section and to the chicken question.

28Ch. 66.6
  • textbook

A marathoner's leg muscles are about 80% one cell type. Which, and why?

Answer: c

Slow-twitch cells are dark and reddish because they are packed with myoglobin and richly supplied with blood vessels, and they hold abundant mitochondria — everything needed to make ATP aerobically for a long time. Option d states the opposite of the truth about mitochondria. Sprinters' legs are about 60% fast-twitch, and the difference is partly genetic.

29Ch. 66.6
  • textbook

Why is chicken breast white and chicken leg dark?

Answer: b

The colour is myoglobin. Ground-dwelling birds run constantly, so the legs are built of slow-twitch cells — myoglobin-rich, vascular, mitochondria-packed, and therefore dark. The breast powers short bursts of flight, so it is fast-twitch — glycogen-rich, anaerobic, low in myoglobin, and white. Option d confuses glycogen with an oxygen store.

30Ch. 66.6
  • textbook

Fast-twitch cells contract more rapidly than slow-twitch cells. What makes them faster?

Answer: a

They carry a form of the enzyme that splits ATP bound to myosin more quickly, so they make and break cross-bridges faster. Their power comes from a separate feature — a wider diameter packed with more actin and myosin. Option d describes slow-twitch cells, which are the richly vascularised ones.

31Ch. 66.7
  • textbook

Which kind of exercise increases muscle size?

Answer: c

To build muscle tone and mass the muscle has to exert more than 75% of its maximum force — the number appears in the section and again in Figure 6.11's caption. Aerobic exercise generally does not increase muscle size; what it does is add blood vessels and mitochondria, improve coordination, and strengthen the skeleton. Aerobic exercise is genuinely valuable, just not for bulk.

32Ch. 66.7
  • textbook

How does a muscle get bigger with resistance training?

Answer: b

The bulk results from an increase in the diameter of the existing muscle cells. The chapter notes a minority view — that heavy exercise splits or tears cells and each part regrows larger — but states diameter as the main explanation. And it does not last: muscle mass begins to disappear two weeks after training stops.

33Ch. 66.7
  • textbook

Why does running downhill produce more soreness two days later than running uphill?

Answer: b

DOMS is especially common after exercise that forces a muscle to lengthen while it is contracting, which is what the quadriceps do going downhill — also walking down stairs, skiing and horseback riding. It is counterintuitive, which is why it gets asked. The cause is not known for certain; microscopic damage and an inflammatory response are the two suggestions.

34Ch. 66.7
  • textbook

Why are Nautilus-type machines useful for resistance training?

Answer: c

Muscles are weaker at some parts of their range of motion than at others, and the machines automatically adjust the resistance — easier where the muscle is weak, harder where it is strong. Option b is also true and the chapter says it, but it is a safety point, not the reason the design is valuable; the question asks why the mechanism matters.

35Ch. 66.7
  • textbook

Anabolic steroids' reproductive side effects differ between the sexes. Which is right?

Answer: a

In males the testicles often become smaller and the user may become sterile and impotent, because anabolic steroids inhibit natural testosterone production. In females the masculine traits are irreversible — deeper voice, body hair, scalp hair loss, smaller breasts, enlarged clitoris. The cardiovascular damage is the other serious category and may not show up for years, which is what makes it invisible to the user.

36Ch. 66.7
  • textbook

A steroid user gains strength quickly and then tears a tendon. Why would that follow?

Answer: b

The chapter states it outright: greater muscle strength is not accompanied by a corresponding increase in the strength of tendons and ligaments, and injuries to those take a long time to heal — which fits what Chapter 5 says about their poor blood supply. Options a, c and d are mechanisms the chapter never claims.

37Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which muscle tissue type is striated but involuntary?

Answer: c

Two are striated and two are involuntary, and they are not the same two. Cardiac is striated but involuntary; skeletal is striated and voluntary; smooth is the only one that is neither. The striations come from the orderly arrangement of actin and myosin in sarcomeres, which cardiac muscle has and smooth muscle does not.

38Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Under the microscope, how do you tell a cardiac cell from a skeletal fiber?

Answer: c

Both are striated, so the stripes cannot separate them. Nuclei and shape do: cardiac cells are short and branched with one central nucleus; skeletal fibers are long cylinders with many nuclei along the periphery. Option b is those two swapped. Spindle-shaped with tapered ends is smooth muscle. Cardiac cells join at intercalated discs carrying gap junctions; skeletal fibers join to nothing.

39Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Why do gap junctions matter in cardiac and smooth muscle?

Answer: a

Gap junctions let a sheet of cells react as one to a single signal — that is how the heart wall contracts together and how peristalsis moves a bolus along a tube. Skeletal muscle has none, which is why it is controlled motor unit by motor unit instead. Smooth muscle cells may also act individually.

40Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Why does a skeletal muscle fiber have many nuclei?

Answer: b

Immature muscle cells fuse during development into a single long fiber, and their nuclei end up spaced along its edge — which is what a cell that can run 30 cm needs. Option c is the tempting structural guess but myofibrils are protein bundles, not compartments with nuclei. Glycogen is stored in the sarcoplasm, not in nuclei.

41Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which structure does the enzyme ATPase sit on?

Answer: c

The lab is explicit: the myosin head carries the enzyme ATPase, which binds and breaks down ATP, and the base of the myosin molecule attaches to a central M protein. That is why the myosin head is the part that both cocks and detaches. Fast-twitch cells owe their speed to carrying a faster form of that same enzyme.

42Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual

Reading across one sarcomere, which band sequence is right?

Answer: b

The lighter I bands sit at the ends, next to the Z discs, where there is thin filament only; the darker A band is the middle, where the thick filaments lie, and the H zone and M line are at its centre. Option a is that inverted. The bands are the lab's terms — Chapter 6 names only the Z line.

43Ch. 6Lab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual

What is a triad in a muscle fiber?

Answer: b

A T tubule flanked by sarcoplasmic reticulum on either side is a triad — three membranes in section. The arrangement increases the contact area between the surface membrane and the calcium store, so the signal and the release happen close together. The lab's image is a finger pushed into a water balloon.

1Ch. 6short answer6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Describe the sliding filament model, including the four steps of the cross-bridge cycle.

Model answer

A muscle contracts when actin filaments slide along myosin filaments, increasing their overlap and shortening the sarcomere — the filaments themselves do not shorten. When many sarcomeres shorten, the whole muscle contracts. At rest the myosin heads have already split ATP into ADP + P_i_, and the energy released has swivelled them out toward the Z lines, cocked like a pistol. Step 1 — cross-bridge attachment: the heads bind the nearest actin filament, bridging thick and thin. Step 2 — power stroke: the stored energy is released, the heads swing back to their bent positions and pull actin toward the midline; ADP and P_i_ leave the head. Step 3 — detachment: new ATP binds the heads and they release actin. Step 4 — reactivation: the heads split that ATP and store the energy, cocking again. The cycle repeats hundreds of times a second.

Marks for the sliding statement with "the sarcomere shortens, the filaments do not", then one for each of the four steps in order. The distinguishing detail is that ATP detaches the head rather than powering the pull — say it and the rigor mortis question answers itself.

2Ch. 6short answer6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Calcium and ATP are both needed for contraction. Explain what each one does, and use rigor mortis to show the difference.

Model answer

Calcium is the switch. At rest the troponin–tropomyosin complex covers the myosin-binding sites on actin. Calcium, released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, binds troponin, which changes shape and shifts tropomyosin off the sites so myosin can attach. Relaxation happens when membrane pumps clear calcium out and the complex re-covers the sites. ATP is the fuel, and it does two separate things: its splitting cocks the myosin head ready for the next stroke, and a newly bound ATP is what detaches the head from actin. Rigor mortis proves they are separate. After death calcium leaks out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and starts contraction, but ATP production has stopped. Without ATP the cross-bridges cannot be broken, so the body stiffens within 3 to 4 hours, and stays stiff until actin and myosin break down after 2 to 3 days. If ATP powered the pull rather than the release, a dead muscle would go limp instead.

One mark for calcium as the switch with troponin and tropomyosin named, one for ATP's two roles, and the rest for using rigor mortis as the discriminating case with its timings.

3Ch. 6short answer6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Trace a nerve impulse from the motor neuron to a contracting sarcomere.

Model answer

One. A nerve impulse reaches the neuromuscular junction — the junction between the tip of a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle cell. Two. The impulse causes acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter, to be released from small packets in the neuron tip. Three. Acetylcholine diffuses across the gap and binds receptors on the muscle cell membrane, changing its permeability and creating an electrochemical message like a nerve impulse. Four. That message travels along the plasma membrane and into the T tubules, which carry it deep into the cell to virtually every sarcomere. Five. At the sarcoplasmic reticulum it opens channels that release calcium. Calcium binds troponin, tropomyosin shifts off the binding sites, and the cross-bridge cycle begins. When the impulse stops, pumps clear the calcium and the muscle relaxes.

Five steps in order, with acetylcholine, the receptor, the T tubule and the sarcoplasmic reticulum named. Saying the T tubule carries the signal, not the calcium is the detail most answers miss.

4Ch. 6short answer6.5
  • textbook

Name the four energy sources a muscle uses and say roughly how long each lasts.

Model answer

One — ATP already stored in the muscle cells, depleted in about 6 seconds of vigorous exercise. Two — creatine phosphate, which carries a high-energy bond and converts ADP back to ATP; a resting muscle holds about six times as much of it as stored ATP, and it supports roughly the next 10 seconds. Diving, weight lifting and sprinting run entirely on these first two. Three — anaerobic pathways, which make ATP about 2.5 times faster than aerobic ones and supply strenuous activity lasting 30 or 40 seconds; pyruvic acid from glycolysis is converted to lactic acid. Burst sports such as tennis and soccer rely on these almost completely. Four — aerobic respiration, which supplies more than 90% of the ATP for intense activity lasting over 10 minutes and nearly 100% of a marathon. The fuel for both pathways is glucose, mostly from glycogen stored in muscle and liver. Afterwards, the oxygen debt is repaid — most of that oxygen generating the ATP that converts lactic acid back to glucose.

Four sources in order with their durations is the answer; the clock is what the question is testing. Adding glycogen as the fuel, and oxygen debt as lactic acid conversion, takes it to full marks.

5Ch. 6short answer6.6
  • textbook

Compare slow-twitch and fast-twitch muscle cells, and say where each predominates.

Model answer

Slow-twitch cells contract slowly but with enormous endurance. They are dark and reddish because they are packed with myoglobin and richly supplied with blood vessels, and they hold abundant mitochondria, so they make ATP aerobically for long periods. Fast-twitch cells contract rapidly and powerfully but fatigue quickly. They carry a form of the ATP-splitting enzyme that works faster, so cross-bridges form and break more quickly; they are wider, with more actin and myosin, which adds power; and they are rich in glycogen and depend on anaerobic ATP production. Distribution: the abdominal muscles contract steadily to balance the powerful slow-twitch back muscles that hold us upright; fast-twitch cells are more common in the arms and legs, which may need to move quickly. People differ partly genetically — marathoners' leg muscles are about 80% slow-twitch, sprinters' about 60% fast-twitch, and a fast-twitch person can build endurance only to a degree.

A full answer contrasts speed, endurance, colour, myoglobin, mitochondria, and aerobic versus anaerobic, then gives the distribution and the athlete percentages. The colour is the thread: dark = myoglobin = oxygen = aerobic = endurance.

6Ch. 6short answerLab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the organisation of a skeletal muscle from the whole muscle down to the sarcomere, naming each connective tissue covering.

Model answer

The whole muscle is wrapped in epimysium. Inside it, muscle fibers are bundled into fascicles, each wrapped in perimysium. Inside a fascicle are the muscle fibers — the muscle cells themselves, which can be several centimetres long and up to 30 cm in the thigh — each wrapped in endomysium. All three sheaths merge and condense at the ends of the muscle to form the tendon. Within a fiber, the plasma membrane is the sarcolemma and the cytoplasm the sarcoplasm; myofibrils run its length and are what make it look striated. Each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres laid end to end — the functional unit, running Z line to Z line — built from thin (actin) and thick (myosin) filaments. Also inside the fiber: the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which stores calcium, and the T tubules, invaginations of the sarcolemma that carry the signal inward; sarcoplasmic reticulum on both sides of a T tubule makes a triad.

The nest in order with all three sheaths correctly placed is most of the marks, and the tendon point — the sheaths merging to form it — is the one that shows the nest is understood rather than memorised. Sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum, T tubule and triad are the lab's named structures and are what a model-labelling question asks for.

1Ch. 6label the diagramName that muscle

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Sternocleidomastoid

    Runs from behind the ear down to the sternum and clavicle. Turns and flexes the head. Its name is its attachments: sterno-cleido-mastoid.

  2. 2name it

    Deltoid

    The cap of the shoulder. Abducts the arm — lifts it away from the midline.

  3. 3name it

    Pectoralis major

    The chest. Adducts and flexes the arm — pulls it toward and across the midline.

  4. 4name it

    Serratus anterior

    The finger-like slips on the lateral chest wall, under the arm. Pulls the scapula forward around the rib cage.

  5. 5name it

    Biceps brachii

    Anterior compartment of the arm. Flexes the forearm, and it is the lab's worked example of a prime mover — with the brachialis and brachioradialis as its synergists.

  6. 6name it

    Rectus abdominis

    The midline strap of the abdominal wall. Flexes the trunk. Rectus means straight.

  7. 7name it

    Abdominal external oblique

    Lateral to the rectus abdominis, fibres running at an angle. Flexes and rotates the trunk. Externus — outside.

  8. 8name it

    Sartorius

    The long thin strap crossing the thigh from the lateral hip to the medial knee. The longest muscle in the body.

  9. 9name it

    Quadriceps group

    Four muscles of the anterior compartment of the thigh — rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis. They extend the leg, and they are the antagonist of the hamstrings.

  10. 10name it

    Tibialis anterior

    The strip on the anterolateral shank, beside the tibia's crest. Dorsiflexes the foot.

  11. 11name it

    Trapezius

    The big diamond across the upper back and neck. Elevates and retracts the scapula.

  12. 12name it

    Latissimus dorsi

    The broad sheet of the lower back. Extends and adducts the arm — the pull-up muscle. Latissimus — widest.

  13. 13name it

    Triceps brachii

    Posterior compartment of the arm. Extends the forearm — the antagonist of the biceps brachii. Tri — three heads.

  14. 14name it

    Gluteus maximus

    The buttock. Extends the thigh. Maximus — the largest of the three glutei.

  15. 15name it

    Hamstring group

    Three muscles of the posterior compartment of the thigh — biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus. They flex the leg, and they are the antagonist of the quadriceps.

  16. 16name it

    Gastrocnemius

    The calf. Plantarflexes the foot; runs into the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, drawn below it.

2Ch. 6label the diagramMuscle organisation, outside in

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Epimysium

    The connective tissue sheath around the whole muscle.

  2. 2name it

    Tendon

    Where all three sheaths merge and condense at the ends of the muscle. Attaches muscle to bone.

  3. 3name it

    Perimysium

    The sheath around one fascicle.

  4. 4name it

    Fascicle

    A bundle of muscle fibers, wrapped in perimysium.

  5. 5name it

    Endomysium

    The sheath around one muscle fiber.

  6. 6name it

    Muscle fiber

    One muscle cell. Can be several centimetres long — up to 30 cm in the thigh.

  7. 7name it

    Nuclei

    Many per fiber, along the periphery — because immature muscle cells fused during development into one long fiber.

  8. 8name it

    Myofibril

    A bundle of contractile proteins running the length of the cell. Their orderly arrangement is what makes the cell look striated.

  9. 9name it

    Sarcomere

    The functional unit of contraction, Z line to Z line. Myofibrils are sarcomeres laid end to end.

  10. 10name it

    Sarcolemma

    The muscle fiber's plasma membrane. Its cytoplasm is the sarcoplasm.

3Ch. 6label the diagramThe sarcomere

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Z disc (Z line)

    Marks each end of the sarcomere. The thin filaments are anchored to it.

  2. 2name it

    I band

    The lighter band — thin filament only, no overlap. It straddles a Z disc, so half belongs to each neighbouring sarcomere.

  3. 3name it

    A band

    The darker band — the full length of the thick filament, overlap included. It does not change length during contraction.

  4. 4name it

    M line

    The central protein the bases of the myosin molecules attach to.

  5. 5name it

    H zone

    The part of the A band with thick filament only — no thin overlap. It narrows as the muscle contracts.

  6. 6name it

    Thin filament (actin)

    Two strands of globular subunits, anchored to the Z disc, extending toward the M line. Each subunit carries a myosin-binding site.

  7. 7name it

    Thick filament (myosin)

    Fibrous, with globular heads projecting toward the thin filaments. The head carries the enzyme ATPase.

  8. 8name it

    Myosin head

    The cross-bridge. It binds actin, swings back in the power stroke, and is released when a new ATP binds it.

  9. 9name it

    Tropomyosin

    The strand lying over the myosin-binding sites on actin, blocking them at rest.

  10. 10name it

    Troponin

    Interspersed along the tropomyosin. Calcium binds here, changing its shape and shifting tropomyosin off the sites.

4Ch. 6label the diagramThe neuromuscular junction

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Motor neuron

    Its axon carries the nerve impulse to the junction. A motor unit is this neuron plus every muscle cell it stimulates — about 150 on average, all contracting together.

  2. 2name it

    Axon terminal

    The tip of the motor neuron. Step 1 is the impulse arriving here.

  3. 3name it

    Synaptic vesicles

    The small packets holding the neurotransmitter, waiting in the terminal.

  4. 4name it

    Acetylcholine

    The neurotransmitter released into the gap. Curare stops it binding; botulinum toxin stops it being released — both give flaccid paralysis, and both kill by paralysing the diaphragm.

  5. 5name it

    Receptors

    On the muscle cell membrane. Acetylcholine binding here changes the membrane's permeability and creates an electrochemical message like a nerve impulse.

  6. 6name it

    Synaptic cleft

    The small gap acetylcholine diffuses across.

  7. 7name it

    Transverse (T) tubule

    An invagination of the sarcolemma carrying the signal — not the calcium — from the surface deep into the cell, to virtually every sarcomere.

  8. 8name it

    Sarcoplasmic reticulum

    Specialised endoplasmic reticulum. It stores the calcium and releases it when the signal arrives. Flanking a T tubule on both sides, it forms a triad.

  9. 9name it

    Calcium ions

    Released last. Ca2+ binds troponin, tropomyosin shifts off the binding sites, and the cross-bridge cycle begins. Relaxation is membrane pumps clearing it back out.

  10. 10name it

    Myofibrils

    What the signal is delivered to. The T tubules dive in around them, which is how a surface signal reaches the middle of a 30 cm cell.

1Ch. 6flashcard6.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The four properties all muscle tissue shares

Back

Excitable (responds to stimuli) · contractile (shortens) · extensible / distensible (stretches) · elastic (returns to resting length).

2Ch. 6flashcard6.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What separates skeletal muscle from cardiac and smooth?

Back

Voluntary control. It is not one of the four shared properties.

3Ch. 6flashcard6.1
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The five functions of skeletal muscle

Back

Movement (including facial expression) · posture against gravity · support for internal organs (abdominal wall, pelvic floor) · moving blood and lymph by squeezing veins and lymphatics · heat generation.

4Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Where is cardiac muscle found, and what does it do?

Back

The walls of the heart, and nowhere else. It contracts to pump blood. Striated but involuntary.

5Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

What does smooth muscle do, and where is it?

Back

Involuntary movement — moves food, moves secretions, involuntary control of respiration, regulates blood flow by narrowing arteries. In the walls of vessels, the digestive and urinary systems, and the iris.

6Ch. 6flashcard6.2
  • textbook

Synergistic vs antagonistic muscles

Back

Synergistic — must contract at the same time to produce a movement. Antagonistic — one contracts while the other relaxes; biceps flexes, triceps extends.

7Ch. 6flashcard6.2
  • textbook

Origin and insertion

Back

Origin — the end on the bone that stays stationary. Insertion — the end on the bone that moves. Defined by which bone moves, not by which end is nearer the body.

8Ch. 6flashcard6.2
  • textbook

Tendinitis — cause and treatment

Back

Inflammation of a tendon from overuse, misuse or age. Treatment is rest — if it hurts, don't use it — because tendons have few blood vessels and heal slowly.

9Ch. 6flashcard6.2
  • textbook

Muscle pull / strain / tear — cause and treatment

Back

Damage to a muscle or its tendons from overstretching, sometimes with bleeding from small vessels. Ice to reduce swelling, and keep the muscle stretched.

10Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The nest, largest to smallest

Back

Muscle → fascicle → fiber (cell) → myofibril → myofilament → sarcomere.

11Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual

Epimysium · perimysium · endomysium

Back

Epi wraps the whole muscle. Peri wraps a fascicle. Endo wraps one fiber. All three merge at the ends to form the tendon.

12Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual

Sarcolemma and sarcoplasm

Back

Sarcolemma — the muscle fiber's plasma membrane. Sarcoplasm — its cytoplasm, where the myofibrils lie.

13Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Sarcomere

Back

The functional unit of contraction, running Z line to Z line. Tens of thousands of them end to end make a myofibril.

14Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Thick filament vs thin filament

Back

Thick = myosin, shaped like two-headed golf clubs; the head carries ATPase, the base attaches to the central M protein. Thin = actin, two twisted strands of globular subunits anchored to the Z disc, each subunit carrying a myosin-binding site.

15Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 2
  • lab manual

The bands across one sarcomere

Back

I band (light) · A band (dark), with the H zone and M line at its centre · I band (light), Z disc to Z disc.

16Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The sliding filament model, in one sentence

Back

Actin slides along myosin, the overlap increases, and the sarcomere shortens — the filaments themselves do not change length.

17Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The four steps of the cross-bridge cycle

Back

1 Attachment — heads bind actin. 2 Power stroke — stored energy swings them back, pulling actin inward; ADP + P_i_ leave. 3 Detachment — new ATP binds and the head lets go. 4 Reactivation — the head splits that ATP and re-cocks.

18Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Calcium's job vs ATP's job

Back

Calcium is the switch — it uncovers the binding sites. ATP is the fuel — it cocks the head, and a new ATP detaches it. ATP does not power the pull.

19Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Troponin and tropomyosin

Back

Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin; troponin is interspersed along it. Calcium binds troponin, which changes shape and shifts tropomyosin off the sites.

20Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Sarcoplasmic reticulum

Back

Specialised smooth endoplasmic reticulum sleeving each myofibril. It stores the calcium and releases it when the signal arrives.

21Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

T tubules — what they carry

Back

Invaginations of the sarcolemma reaching deep into the cell. They carry the signal, not the calcium, to virtually every sarcomere. T tubule + sarcoplasmic reticulum on both sides = a triad.

22Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Rigor mortis — the mechanism and the timings

Back

Calcium leaks out after death and starts contraction; ATP production stops, and it takes ATP to break a cross-bridge. Stiff within 3–4 hours; relaxes after 2–3 days as actin and myosin break down.

23Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The neuromuscular junction, step by step

Back

Impulse arrives → acetylcholine released from the neuron tip → diffuses the gap and binds receptors on the muscle membrane → message runs into the T tubules → sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium.

24Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Curare vs botulinum toxin

Back

Curare blocks acetylcholine from binding the receptor. Botulinum blocks acetylcholine from being released. Both → flaccid paralysis; both kill by paralysing the diaphragm, which is skeletal muscle.

25Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook

Duchenne muscular dystrophy

Back

Defective gene for dystrophin → too much calcium enters the cell → it destroys proteins and the cell dies. Dead cells are replaced by fat and connective tissue.

26Ch. 6flashcard6.3
  • textbook

Muscle cramp — possible causes and relief

Back

Forceful involuntary contraction, possibly from low blood calcium, magnesium or potassium. Usually relieved by stretching or gently rubbing.

27Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Motor unit

Back

A motor neuron and all the muscle cells it stimulates — all of them contract together. About 150 cells on average; its cells are spread through the muscle.

28Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook

Motor unit size and precision

Back

Inversely related. An eye-muscle neuron may control 3 cells; a calf-muscle neuron thousands. Fine control = small units.

29Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Recruitment

Back

Raising the strength of contraction by stimulating more motor units. One unit alone makes the whole muscle contract, but only weakly.

30Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook

Muscle tone

Back

Some motor units are always active in a resting muscle, and they rotate — so it stays firm and solid. A muscle without tone is limp.

31Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook

Twitch · summation · tetanus

Back

Twitch — one stimulus: latent period, short contraction, longer relaxation. Summation — a second stimulus before full relaxation, giving a stronger contraction. Tetanus — stimuli so frequent there is no relaxation at all; sustained maximal contraction.

32Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook

Latent period

Back

The interval between reception of the stimulus and the beginning of contraction.

33Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What are twitches actually good for?

Back

They are too brief for normal movement, but they generate heat when we shiver.

34Ch. 6flashcard6.4
  • textbook

Muscle fatigue — the two stated causes

Back

The muscle cannot produce enough ATP, and lactic acid accumulates — so it stops contracting even though stimulation continues.

35Ch. 6flashcard6.5
  • textbook

The four energy sources, on the clock

Back

Stored ATP 6 s → creatine phosphate 10 s more → anaerobic pathways ~30–40 s → aerobic respiration for anything longer.

36Ch. 6flashcard6.5
  • textbook

Creatine phosphate

Back

The muscle's short-term store — a high-energy bond between creatine and phosphate, used to convert ADP back to ATP. A resting muscle holds about six times as much as stored ATP.

37Ch. 6flashcard6.5
  • textbook

Anaerobic vs aerobic — the trade

Back

Anaerobic is ~2.5× faster but ends in lactic acid; it fuels bursts (tennis, soccer). Aerobic supplies >90% of ATP for intense effort over 10 minutes and nearly 100% of a marathon.

38Ch. 6flashcard6.5
  • textbook

Glycogen in muscle

Back

The stored carbohydrate broken down to glucose, the primary fuel for either pathway. About 1.5% of a muscle cell's weight. Running it out is "hitting the wall".

39Ch. 6flashcard6.5
  • textbook

Myoglobin vs hemoglobin

Back

Myoglobin — an oxygen-binding pigment inside muscle cells. Hemoglobin — carries oxygen in the blood. Both supply oxygen during prolonged activity.

40Ch. 6flashcard6.5
  • textbook

Oxygen debt — what the extra oxygen is mostly for

Back

Converting lactic acid back to glucose. Also replacing myoglobin's oxygen and restoring glycogen and creatine phosphate.

41Ch. 6flashcard6.6
  • textbook

Slow-twitch cells

Back

Dark and red — packed with myoglobin, richly vascularised, abundant mitochondria, aerobic, enormous endurance. Marathoners' legs ≈ 80% slow-twitch.

42Ch. 6flashcard6.6
  • textbook

Fast-twitch cells

Back

Pale — a faster ATP-splitting enzyme, wider with more actin and myosin, glycogen-rich, anaerobic, powerful but tire quickly. Sprinters' legs ≈ 60% fast-twitch.

43Ch. 6flashcard6.6
  • textbook

White meat and dark meat

Back

Dark = slow-twitch = myoglobin — the legs of a bird that runs constantly. White = fast-twitch — the breast, for short bursts of flight.

44Ch. 6flashcard6.7
  • textbook

What does aerobic exercise change, and what does it not?

Back

Adds blood vessels and mitochondria, improves coordination and digestive movement, strengthens bone, enlarges the heart. It does not increase muscle size.

45Ch. 6flashcard6.7
  • textbook

The threshold for building muscle mass

Back

The muscle must exert more than 75% of its maximum force. A few minutes every other day for a year can build 50% more muscle — and it starts disappearing 2 weeks after you stop.

46Ch. 6flashcard6.7
  • textbook

How does a muscle get bigger?

Back

The existing cells increase in diameter. (A minority view is that heavy exercise splits or tears cells and each part regrows larger.)

47Ch. 6flashcard6.7
  • textbook

DOMS

Back

Delayed onset muscle soreness — a day or two after intense exercise, especially where a muscle lengthens while contracting (running downhill, stairs, skiing). Cause not known for certain.

48Ch. 6flashcard6.7
  • textbook

Anabolic steroids — the three most serious systems affected

Back

Liver · cardiovascular · reproductive. Cardiovascular damage may take years to appear; reproductive effects are immediate, and in females irreversible.

49Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Skeletal, cardiac, smooth — down the microscope

Back

Skeletal — long cylinders, many peripheral nuclei, striated, joined to nothing. Cardiac — short and branched, one central nucleus, striated, intercalated discs. Smooth — short spindle shape with tapered ends, one nucleus, no striations, gap junctions.

50Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Which types have gap junctions, and why does it matter?

Back

Cardiac and smooth, not skeletal. They let a sheet of cells react as one to a single signal — the heart wall contracting together, and peristalsis.

51Ch. 6flashcardLab 8 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Why is smooth muscle not striated?

Back

Its myofilaments are arranged differently — not in sarcomeres. That is also why it can shorten in several directions at once rather than only end to end.

Lab 5 — Intro to Anatomy, Tissues & Integumentary

Week 6 · study page · 22 multiple choice · 5 short answer · 34 flashcards · 2 diagrams, 21 labels · Ran Mon 09/21 after the Unit 1 exam took its original period.

1Lab 5Block 1
  • lab manual

Which plane separates the body into anterior and posterior?

Answer: c

The pairing is the whole topic. Sagittal → right and left. Frontal (coronal) → anterior and posterior. Transverse → superior and inferior (or proximal and distal on a limb). Mid-sagittal is the specific sagittal cut that divides right and left into equal halves — it is the midline that medial and lateral are measured from.

2Lab 5Block 2
  • lab manual

Which pair of directional terms may be used only on a limb or a tubular structure?

Answer: d

Proximal (closer to the point of origin) and distal (further from it) require a reference position on a limb or a tubular structure — using them on the trunk is wrong. The lab puts that restriction in a parenthesis, which is exactly the kind of detail a lab exam picks up. The other named restriction: intermediate references at least two other positions and is meaningless alone.

3Lab 5Block 2
  • lab manual

A patient is lying face down. What is that position called?

Answer: b

Prone is face down; supine is face up — the mnemonic is that you lie on your spine when supine. Dorsal and caudal are directions, not positions: dorsal means toward the back (the same as posterior), caudal means toward the tail. Every description is made relative to anatomical position, whatever the body is actually doing.

4Lab 5Block 3
  • lab manual

Which regional term names the front of the elbow?

Answer: c

Antecubital — the front of the elbow; olecranal — the back of it. That pair is one of five the block singles out as confusable: also brachial (arm) vs antebrachial (forearm), carpal (wrist) vs tarsal (ankle), crural (leg) vs sural (calf), and pollex (thumb) vs hallux (great toe). None of this vocabulary is in Chapter 4 — it is lab-exam material end to end.

5Lab 5Block 3
  • lab manual

Which regional term names the back of the knee?

Answer: b

Popliteal — the back of the knee; patellar is the kneecap on the front. Sural is the calf and crural is the leg — the other pair worth separating on the sheet. Learn the adjective form of every regional term, because the adjective is the one that gets used in a description.

6Lab 5Block 4
  • lab manual

Which cavity holds the great vessels, trachea and esophagus?

Answer: c

Inside the thoracic cavity sit the pleural cavities (right and left lungs), the pericardial cavity (heart), and the mediastinum — the cavity holding the great vessels, trachea and esophagus. Worth knowing the nesting: the pericardial cavity sits within the mediastinum. Mediastinum is lab vocabulary; Chapter 4 does not use it.

7Lab 5Block 4
  • lab manual

What separates the abdominal cavity from the pelvic cavity?

Answer: c

There is no physical structure between them — both are in the abdomen, and the boundary is a bony landmark, the superior aspect of the hip bones (iliac crest). Below it is the pelvic cavity (bladder, uterus, ovaries); above it and below the diaphragm is the abdominal cavity (most of the digestive tract, spleen, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, kidneys, ureters). The diaphragm is the real physical divider — but between thoracic and abdominopelvic.

8Lab 5Block 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Epithelial tissue has three defining characteristics. Which is one of them?

Answer: b

Avascular + free surface + basement membrane is the lab's three-part definition. All nutrition diffuses out of blood vessels in the connective tissue deep to the basement membrane — which is the single fact explaining why the outer layers of a stratified epithelium die. Option c describes connective tissue, the opposite arrangement: cells scattered in a matrix.

9Lab 5Block 5
  • lab manual

A stratified epithelium is named for the shape of which layer?

Answer: c

Named for the apical layer, not the basal one — which matters because in stratified squamous epithelium the basal cells are cuboidal and only flatten as they rise. That is also why the basal layer is the one that retains the ability to divide: it is the layer nearest the nutrition.

10Lab 5Block 5
  • lab manual

Which epithelium lines the bladder, and why that one?

Answer: a

Transitional epithelium lines the bladder, urethra and ureters, and its job is to let the urinary organs expand and stretch. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar is the trachea and Fallopian tubes — it only appears layered, being one layer packed so tightly the nuclei sit at different heights, and its cilia move mucus and trapped particles out.

11Lab 5Block 6
  • lab manual

Which connective tissue has collagen running in one direction, and where is it?

Answer: b

Dense regular packs collagen in a single direction, giving tensile strength along that one line — tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular runs collagen in multiple directions, to resist tearing from any of them: fascia, joint capsules and the dermis of the skin. Dense irregular is lab vocabulary — Chapter 4 does not make the regular/irregular distinction, though Whalen's deck does.

12Lab 5Block 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which two connective tissues are the exception to good blood supply?

Answer: d

Connective tissues typically have a very good blood supply — except dense connective tissue and cartilage, and that is why both have long healing times. Bone is the counter-example people reach for and it is wrong: bone is well vascularised and heals promptly. Blood is itself a fluid connective tissue.

13Lab 5Block 7
  • lab manual

You are looking at a slide of striated muscle with a single central nucleus per cell. What is it?

Answer: b

The lab gives a two-question decision tree. Striated or not? Not striated → smooth. If striated, where are the nuclei? Many, at the periphery → skeletal. One, central → cardiac. Put the tree on the sheet rather than three separate descriptions; it is faster and it is what a slide question actually needs.

14Lab 5Block 8
  • lab manual

On a nervous tissue slide, how do you recognise neuroglia?

Answer: b

Neurons appear as large branching cells with a single nucleus; neuroglia are significantly smaller, and you will generally only see their dark-staining nucleus. They outnumber neurons about ten to one. Option a describes the neuron; option d is cartilage.

15Lab 5Block 9
  • lab manual

Which epidermal layer is the only one that divides?

Answer: c

The stratum basale is the deepest — a single layer of keratinocytes, sitting on the basement membrane where the nutrition is, and the only layer that divides. When one divides, the cell on the membrane stays and the new cell is pushed outward. Melanocytes and Merkel cells are interspersed here too.

16Lab 5Block 9
  • lab manual

Put the epidermal strata in order from deepest to most superficial.

Answer: a

Basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum → corneum. Learn it from the bottom up, because that is the order a cell actually travels and it explains why it dies: the epidermis is avascular, so the further a cell gets from the basement membrane, the less nutrition reaches it. Option b is the same list read downward.

17Lab 5Block 9
  • lab manual

Which cell in the epidermis detects discriminative touch?

Answer: c

Merkel cells are modified receptors for sensory neurons and detect discriminative touch; they sit in the stratum basale, and the sensory neurons that connect to them are in the papillary layer of the dermis. Melanocytes in the same stratum make melanin and distribute it in granules to the keratinocytes above, protecting them from UV.

18Lab 5Block 9
  • lab manual

Which corpuscle detects deep pressure and vibration, and where is it?

Answer: b

Pacinian — deep pressure and vibration, in the reticular layer. Meissner — touch, in the papillary layer. Ruffini — stretch and body position, also in the reticular layer. The two dermal layers differ: papillary is superficial areolar connective tissue with the vessels that feed the epidermis; reticular is much thicker dense irregular connective tissue.

19Lab 5Block 9
  • lab manual

How do you know from a slide that you have reached the hypodermis?

Answer: c

Moving away from the epidermis, when you see significant amounts of adipocytes you are in the hypodermis. It is areolar connective tissue plus a significant amount of adipose, with the larger blood and lymph vessels that supply the dermal ones, and it is not actually part of the skin — it connects the skin to deeper tissues.

20Lab 5Block 10
  • lab manual

Which is true of thick skin?

Answer: b

Thick skin: palms and soles; no hairs, no oil glands; a stratum lucidum (so five layers); 15–30 layers of dead cells in the stratum corneum. Thin skin: everywhere else; four layers, no stratum lucidum; hair in most cases; few layers in the stratum corneum. Thick skin is the one without hair — which is the part people get backwards.

21Lab 5Block 11
  • lab manual

Hair and nails are both made of what, produced how?

Answer: c

Both are keratin developing from epithelial tissue, by the same mechanism as the epidermis: the deep layers divide, the cells are pushed away from the dividing line, die, and the keratin remains. The keratin is the same protein as in the epidermis — hair and nails simply have much more of it, which is what makes them hard. Hair originates in the hair follicle; nails from the dividing tissue of the nail root.

22Lab 5Block 11
  • lab manual

Which three glands does the lab ask you to identify, by name and by region?

Answer: a

Activity 6 section C, "Accessory Organs to the Skin", labels the sebaceous gland, the apocrine sweat gland and the eccrine sweat gland on the model, then asks which is found in the scalp, the axilla and the palm or sole. The Canvas activity tab names only the sebaceous gland, which is why this looked like a gap until the lab document was captured. Prepare all three by name and by region.

1Lab 5short answerBlocks 1–3
  • lab manual

Name the three planes of dissection and say what each separates. Then define the directional terms you would use to describe a lump on the front of the forearm, just above the wrist.

Model answer

Planes of dissection are imaginary lines drawn through an object, separating specific regions or sections — they matter for reading histology and diagnostic imaging, because they tell you where a structure sits in the picture. Sagittal runs longitudinally, head to feet, separating right from left; mid-sagittal is the sagittal cut that divides them into equal halves and is the midline that medial and lateral are measured against. Frontal (coronal) also runs head to feet but separates anterior from posterior. Transverse cuts across the width, separating superior from inferior — or, on a limb or tube, proximal from distal.
