The description: "the mass is on the right anterior antebrachium, just proximal to the carpal region." Anterior — toward the front. Antebrachial — the forearm region. Proximal — closer to the point of origin. Carpal — the wrist. Everything is stated relative to anatomical position, so it does not matter if the patient lifts the arm; the description is unchanged.

Three planes with the pair each separates, then the worked description. The two lab restrictions are worth adding: proximal and distal only on a limb or tubular structure, and intermediate references at least two other positions.

2Lab 5short answerBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the body cavities and their subdivisions, and say what divides each from the next.

Model answer

Dorsal body cavity → the cranial cavity, within the skull, holding the brain and brain-stem structures; and the vertebral (spinal) cavity, the remainder outside the cranial vault, holding the spinal cord. Ventral body cavity → the thoracic cavity and the abdominal and pelvic cavities. Inside the thoracic cavity, within the chest wall and surrounded by ribs: the pleural cavities holding the right and left lungs; the pericardial cavity holding the heart; and the mediastinum, holding the great vessels, trachea and esophagus — with the pericardial cavity sitting inside the mediastinum. What divides what: the diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal and pelvic cavities — a real physical sheet of muscle. The abdominal and pelvic cavities have no physical structure between them; the boundary is the superior aspect of the hip bones, the iliac crest. Below the iliac crest is the pelvic cavity — bladder, uterus and ovaries in the female, plus any gastrointestinal or urinary tract running into the region. Above it and below the diaphragm is the abdominal cavity — most of the digestive tract, spleen, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, kidneys and ureters.

Both main cavities with their subdivisions and contents, then the two boundaries with the crucial difference between them — one is a muscle, the other is a bony landmark with nothing in between. Getting those the wrong way round is the trap the block flags.

3Lab 5short answerBlock 9
  • lab manual

Describe the epidermis layer by layer, and explain why its outer cells are dead.

Model answer

The epidermis is the outermost layer of the skin, made of stratified squamous epithelial tissue — four layers, five in thick skin. Stratum basale — the deepest, a single layer of keratinocytes, and the only layer that divides; when a cell divides the one on the basement membrane stays and the new one is pushed outward. Melanocytes (making melanin, distributed in granules to the keratinocytes above to protect them from UV) and Merkel cells (modified sensory receptors for discriminative touch) are interspersed here. On UV exposure the basal keratinocytes also produce an inactive form of vitamin D, essential for calcium regulation. Stratum spinosum — multiple layers of keratinocytes. Stratum granulosum — 3–5 layers, granular from keratin granules accumulating as the cells begin to die; the cells start to flatten. Stratum lucidum — only in thick skin; remnants of dead keratinocytes, keratin and lipid, appearing translucent. Stratum corneum — most superficial, flattened angular dead keratinocytes. Why they die: epithelial tissue has no blood vessels. Nutrients diffuse from the dermis into the epidermis and wastes diffuse back; the layers furthest from the basement membrane receive very little nutrition, so they die. What they leave behind — keratin, granules and lipid membranes — is the barrier against pathogens and chemicals, the waterproof barrier against water loss, and the protection against physical trauma and abrasion.

Five strata in order with what happens at each, then the avascularity explanation. The strata names are lab-only vocabulary and the ordering question is nearly certain; the "why they die" paragraph is what converts a list into an answer.

4Lab 5short answerBlock 9
  • lab manual

Compare the papillary and reticular layers of the dermis, and say what the dermal papillae are for.

Model answer

The dermis lies deep to the epidermis and is a significant amount of loose and dense irregular connective tissue surrounding nerves, blood and lymph vessels, glands and follicles. Papillary layer — the superficial one, running from the basement membrane to the base of the papillae. It is areolar connective tissue with the blood vessels that exchange nutrients and wastes with the epidermis above. It contains the sensory neurons connecting to the Merkel cells and the Meissner corpuscles for touch. Reticular layer — dense irregular connective tissue, with blood vessels and glands. It is much thicker than the papillary layer and more dense with collagen and elastic fibres, and it contains Pacinian corpuscles (deep pressure and vibration) and Ruffini corpuscles (stretch and body position). Dermal papillae are the foldings between dermis and epidermis; they increase the surface area of the connection between the two layers — which matters because the epidermis has no vessels of its own and depends entirely on diffusion across that boundary.

Two layers with tissue type, thickness and the receptors each holds, then the papillae with their function. The three corpuscles are lab-only and are exactly the sort of thing a labelling question asks for.

5Lab 5short answerCoverage
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The lab's eleven printed topics do not cover everything on Whalen's Ch. 4 study guide. Which objectives have no board block behind them?

Model answer

Six, and they are all on the Ch. 4 tab rather than on the sheet. Cell junctions — tight, gap and adhesion, which the guide asks you to compare and contrast, with examples. The four membrane types — mucous, serous, synovial, cutaneous. Glands as a category — the endocrine / exocrine distinction; Block 11 covers the integument's glands, which is a different question. Skin colour and melanin — how melanin is produced and what it does; the lab's own graded summary questions ask for melanocytes, and no board topic prepares it. How keratin protects, and how lipid-soluble medications cross the skin. The whole of §4.3 — homeostasis: negative and positive feedback with examples, the three components of a homeostatic mechanism, and thermoregulation. The sharpest gap is positive feedback: the study guide asks for it with examples, alongside negative feedback — and it has no board block, and Lecture 3 covers negative feedback in detail and positive feedback not at all. Prepare the eleven blocks for the sheet; do not mistake the sheet for the chapter.

This is not a content question so much as a coverage check, and it is the one worth doing the night before: everything above is examinable and none of it is on the board sheet. If a question on positive feedback appears, nothing in this course's lectures or labs prepared it.

1Lab 5label the diagramPlanes and directional terms

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Mid-sagittal plane

    The sagittal cut that divides right and left into equal halves. This is the midline that medial and lateral are measured against.

  2. 2name it

    Frontal (coronal) plane

    Longitudinal, head to feet, separating anterior from posterior.

  3. 3name it

    Transverse plane

    Cross-wise across the width, separating superior from inferior — or, on a limb or tubular structure, proximal from distal.

  4. 4name it

    Brachial region

    The arm. Not to be confused with antebrachial, the forearm.

  5. 5name it

    Femoral region

    The thigh. Below it, patellar at the front of the knee and popliteal behind it, then crural (leg) and sural (calf).

  6. 6name it

    Crural region

    The leg — below the knee. Sural is the calf specifically, and tarsal the ankle.

  7. 7name it

    Superior

    Above. Its partner is inferior, below.

  8. 8name it

    Inferior

    Below. Directional terms always come in pairs, and everything is stated relative to anatomical position whatever the body is actually doing.

  9. 9name it

    Medial and lateral

    Medial — toward the midline. Lateral — away from it.

  10. 10name it

    Proximal

    Closer to the point of origin. Only usable on a limb or a tubular structure — the lab says so in a parenthesis, which is exactly the kind of restriction a lab exam tests.

  11. 11name it

    Distal

    Further from the point of origin. Same restriction.

2Lab 5label the diagramThe epidermal strata

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Stratum corneum

    The most superficial layer — flattened, angular, dead keratinocytes. 15–30 layers in thick skin, few in thin skin.

  2. 2name it

    Stratum lucidum

    Only in thick skin — palms and soles. Remnants of dead keratinocytes, keratin and lipid, appearing translucent.

  3. 3name it

    Stratum granulosum

    3–5 layers, granular in appearance from keratin granules accumulating as the cells begin to die from lack of nutrition. The cells start to flatten here.

  4. 4name it

    Stratum spinosum

    Multiple layers of keratinocytes, between the basale and the granulosum.

  5. 5name it

    Stratum basale

    The deepest — a single layer of keratinocytes, and the only layer that divides. When one divides, the cell on the basement membrane stays and the new cell is pushed outward.

  6. 6name it

    Basement membrane

    The boundary the epidermis sits on. Nutrients diffuse across it from the dermis, and wastes diffuse back.

  7. 7name it

    Keratinocyte

    The main cell of the epidermis. As it is pushed away from its supply it flattens, fills with keratin and dies — and what it leaves behind is the barrier against pathogens, the waterproofing, and the protection from abrasion.

  8. 8name it

    Melanocyte

    In the stratum basale. Produces melanin, distributed in granules to the keratinocytes above, protecting them from UV damage. Production increases in response to UV.

  9. 9name it

    Merkel cell

    Also in the stratum basale. A modified receptor for a sensory neuron, detecting discriminative touch.

  10. 10name it

    Dermis

    Below the basement membrane — and the layer with the blood vessels. That single fact is why the outer epidermal cells die, why tattoos are permanent, and why a blister forms between the two.

1Lab 5flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual

The three planes, and what each separates

Back

Sagittal → right / left. Frontal (coronal) → anterior / posterior. Transverse → superior / inferior (or proximal / distal). Mid-sagittal → equal right and left halves; the midline.

2Lab 5flashcardBlock 2
  • lab manual

Prone and supine

Back

Prone — lying face down. Supine — lying face up.

3Lab 5flashcardBlock 2
  • lab manual

Superficial / deep · proximal / distal

Back

Superficial — toward the surface. Deep — away from it. Proximal — closer to the point of origin. Distal — further from it. Proximal and distal are limb-and-tube only.

4Lab 5flashcardBlock 2
  • lab manual

Medial and lateral

Back

Medial — toward the midline. Lateral — away from it. The midline is the mid-sagittal plane.

5Lab 5flashcardBlock 3
  • lab manual

The five confusable regional pairs

Back

Antecubital (front of elbow) / olecranal (back). Brachial (arm) / antebrachial (forearm). Carpal (wrist) / tarsal (ankle). Crural (leg) / sural (calf). Pollex (thumb) / hallux (great toe).

6Lab 5flashcardBlock 3
  • lab manual

Regional terms — head and neck

Back

Frontal forehead · orbital/ocular eye · buccal cheek · otic ear · nasal nose · oral mouth · mental chin · cranial skull · facial face · cephalic head · cervical neck.

7Lab 5flashcardBlock 3
  • lab manual

Regional terms — trunk

Back

Thoracic chest · mammary breast · abdominal · umbilical navel · pelvic · inguinal groin · pubic · axillary armpit · dorsal back · lumbar loin · sacral · gluteal buttock · coxal hip · acromial shoulder.

8Lab 5flashcardBlock 3
  • lab manual

Regional terms — limbs

Back

Brachial arm · antecubital / olecranal elbow · antebrachial forearm · carpal wrist · manual / palmar hand and palm · femoral thigh · patellar / popliteal knee · crural leg · sural calf · tarsal ankle · calcaneal heel · pedal / plantar foot and sole.

9Lab 5flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The dorsal body cavity

Back

Cranial cavity — brain and brain-stem structures. Vertebral (spinal) cavity — the spinal cord.

10Lab 5flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual

Inside the thoracic cavity

Back

Pleural cavities — the lungs. Pericardial cavity — the heart. Mediastinum — great vessels, trachea, esophagus. The pericardial cavity sits within the mediastinum.

11Lab 5flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual

What divides the body cavities?

Back

Diaphragm — thoracic from abdominopelvic; a real physical sheet. Iliac crest — abdominal from pelvic; a bony landmark, with no membrane between them.

12Lab 5flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual

Epithelial tissue — the three-part definition

Back

Avascular (fed by diffusion from the connective tissue below) · a free surface · a basement membrane. Tightly packed cells with very little matrix.

13Lab 5flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual

Pseudostratified epithelium

Back

One layer that only appears layered — cells packed so tightly the nuclei sit at different levels. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar lines the trachea and Fallopian tubes; its cilia move mucus and particles out.

14Lab 5flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual

Transitional epithelium

Back

Bladder, urethra, ureters. It lets the urinary organs expand and stretch.

15Lab 5flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual

How is a stratified epithelium named?

Back

For the shape of its apical layer, not its basal one. Simple = one layer, stratified = more than one; shapes are squamous, cuboidal, columnar.

16Lab 5flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

The three connective tissue fibre types, as the lab describes them

Back

Reticular — thin, branching, dark; support and attachment. Elastic — thin coiled purple; elasticity. Collagen — thick, pink; strength and resistance to stretching. All made by fibroblasts.

17Lab 5flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

Dense regular vs dense irregular

Back

Regular — collagen in one direction; tendons and ligaments. Irregular — collagen in multiple directions; fascia, joint capsules, the dermis.

18Lab 5flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Areolar connective tissue

Back

Contains all three fibre types and all the cell types, loosely criss-crossed. Support and attachment in multiple directions — the universal packing material.

19Lab 5flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

Adipose tissue, on a slide

Back

Fat cells with very little matrix or fibres; the fat droplet pushes the nucleus to the periphery. White fat = one large droplet, brown fat = many small. Cushions, stores energy, insulates.

20Lab 5flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

Which connective tissues heal slowly, and why?

Back

Dense connective tissue and cartilage — the two exceptions to connective tissue's usually good blood supply.

21Lab 5flashcardBlock 7
  • lab manual

The muscle-slide decision tree

Back

Striated? No → smooth. Yes → where are the nuclei? Many, at the periphery → skeletal. One, central → cardiac.

22Lab 5flashcardBlock 8
  • lab manual

Neuron anatomy

Back

One cell body (soma) with the nucleus and mitochondria · multiple dendrites that receive and carry the impulse to the soma · one axon that carries it away, sometimes up to a metre.

23Lab 5flashcardBlock 8
  • lab manual

Neurons vs neuroglia on a slide

Back

Neurons — large branching cells with a single nucleus. Neuroglia — significantly smaller; usually only the dark-staining nucleus is visible. They outnumber neurons ten to one.

24Lab 5flashcardBlock 9
  • lab manual

The epidermal strata, deep to superficial

Back

Basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum → corneum. Four layers in thin skin; lucidum only in thick skin.

25Lab 5flashcardBlock 9
  • lab manual

Stratum basale

Back

A single layer of keratinocytes on the basement membrane — the only layer that divides. Holds the melanocytes and Merkel cells, and makes inactive vitamin D on UV exposure.

26Lab 5flashcardBlock 9
  • lab manual

Merkel cells

Back

Modified receptors for sensory neurons in the stratum basale; they detect discriminative touch.

27Lab 5flashcardBlock 9
  • lab manual

Papillary vs reticular dermis

Back

Papillary — superficial, areolar, holds the vessels feeding the epidermis, Meissner corpuscles (touch) and the neurons to the Merkel cells. Reticular — much thicker, dense irregular, holds Pacinian (deep pressure, vibration) and Ruffini (stretch, position) corpuscles.

28Lab 5flashcardBlock 9
  • lab manual

Dermal papillae

Back

Foldings between dermis and epidermis that increase the surface area of the connection — which matters because the epidermis is fed entirely by diffusion across it.

29Lab 5flashcardBlock 9
  • lab manual

How do you know you have reached the hypodermis?

Back

Significant amounts of adipocytes. It is areolar connective tissue plus adipose, holds the larger vessels supplying the dermis, and is not part of the skin.

30Lab 5flashcardBlock 10
  • lab manual

Thick skin vs thin skin — the three discriminators

Back

Stratum lucidum present? Hair present? How deep is the stratum corneum? Thick: palms and soles, five layers, no hair, no oil glands, 15–30 corneum layers. Thin: everywhere else, four layers, usually hair, few corneum layers.

31Lab 5flashcardBlock 11
  • lab manual

Hair follicle anatomy

Back

Shaft = medulla, cortex, cuticle. Follicle = inner and outer root sheath. Base = hair bulb, hair matrix (the dividing cells) and hair papilla. The arrector pili muscle and sebaceous gland attach to it.

32Lab 5flashcardBlock 11
  • lab manual

Nail anatomy

Back

Nail body · free edge · lunula · nail root · eponychium (proximal) · hyponychium (under the free edge) · proximal and lateral nail folds. Nails originate from the dividing tissue of the nail root.

33Lab 5flashcardBlock 11
  • lab manual

The three glands the lab wants, and their regions

Back

Sebaceous — scalp. Apocrine sweat — axilla. Eccrine sweat — palm and sole. From Activity 6 section C, "Accessory Organs to the Skin".

34Lab 5flashcardCoverage
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What the Lab 5 board sheet does not cover

Back

Cell junctions · the four membranes · endocrine vs exocrine glands · melanin and skin colour · keratin and transdermal absorption · all of homeostasis — including positive feedback, which no lecture covered either. All of it is on the Ch. 4 tab.

Lab 6 — Cellular Respiration & Digestive

Week 7 · study page · 22 multiple choice · 4 short answer · 31 flashcards · 1 diagrams, 11 labels

1Lab 6Boardwork topics
  • lab manual
  • lecture

The board sheet asks four things of each respiration phase. Which four?

Answer: a

That grid is the whole of Block 1 and it is printed four times on the sheet, once per phase. Whalen called the same thing a 10-point fill-in-the-blank story, and it is also the four Activity 1 tables and the graded summary table at the back of the lab document. Nothing else on this lab pays out three times.

2Lab 6Block 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Where does each phase happen? Which row is wrong?

Answer: c

The citric acid cycle is in the mitochondrial matrix, not the cytoplasm. Only glycolysis is cytoplasmic — and so is fermentation, entirely. The chain is the one embedded in the inner membrane, which is what lets it pump H+ into the intermembrane space.

3Lab 6Block 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Which phase produces no direct ATP and no CO2?

Answer: d

The chain makes no ATP directly — its 32 come through ATP synthase, driven by the H+ gradient, which is oxidative rather than substrate-level phosphorylation — and its product is water, not CO2. The transition reaction is the tempting answer: it makes no ATP at all, but it does release 2 CO2, so it fails the second half.

4Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 1
  • lab manual

What is substrate-level phosphorylation?

Answer: a

A phosphate already covalently attached to another molecule is transferred to ADP — one to one, catalysed by an enzyme. It is how glycolysis and the citric acid cycle make their ATP. Option b is oxidative phosphorylation, which is the chain and nothing else, and the lab names the two as a pair.

5Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Why does FADH2 yield less ATP than NADH?

Answer: b

NADH unloads at complex I; FADH2 unloads at complex II — and complex II does not contain a hydrogen ion pump. Fewer protons pumped means a smaller gradient and less ATP through ATP synthase. The lab states the complex II point explicitly, which is what makes it examinable here rather than in the chapter.

6Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 1
  • lab manual

Put the electron transport chain components in the order an electron meets them.

Answer: a

NADH hands electrons to complex I; mobile Q carries them to complex III; mobile cytochrome c carries them to complex IV; complex IV hands them to oxygen, making water. FADH2 joins at complex II, which feeds Q — bypassing complex I's proton pump, and that is why it is worth less.

7Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

What happens to the lactate produced during anaerobic respiration in muscle?

Answer: c

Reducing pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep going — that is the point of it, not the 2 ATP. The lactate is then carried to the liver and recycled back to pyruvate. Whalen and the chapter agree; the lab's Activity 1 says the same thing in the Fate of Pyruvate paragraph.

8Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 2
  • lab manual

What are the four basic functions of the digestive system?

Answer: a

The lab opens Activity 2 with exactly these four: ingestion — taking in food and nutrients; digestion — breaking macromolecules down to their monomers; absorption — moving small molecules from the lumen into the body; excretion — expelling the waste. The distractors all mix in real processes that are not on the list of four.

9Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 2
  • lab manual

The mucosa has three sublayers. Which?

Answer: b

Epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae — the lab's breakdown of the innermost layer. The lamina propria carries the small blood vessels, glands and lymphatic tissue, which is what distinguishes it from the submucosa beneath, whose vessels are larger. Whalen excused the muscularis mucosae from Bio 5 testing, but the lab prints it.

10Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 2
  • lab manual

When does the GI tract wall have a serosa rather than an adventitia?

Answer: b

Serosa — areolar connective tissue covered by a layer of epithelium — surrounds the tract inside the abdominal cavity and holds it in place. Adventitia has a similar function outside the abdominal cavity, but is comprised only of connective tissue — no epithelium. One or the other, never both, and the deciding factor is location.

11Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which layer is responsible for segmentation and peristalsis, and how is it arranged?

Answer: c

Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle. Circular contraction constricts; longitudinal contraction shortens the tube. Together they segment (mix) and peristalse (propel). The stomach is the exception, with an additional oblique layer innermost, which is what lets it store and churn as well as propel.

12Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of these is not an accessory organ to the digestive tract?

Answer: d

The duodenum is part of the GI tract itself — the first region of the small intestine. The accessory organs are salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas: they are attached to the tract by ducts and release secretions that aid digestion, but food never passes through them.

13Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 3
  • lab manual

Which pancreatic cells make the digestive enzymes, and which make the bicarbonate?

Answer: a

Acinar cells → lipase, amylase, nucleases and proteases. Ductal cells → bicarbonate, which raises the pH of the chyme in the duodenum so those enzymes work and the small intestine is not damaged. The islets of Langerhans are the endocrine side entirely — insulin, glucagon and somatostatin into the blood.

14Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Bile emulsifies fat. Which kind of digestion is that, and why does it matter?

Answer: b

Emulsification is mechanical digestion: it breaks a large fat globule into small ones, which increases the surface area so lipase — a water-soluble enzyme that can only act at a surface — has somewhere to work. Bile is not an enzyme and splits nothing. It is made by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released when CCK arrives.

15Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where does all the blood leaving the digestive tract go first, and by what route?

Answer: b

All of the blood from the digestive tract goes first to the liver through the hepatic portal vein, so the liver processes the nutrients before they are delivered to the rest of the body. The exception is lipids, which enter the lacteals as chylomicrons and travel by lymph — too large for a capillary.

16Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual

Which cell type secretes hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?

Answer: b

The lab gives four gastric cell types: parietal → HCl and intrinsic factor · chief → pepsinogen and gastric lipase · G cells → gastrin, a hormone · mucous cells → mucus. Intrinsic factor matters downstream — B12 is too large to diffuse and needs it, plus specific transporters in the ileum, to be absorbed.

17Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual

What activates trypsinogen, and where?

Answer: c

Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) is produced by the duodenal enterocytes — part of the intestinal brush border — and activates trypsin when trypsinogen arrives. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen in a positive feedback and also activates the other pancreatic proteases. Option a is the stomach's parallel: HCl activating pepsinogen into pepsin.

18Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual

Why are the pancreatic proteases released in an inactive form?

Answer: b

The lab says it outright: the proteases are released in inactive forms and this is very important to prevent the pancreatic enzymes from digesting the pancreas as they are produced. The same logic explains pepsinogen in the stomach. Activation happens only after they arrive in the duodenum and meet enterokinase.

19Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which enzyme's products are individual amino acids rather than shorter peptides?

Answer: d

Carboxypeptidase is the row that finishes the job — it takes amino acids off the carboxyl end of a peptide, giving individual amino acids. Pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin all stop at polypeptides or smaller fragments. The brush-border aminopeptidase works from the amino end and dipeptidase splits dipeptides.

20Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual

Where is most absorption in the small intestine, and what is the ileum's special job?

Answer: b

Most water and nutrient absorption occurs in the jejunum. Vitamin B12 is the exception — very large, so it must be absorbed with intrinsic factor, through specific transporters in the ileum. The duodenum is where the chyme arrives and is neutralised and enzymatically worked on, not the main absorptive site.

21Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which vitamins are absorbed along with lipids?

Answer: b

Lipid-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed along with the lipids — so anything that blocks fat absorption blocks them too. Most water-soluble vitamins are absorbed through simple diffusion, and B12 is the exception to the exception, needing intrinsic factor and its own transporters.

22Lab 6Lab 6 Activity 4
  • lab manual

The lab prints an enzyme table for nucleic acids. Which enzymes are on it?

Answer: a

Brush border: nucleosidases and phosphatases, breaking nucleotides into phosphates, nitrogenous bases and pentoses. Pancreatic acinar cells: nucleases — ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease. This matters because Table 15.2 of the chapter has no nuclease row at all, while Table 15.3, both lectures and this lab all include nucleic acid digestion. The lab exam wants them.

1Lab 6short answerBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fill in the four-phase grid: for each phase of cellular respiration, give its location, its ins and outs, its direct ATP, and its electron carriers.

Model answer

Glycolysis. Location: cytoplasm. In: 1 glucose (6C) + 2 ATP. Out: 2 pyruvate (3C). Direct ATP: 4 made, 2 spent — net 2. Carriers: 2 NADH. Oxygen not required. Transition reaction. Location: mitochondrion (matrix). In: 2 pyruvate + 2 CoA. Out: 2 acetyl-CoA + 2 CO2. Direct ATP: none. Carriers: 2 NADH. Citric acid cycle. Location: mitochondrion (matrix). In: 2 acetyl-CoA. Out: 4 CO2. Direct ATP: 2, by substrate-level phosphorylation. Carriers: 6 NADH + 2 FADH2. Electron transport chain. Location: inner mitochondrial membrane. In: 10 NADH + 2 FADH2 + O2. Out: H2O. Direct ATP: none directly — 32 via ATP synthase. Carriers: where they unload. Oxygen required. Total: 2 + 2 + 32 = 36 ATP per glucose.

The grid is the answer, and every cell of it is worth something. The four things the sheet asks for are exactly the four rows. Whalen's number for the chain is 32, not 34 — he said so explicitly for the exam.

2Lab 6short answerBlock 3 / Activity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Draw and describe the four layers of the GI tract wall, from the lumen outward.

Model answer

Mucosa — the inner layer lining the lumen, with three sublayers: epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae. It is responsible mainly for mucous secretions, protection, digestive secretions and absorption, and it varies along the tract to suit the job of each region. The lamina propria carries small blood vessels, glands and lymphatic tissue. Submucosa — connective tissue with larger blood vessels, glands and nerves, responsible for local secretions on a wider scale. Muscularis — generally two layers of smooth muscle, inner circular and outer longitudinal, producing segmentation (mixing) and peristalsis (propulsion). The stomach is the exception: it has a third, obliquely oriented layer inside the circular one, which is what lets it store and churn as well as propel. Serosa or adventitia — serosa is areolar connective tissue covered by epithelium, found inside the abdominal cavity, surrounding the tract and holding it in place. Adventitia does the same job outside the abdominal cavity but is connective tissue only, with no epithelium.

Four layers in order with a function each. The two lab-specific details that earn extra: the mucosa's three sublayers, and serosa versus adventitia decided by whether the stretch is inside the abdominal cavity. The stomach's third muscle layer is the other near-certain mark.

3Lab 6short answerBlock 4 / Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the accessory organs of digestion — where each is, what it secretes, and where that secretion acts.

Model answer

Salivary glands. Sublingual inside the oral cavity, submandibular and parotid adjacent to it. They secrete saliva — water, mucus, ions, glycoproteins, enzymes and antibodies — which moistens the food for mechanical and chemical digestion and carries salivary amylase, starting carbohydrate digestion in the mouth. It works until denatured by the low pH of the stomach. Liver. Inferior to the diaphragm, in the superior aspect of the abdominal cavity. It produces bile, stored in the gallbladder, which emulsifies lipids — mechanical digestion — so lipase can reach them. All blood leaving the digestive tract reaches the liver first by the hepatic portal vein, so it processes the nutrients before the rest of the body sees them; it also handles detoxification, lipid synthesis, glucose regulation and protein synthesis. Gallbladder. Inferior to the liver, on the right. It stores and concentrates bile and releases it when CCK signals that lipids have arrived; the cystic duct joins the hepatic duct to form the common bile duct, which meets the pancreatic duct and empties into the duodenum. Pancreas. Inferior and posterior to the stomach. Exocrine: acinar cells secrete lipase, amylase, nucleases and proteases, and ductal cells secrete bicarbonate, which raises the pH of the chyme so those enzymes can work and the duodenum is not damaged. Endocrine: the islets of Langerhans release insulin, glucagon and somatostatin into the bloodstream for glucose regulation.

Four organs, each with location, secretion and site of action. The pancreas's exocrine/endocrine split, the bicarbonate's purpose, and the hepatic portal vein are the three lab-specific details that separate a full answer from a textbook one.

4Lab 6short answerBlock 5 / Activity 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Take one macromolecule of your choice and trace its digestion from mouth to absorption, naming every enzyme.

Model answer

Carbohydrate. Mouth: teeth break the food into smaller pieces and the tongue mashes it; salivary amylase begins breaking polysaccharides into disaccharides and trisaccharides. It works best around pH 6.5 and keeps working inside the swallowed bolus. Stomach: the pH is too low, so salivary amylase becomes inactive; mechanical digestion continues with the churning, and chemical digestion of carbohydrate stops. Small intestine: pancreatic amylase is released from the acinar cells into the duodenum and breaks the remaining polysaccharides into α-dextrins, disaccharides and trisaccharides. The intestinal cells then release the brush-border enzymes for the final break to monosaccharides: α-dextrinase (α-dextrins → glucose), maltase (maltose → glucose), sucrase (sucrose → glucose + fructose) and lactase (lactose → glucose + galactose). Absorption: the monosaccharides — glucose, galactose and fructose — are absorbed mainly in the jejunum, crossing the enterocyte and entering the capillary in the villus, then travelling by the hepatic portal vein to the liver. The surface that makes it possible: large circular folds, villi, and microvilli on the enterocytes.

Follow one macromolecule the whole way and name every enzyme with its source and product. The three brush-border enzymes are the ones the lectures skipped and the lab prints; monosaccharides are the only carbohydrate form that can be absorbed is the sentence to end on.

1Lab 6label the diagramThe four layers of the GI tract wall

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Lumen

    The hollow space the food is actually in. Nothing in here is inside you until it crosses the wall.

  2. 2name it

    Epithelium

    The innermost sublayer of the mucosa, facing the lumen. Where absorption happens, and where the villi and microvilli are in the small intestine.

  3. 3name it

    Lamina propria

    The middle sublayer of the mucosa — connective tissue carrying the small blood vessels, glands and lymphatic tissue.

  4. 4name it

    Muscularis mucosae

    The outermost sublayer of the mucosa, separating it from the submucosa. Whalen named it and then excused it from Bio 5 testing — but the lab prints it, so know it for the lab paper.

  5. 5name it

    Mucosa

    The whole inner layer — epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae. Mucous secretions, protection, digestive secretions and absorption. It varies along the tract to suit each region.

  6. 6name it

    Submucosa

    Connective tissue carrying the larger blood vessels, glands and nerves — secretions on a wider scale than the mucosa's local ones.

  7. 7name it

    Circular muscle

    The inner layer of the muscularis. Contracting, it constricts the tube — this is segmentation, which mixes.

  8. 8name it

    Longitudinal muscle

    The outer layer of the muscularis. Contracting, it shortens the tube — this is peristalsis, which propels.

  9. 9name it

    Muscularis

    Both muscle layers together. The stomach is the exception with three — an extra oblique layer innermost, which is what lets it churn.

  10. 10name it

    Serosa

    Areolar connective tissue covered by a layer of epithelium, wrapping the tract and holding it in place. Only inside the abdominal cavity.

  11. 11name it

    Adventitia

    The same job outside the abdominal cavity, but connective tissue only — no epithelium. One or the other, never both.

1Lab 6flashcardBoardwork topics
  • lab manual

The four things the board sheet asks of each respiration phase

Back

Location · ins and outs · direct ATP produced · electron carriers. Printed four times, once per phase.

2Lab 6flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Glycolysis — the board row

Back

Cytoplasm. In: glucose (6C) + 2 ATP. Out: 2 pyruvate. Direct ATP: net 2 (4 made, 2 spent). Carriers: 2 NADH. No oxygen needed.

3Lab 6flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Transition reaction — the board row

Back

Mitochondrial matrix. In: 2 pyruvate + 2 CoA. Out: 2 acetyl-CoA + 2 CO2. Direct ATP: none. Carriers: 2 NADH.

4Lab 6flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Citric acid cycle — the board row

Back

Mitochondrial matrix. In: 2 acetyl-CoA. Out: 4 CO2. Direct ATP: 2. Carriers: 6 NADH + 2 FADH2.

5Lab 6flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Electron transport chain — the board row

Back

Inner mitochondrial membrane. In: 10 NADH + 2 FADH2 + O2. Out: H2O. Direct ATP: none — 32 via ATP synthase. It is where the carriers unload.

6Lab 6flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

Substrate-level vs oxidative phosphorylation

Back

Substrate-level — an enzyme transfers a phosphate already attached to another molecule onto ADP; glycolysis and the cycle. Oxidative — the H+ gradient drives ATP synthase; the chain only.

7Lab 6flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

The chain, component by component

Back

NADH → complex I. FADH2 → complex II. Mobile Q then complex III, mobile cytochrome c then complex IV, which hands the electron to oxygen, making water.

8Lab 6flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

Why is FADH2 worth less than NADH?

Back

It enters at complex II, which has no H+ pump — so fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made.

9Lab 6flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

Chemiosmosis, in one line

Back

H+ is pumped into the intermembrane space against its gradient; it returns through ATP synthase, and that is the ATP. Steeper gradient → faster ATP.

10Lab 6flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The fate of pyruvate

Back

Aerobic — into the mitochondrion for the transition reaction. Anaerobic — reduced to lactate in the cytosol, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis continues; net 2 ATP, and the lactate goes to the liver to be recycled to pyruvate.

11Lab 6flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

The four basic digestive functions

Back

Ingestion · digestion · absorption · excretion.

12Lab 6flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

The mucosa's three sublayers

Back

Epithelium · lamina propria · muscularis mucosae. The lamina propria carries the small vessels, glands and lymphatic tissue.

13Lab 6flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

Submucosa

Back

Connective tissue with the larger blood vessels, glands and nerves — secretions on a wider scale than the mucosa's local ones.

14Lab 6flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

Serosa vs adventitia

Back

Serosa — areolar connective tissue covered by epithelium; inside the abdominal cavity. Adventitia — connective tissue only; outside it. Same job: wrap the tract and hold it in place.

15Lab 6flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The stomach's extra muscle layer

Back

An oblique layer of smooth muscle inside the circular layer — only the stomach has it, and it is what lets the stomach store and churn, not just propel.

16Lab 6flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual

The four accessory organs

Back

Salivary glands · liver · gallbladder · pancreas. Attached to the tract by ducts; they secrete into it but food never passes through them.

17Lab 6flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual

The pancreas — exocrine and endocrine

Back

Exocrine: acinar cells → enzymes (lipase, amylase, nucleases, proteases); ductal cells → bicarbonate, raising the chyme's pH. Endocrine: islets of Langerhans → insulin, glucagon, somatostatin into the blood.

18Lab 6flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Hepatic portal vein

Back

Carries all the blood leaving the digestive tract to the liver first, so the liver processes the nutrients before the body sees them. Lipids are the exception — they go by lymph.

19Lab 6flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual

The bile duct route

Back

Hepatic duct (liver) + cystic duct (gallbladder) → common bile duct → meets the pancreatic duct → duodenum.

20Lab 6flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What releases bile, and what does bile do?

Back

CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction. Bile's bile salts emulsify lipids — mechanical digestion — breaking globules into droplets so lipase has surface area.

21Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

The four gastric cell types

Back

Parietal → HCl + intrinsic factor. Chief → pepsinogen + gastric lipase. G cells → gastrin. Mucous cells → mucus.

22Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

Two zymogens and their activators

Back

Pepsinogen → pepsin, by HCl, pH 2. **Trypsinogen → trypsin, by enterokinase** from the duodenal brush border, pH 7.5. Each then activates more of itself.

23Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

Why are proteases secreted inactive?

Back

To stop them digesting the gland that made them — the pancreas, or the stomach lining.

24Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

The brush-border enzymes

Back

α-dextrinase · maltase · sucrase · lactase (carbohydrates) · nucleosidases and phosphatases (nucleotides) · enterokinase (activates trypsinogen) · aminopeptidase and dipeptidase (peptides). Made and used in the small intestine.

25Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

The pancreatic enzymes

Back

Pancreatic amylase · pancreatic lipase · trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidase · nucleases (ribonuclease, deoxyribonuclease). All from the acinar cells.

26Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which enzyme finishes protein digestion?

Back

Carboxypeptidase — its products are individual amino acids, from the carboxyl end. Trypsin and chymotrypsin stop at fragments; aminopeptidase works the amino end and dipeptidase splits dipeptides.

27Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

The two lipases before the pancreas

Back

Lingual lipase from the lingual glands, and gastric lipase from the chief cells — both act on triglycerides, both only a little, because lipids clump and the environment is watery.

28Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

Where does absorption actually happen?

Back

Most in the jejunum. Water mostly in the small intestine, some in the large. Minerals and electrolytes by active transport in both. B12 in the ileum, with intrinsic factor and specific transporters.

29Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which vitamins ride in with the lipids?

Back

Fat-soluble A, D, E and K. Water-soluble vitamins cross by simple diffusion — except B12, which is too large.

30Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual

What is absorbed, by macromolecule

Back

Carbohydrates → monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose). Proteins → single amino acids, dipeptides, tripeptides. Triglycerides → monoacylglycerides, glycerol, free fatty acids. Nucleic acids → pentose sugars, phosphates, nitrogenous bases.

31Lab 6flashcardActivity 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The nuclease question

Back

Table 15.2 of the chapter has no nuclease row — but Table 15.3, both lectures and the lab's own Activity 4 table all include nucleic acid digestion. The lab exam wants nucleosidases, phosphatases and the pancreatic nucleases.

Lab 7 — Skeletal

Week 8 · study page · 23 multiple choice · 5 short answer · 32 flashcards · 1 diagrams, 9 labels

1Lab 7Block 1
  • lab manual

Which four bone structures does the topic list name?

Answer: b

The lab's four bone terms are not the chapter's four bone terms. The sheet asks for diaphysis, epiphysis, medullary cavity and epiphyseal plate; Chapter 5 calls the first three the shaft, the ends or heads, and the marrow cavity, and only epiphyseal plate appears under the lab's own name. Use the lab's words on the sheet — option a is the same four structures in the textbook's vocabulary.

2Lab 7Block 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is in the medullary cavity of an adult long bone?

Answer: c

Yellow marrow — fat, for energy storage — fills the medullary cavity of the shaft in an adult. Red marrow is in the spongy bone of the epiphyses and of flat bones (ribs, pelvis, backbone, skull, sternum), and it is where blood cells form. Location alone answers the question, which is exactly how the board topic frames it.

3Lab 7Block 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which structure carries the cells for bone growth and repair?

Answer: c

The periosteum is the membrane over compact bone. It carries blood vessels, nerves, and the cells for growth and repair — the osteoprogenitor cells of its inner cellular layer, which become the fibroblasts and osteoblasts of a fracture repair. It is also why most of the pain from a bruised or broken bone is periosteum.

4Lab 7Block 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What actually happens at the epiphyseal plate to lengthen a bone?

Answer: b

The plate's cartilage cells divide and force the end farther from the shaft, while bone replaces the older cartilage nearer the shaft — so the bone gets longer from the middle of the plate outward. It fuses and lengthening stops at about 18 in females and 21 in males; after that a bone can still widen but not lengthen.

5Lab 7Block 2
  • lab manual
  • lecture

What makes a structure an osteon?

Answer: b

The osteon is the microscopic repeating structural unit of compact bone — mature bone cells in concentric rings around a central canal. Option a is the trap: osteocytes in lacunae are present in spongy bone too, so that feature cannot distinguish them. The central canal is the discriminator, and drawing it is what Activity 1 asks for.

6Lab 7Block 2
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

How does an osteocyte several rings out get fed?

Answer: b

Tiny canals — canaliculi — connect nearby lacunae and eventually the central canal, and osteocytes send projections through them to touch neighbouring cells, so nutrients, oxygen and wastes pass cell to cell to and from the vessels in the canal. Canaliculi is the lab's word for a structure Chapter 5 describes without naming — it is tagged (n) on the sheet for that reason.

7Lab 7Block 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What would a bone be like with its collagen removed but its minerals intact?

Answer: b

Hardness comes from the mineral salts — mainly calcium and phosphorus. Resilience comes from the collagen. Take the collagen and you keep hardness but lose resilience: brittle and crumbly, like chalk. Options a and d are the other half of the pair — what happens when the minerals go, which is rickets.

8Lab 7Block 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Compact and spongy bone differ in what?

Answer: c

Arrangement, not composition. Compact bone is densely packed with osteons and has few internal spaces; spongy bone is a latticework of tiny beams and thin plates with open areas between. Both are hardened by calcium and phosphorus and both contain osteocytes in lacunae. This is the chapter's own end-of-chapter question and the lab's callout.

9Lab 7Block 3
  • lab manual

What are the three things spongy bone does?

Answer: a

Strength without weight — the lattice braces along the lines of stress using a fraction of the material solid bone would need. Houses red marrow, so it is where blood cell production happens. Absorbs and distributes force arriving at the joint surface, spreading it into the shaft rather than letting it land on one point. Yellow marrow and the shaft wall belong to the other two structures.

10Lab 7Block 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pair of bones makes up the pectoral girdle?

Answer: b

Scapulae and clavicles. Each clavicle forms a relatively rigid bridge between a scapula and the sternum, and one corner of the roughly triangular scapula carries the socket that takes the humerus. The humerus is the limb bone, not part of the girdle, and the sternum is axial.

11Lab 7Block 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which girdle is more rigid, and what does that buy?

Answer: d

The pelvic girdle is much more rigid than the pectoral girdle, because it carries the body's weight into the legs: the two pelvic bones attach behind to the sacrum and meet in front at the cartilage disk of the pubic symphysis. The pectoral girdle is loose by design, which is what gives the shoulder its range. The trade-off between them is the point of the topic.

12Lab 7Block 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What are the two ways the lab gives for sexing a skeleton?

Answer: b

The clavicles are more curved in males than in females, and the opening of the pelvic girdle is wider in the female, to facilitate childbirth. Both are stated outright in the same section, which is unusual enough that a question is likely. Nothing in the source supports the other three pairs.

13Lab 7Block 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In carpal tunnel syndrome, what is compressed and by what?

Answer: a

The tunnel carries a nerve — controlling sensation in the fingers and some hand muscles — plus tendons. Repetitive motion inflames the tendons so that they press against the nerve, giving numbness or tingling in the hand and pain in wrist, hand and fingers. The tendons inflame; the nerve is what hurts. A question asking what is compressed wants the nerve.

14Lab 7Block 5
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

The vertebral column has how many of each?

Answer: a

26 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum (5 fused), 1 coccyx (4 fused). Whalen's mnemonic is breakfast, lunch and dinner — 7, 12, 5. Every wrong option is those same three numbers reordered, which is exactly how the question gets set. The sacrum fuses for strength where the column meets the pelvic girdle.

15Lab 7Block 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which is the correct count for the skull?

Answer: b

8 cranial — frontal, 2 parietal, occipital, 2 temporal, sphenoid, ethmoid — and 14 facial, including the maxillae, mandible, zygomatics, nasals, lacrimals and vomer. Option a is the pair reversed. The counts are the most testable thing in this block, along with 80 axial bones and 12 rib pairs, the upper 10 reaching the sternum.

16Lab 7Block 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture

A disk bulges outward against a spinal nerve. What follows?

Answer: b

Direction decides the symptom. Outward presses a spinal nerve and causes great pain — the sciatic nerve down the back of the leg is the one most often affected, giving sciatica. Inward presses the spinal cord, interfering with muscle control and the perception of incoming stimuli — which is option a. And the disk never slips: it bulges.

17Lab 7Block 6
  • lab manual

The lab classifies joints functionally. Which term means "freely mobile"?

Answer: c

Synarthrosis — immobile or nearly so. Amphiarthrosis — limited movement. Diarthrosis — freely mobile. These three words are the lab's functional classification and they do not appear in Chapter 5 at all, which classifies joints only structurally as fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial. A symphysis is a structural subtype of cartilaginous joint, not a functional class.

18Lab 7Block 6
  • lab manual

Which pairing of functional class to example is right?

Answer: c

Amphiarthrosis — between the vertebrae, where the fibrocartilage intervertebral disk cushions and allows a small amount of flexibility; structurally it is a symphysis. Synarthrosis is the skull sutures, the manubrium-to-sternum joint, and the tooth in its socket held by the periodontal ligament. Diarthrosis is most of the appendicular skeleton — knee, elbow, shoulder, hip.

19Lab 7Block 6
  • lab manual

Which are the only ball-and-socket joints in the body?

Answer: a

The hip and shoulder — the lab says outright these are the only ball-and-socket joints in the body and that they move in all planes. Elbow and knee are hinges, moving in one plane. The wrist is condyloid — the radiocarpal joint. Of the six synovial types, the ones with a single named example each are worth keeping: pivot (C1–C2), saddle (thumb, trapezium to metacarpal 1), plane (between the tarsals).

20Lab 7Block 6
  • lab manual

Which synovial joint type allows rotation around an axis, and where is the lab's example?

Answer: b

A pivot joint allows rotation around an axis, and the lab's example is between the first and second cervical vertebrae — the side-to-side rotation of the head. Saddle is the trapezium to first metacarpal, at the base of the thumb; plane joints give limited gliding, as between the tarsals; hinge works like a door hinge.

21Lab 7Block 6
  • lab manual

In which plane does abduction occur, and what does it do?

Answer: b

Abduction moves a body part away from the midline, in the coronal (medial–lateral) plane — the limb or hand laterally away from the body, or spreading the fingers or toes. Adduction is its partner, moving toward or across the midline. Flexion and extension are the sagittal pair. The planes are the lab's addition; Figure 5.14 gives the movements without them.

22Lab 7Block 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The lab defines flexion as narrowing the joint space; the textbook says it decreases the angle between the bones. What should you conclude?

Answer: c

Narrowing the joint space and decreasing the angle between the bones are the same thing — the apparent conflict softens completely on reading, which is the test the course's conventions set for whether something is a real conflict. Use whichever wording the question invites. Note also that for the head and vertebral column, anterior bending is flexion and any posterior-going movement is extension.

23Lab 7Block 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which movements does the lab's list omit that Figure 5.14 supplies?

Answer: c

Figure 5.14 gives eight movements with the textbook's definitions — including supination and pronation, which the lab never mentions. What the lab's Activity 4 adds instead is what the figure lacks: the sagittal and coronal planes, medial versus lateral (internal versus external) rotation, and the named joints each movement occurs at. Learn the union of the two — that is the whole topic.

1Lab 7short answerBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Name the six functions of bone and the four structures of a long bone the board sheet asks for.

Model answer

The six functions. Support — a rigid framework holding soft tissues; the leg bones and backbone hold the body upright, and the pelvic girdle supports the abdominal organs. Movement — attachment points for muscles, so bones move at joints when muscles contract. Protection — heart and lungs in the chest cavity, brain in the skull. Mineral storage — particularly calcium and phosphorus, released to the body when needed. Fat storage — energy-rich fat in the yellow marrow. Blood cell production — in the red marrow. The four structures, in the lab's own vocabulary. Diaphysis — the shaft, mostly compact bone. Epiphysis — the enlarged end, mostly spongy bone under a compact shell, capped with cartilage where it glides on another bone. Medullary cavity — the space inside the shaft, holding yellow marrow in an adult. Epiphyseal plate — the cartilage growth plate between epiphysis and diaphysis; its cartilage cells divide and force the end farther from the shaft while bone replaces the older cartilage nearer the shaft, and it fuses at about 18 in females and 21 in males. Add the periosteum, the membrane over compact bone carrying blood vessels, nerves and the cells for growth and repair — and the source of most of the pain from a bruise or break.

Six functions and four structures, in the lab's words rather than the chapter's. The vocabulary gap is real — Chapter 5 says shaft, ends and marrow cavity — and the sheet asks for the formal terms.

2Lab 7short answerBlock 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture

Describe the structure of compact bone, and explain how its cells are kept alive.

Model answer

Compact bone is very dense, with few internal spaces. It forms most of the diaphysis of a long bone and the outer shell everywhere else. Its microscopic repeating structural unit is the osteon: mature bone cells — osteocytes — arranged in concentric rings of matrix around a central canal, which carries a blood vessel. Each osteocyte lies in a lacuna, a small space in the hardened matrix. Tiny canals — canaliculi — connect nearby lacunae and eventually reach the central canal, and osteocytes send projections through them to touch their neighbours, so nutrients, oxygen and wastes pass cell to cell to and from the vessels in the canal. What the matrix is made of: hardness from mineral salts, mainly calcium and phosphorus; resilience from collagen, a strong elastic protein woven through it. Without the mineral salts bone would be rubbery like a garden hose; without collagen it would be brittle and crumbly like chalk. What it does: bears weight and compression, which is why it is thickest along the shaft where the load runs; and provides the attachment surface for tendons and ligaments.

This is Activity 1's whole drawing turned into prose — osteon, central canal, concentric rings, osteocyte, lacuna, canaliculi, blood vessel. The two-component matrix with both failure similes is the other half, and it is the same question the chapter asks.

3Lab 7short answerBlocks 2–3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Compare compact and spongy bone: what each is, where it is, and what it does.

Model answer

Compact bone. Very dense with few internal spaces, packed with osteons. Found in most of the diaphysis and as the outer shell of every bone. It bears weight and compression, which is why it is thickest along the shaft where the load runs, and it provides the attachment surface for tendons and ligaments. Spongy bone. A latticework of tiny beams and thin plates — trabeculae — with open areas between, bracing the bone from within. Found in small flat bones such as most of the skull, and in the epiphyses and near the ends of the shafts of long bones. It does three things: strength without weight, bracing along the lines of stress with a fraction of the material solid bone would need; housing red marrow in its open spaces, so it is where blood cells are formed; and absorbing and distributing force arriving at the joint surface, spreading it into the shaft rather than letting it land on one point. They differ in arrangement, not composition — both are hardened by calcium and phosphorus, and both hold osteocytes in lacunae. Say where each one is as well as what it is: a question that gives you a location is asking which kind of bone. And spongy bone is where remodeling shows first — weight-bearing thickens it, disuse thins it, and osteoporosis is that balance tipped the wrong way; the lattice is what thins.

Two topics on the sheet, and the exam will treat them as a pair. The framing that earns marks is arrangement, not composition, followed by location and by three functions each.

4Lab 7short answerBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Classify joints structurally and functionally, and map the two systems onto each other.

Model answer

Joints are the locations where bones come together with other bones or cartilage, and they are classified two ways. Structurally — by what holds them together. Fibrous: fibrous tissue between the bones, no joint cavity, little or no movement — the sutures of the adult skull. Cartilaginous: fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage between the bones, none to slight movement — between the vertebrae, the ribs to the sternum, and the pubic symphysis. Synovial: a capsule enclosing a fluid-filled cavity, reinforced by ligaments; freely movable, and most joints of the body. Functionally — by how much the joint moves. Synarthrosis: immobile or nearly so, providing stability where that protects what is underneath — structurally fibrous or cartilaginous; examples are the skull sutures, the manubrium-to-sternum joint, and the tooth held by the periodontal ligament. Amphiarthrosis: limited movement — stability with a small degree of flexibility; structurally cartilaginous; the example is between the vertebrae, where the intervertebral disk cushions and allows some flexibility in the spine. Diarthrosis: freely mobile; structurally synovial; most of the appendicular skeleton — knee, elbow, shoulder, hip. The mapping: fibrous and cartilaginous joints are synarthroses or amphiarthroses; every diarthrosis is a synovial joint. The lab's objective asks for the functional three, and those three words are not in Chapter 5 at all.

Both classifications with an example each, then the mapping between them. The functional triad is lab-only vocabulary and is what the activity's own objective names — a structural-only answer would miss the question being asked.

5Lab 7short answerBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe everything a synovial joint contains, and how such a joint fails.

Model answer

Hyaline cartilage covers the articular surfaces — the areas where the bones may come into contact — reducing friction and damage to the bone and protecting against compressive forces. A two-layered capsule, whose inner layer, the synovial membrane, secretes viscous clear synovial fluid into the joint cavity, which lubricates and cushions. Ligaments — strong straps of dense regular connective tissue that hold the bones together, support the joint and direct the movement; because synovial joints are freely movable, the ligaments are what add the stability back. Bursae — fluid-filled sacs lined with synovial membrane, found where skin rubs over bone and between tendons, muscles or ligaments and bone. How many directions: uniaxial one, biaxial two, multiaxial several — a multiaxial joint such as the hip allows anterior–posterior, medial–lateral and rotational movement. The failures. Sprain — damage to a ligament, from slight overstretching to a full tear; ligaments are dense in pain receptors sensitive to stretching and swelling, so the injury may be less severe than the pain suggests. Ice first, then heat — ice constricts vessels and reduces bleeding, heat then dilates them to bring in nutrients, oxygen and anti-inflammatory chemicals; ligaments, like tendons, have few blood vessels and heal slowly. Bursitis — an inflamed bursa: intense pain, worse on movement, not relieved by resting in any position, usually settling in a week or two. Osteoarthritis — wear; cartilage degenerates until the bones grind, in weight-bearing joints (hip, knee, spine); partly preventable by controlling weight and exercising. Rheumatoid arthritis — autoimmune; the body attacks its own synovial membranes, fluid accumulates, cartilage is destroyed and may be replaced by fibrous tissue. Permanent.

Five structures, the axis count, then four failures with the discriminating fact for each. Naming the articular cartilage as hyaline is a mark on its own — Whalen asked for it twice — and osteoarthritis is wear, rheumatoid is autoimmune is the one-line contrast the exam wants.

1Lab 7label the diagramA synovial joint

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Bone

    The two articulating bones. A joint is simply where bones come together with other bones or cartilage.

  2. 2name it

    Ligament

    A strong strap of dense regular connective tissue. It holds bone to bone, supports the joint and directs the movement — the thing that adds stability back to a freely movable joint. Damage to one is a sprain.

  3. 3name it

    Articular cartilage

    Hyaline. Covers the surfaces that may come into contact, reducing friction and damage and protecting against compressive forces.

  4. 4name it

    Synovial membrane

    The inner layer of the capsule. It secretes the synovial fluid.

  5. 5name it

    Joint (synovial) cavity

    The space holding the synovial fluid, which lubricates and cushions the joint.

  6. 6name it

    Tendon

    Muscle to bone — not part of the joint itself, but it crosses it, which is why a bursa sits underneath.

  7. 7name it

    Joint capsule

    Two-layered, enclosing the cavity. Its outer layer is continuous with the coverings of the bones.

  8. 8name it

    Bursa

    A fluid-filled sac lined with synovial membrane, found where skin rubs over bone and between tendons, muscles or ligaments and bone. Inflamed, it gives bursitis — intense pain, worse on movement, not relieved by rest in any position.

  9. 9name it

    Diarthrosis

    The functional class this joint belongs to — freely mobile. Structurally it is synovial. The other two functional classes are synarthrosis (immobile — skull sutures) and amphiarthrosis (limited — between the vertebrae).

1Lab 7flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual

The lab's four bone terms vs the chapter's

Back

Lab: diaphysis · epiphysis · medullary cavity · epiphyseal plate. Chapter: shaft · ends or heads · marrow cavity · growth plate. Only "epiphyseal plate" is shared. Use the lab's on the sheet.

2Lab 7flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The six functions of bone

Back

Support · movement · protection · mineral storage (calcium and phosphorus) · fat storage (yellow marrow) · blood cell production (red marrow).

3Lab 7flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Red marrow vs yellow marrow — location

Back

Red — in spongy bone: ribs, pelvis, backbone, skull, sternum, long-bone ends. Makes blood cells. Yellow — in the medullary cavity of the shaft. Stores fat.

4Lab 7flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture

The periosteum

Back

The membrane over compact bone. Carries blood vessels, nerves, and the cells for growth and repair. Most of the pain from a bruised or broken bone is periosteum.

5Lab 7flashcardBlock 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

How does the epiphyseal plate lengthen a bone?

Back

Its cartilage cells divide and force the end farther from the shaft; bone replaces the older cartilage nearer the shaft. It fuses at about 18 in females, 21 in males — after which the bone can widen but not lengthen.

6Lab 7flashcardBlock 2
  • lab manual
  • lecture

The osteon, drawn

Back

Concentric rings of matrix around a central canal with a blood vessel in it; osteocytes in lacunae between the rings; canaliculi running lacuna to lacuna and out to the canal, with cell projections reaching through them.

7Lab 7flashcardBlocks 2–3
  • lab manual
  • lecture

What distinguishes an osteon from a trabecula?

Back

The central canal. Osteocytes in lacunae are in both, so that feature cannot separate them.

8Lab 7flashcardBlock 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The two matrix components and their failure modes

Back

Mineral salts (calcium, phosphorus) → hardness. Collagen → resilience. No salts → rubbery, like a hose. No collagen → brittle, like chalk.

9Lab 7flashcardBlock 2
  • lab manual

Compact bone — what and where

Back

Very dense, few internal spaces, packed with osteons. Most of the diaphysis and the outer shell everywhere. Bears weight and compression; the attachment surface for tendons and ligaments.

10Lab 7flashcardBlock 3
  • lab manual

Spongy bone — the three functions

Back

Strength without weight (lattice along the lines of stress) · houses red marrow, so blood cell production · absorbs and distributes force from the joint surface into the shaft.

11Lab 7flashcardBlocks 2–3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Compact vs spongy — the one-line answer

Back

They differ in arrangement, not composition. Both are hardened by calcium and phosphorus; both hold osteocytes in lacunae. One is packed with osteons, the other is an open latticework.

12Lab 7flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The pectoral girdle and the arm, in order

Back

Scapula + clavicle → humerus → radius and ulna → 8 carpals → 5 metacarpals → phalanges. The elbow is formed by the extension of the ulna past its junction with the humerus.

13Lab 7flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The pelvic girdle and the leg, in order

Back

Two pelvic bones + sacrum → femur → tibia and fibula (patella over the knee) → tarsals → metatarsals → phalanges. Joined in front at the pubic symphysis.

14Lab 7flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Pectoral vs pelvic girdle — the trade-off

Back

Pectoral — loose, greater range of movement; attaches the arms to the rib cage via the sternum. Pelvic — much more rigid, weight-bearing; attaches the legs to the vertebral column via the sacrum.

15Lab 7flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Sexing a skeleton — the two ways in this topic

Back

Clavicles are more curved in males. The female pelvic opening is wider, for childbirth.

16Lab 7flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Phalanges, hands and feet

Back

Each finger has three; the thumb has two. Toes use the same word — phalanges.

17Lab 7flashcardBlock 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Carpal tunnel syndrome

Back

Repetitive motion inflames the tendons in the tunnel, and they press on the nerve. Numbness or tingling in the hand, pain in wrist, hand and fingers. The nerve is what is compressed.

18Lab 7flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The axial counts

Back

80 axial bones. Cranium 8 (frontal, 2 parietal, occipital, 2 temporal, sphenoid, ethmoid). Face 14. Vertebrae 26 (7 / 12 / 5 / sacrum / coccyx). Ribs 12 pairs, the upper 10 reaching the sternum.

19Lab 7flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Foramen magnum and the sinuses

Back

Foramen magnum — the opening in the occipital bone for the spinal cord. Sinuses — air spaces that lighten the head and act as resonating chambers for the voice.

20Lab 7flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The two "smallest" bones

Back

Ethmoid — smallest of the cranium. Lacrimal — smallest of the face.

21Lab 7flashcardBlock 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why does the sacrum fuse, and what is the coccyx for?

Back

The sacrum fuses for strength where the column meets the pelvic girdle. The coccyx has no function — a vestigial tail — but its upper part is nerve-supplied and extremely painful when injured.

22Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

The three functional joint classes

Back

Synarthrosis — immobile or nearly so. Amphiarthrosis — limited movement. Diarthrosis — freely mobile. None of these three words is in Chapter 5.

23Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

The functional classes, with examples

Back

Synarthrosis — skull sutures, manubrium to sternum, the tooth in its socket (periodontal ligament). Amphiarthrosis — between the vertebrae, the intervertebral disk, a symphysis. Diarthrosis — most of the appendicular skeleton.

24Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The three structural joint classes

Back

Fibrous — fibrous tissue, no cavity, little or no movement; skull sutures. Cartilaginous — fibrocartilage or hyaline; vertebrae, ribs to sternum, pubic symphysis. Synovial — capsule, cavity, ligaments; freely movable.

25Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

The six synovial joint types

Back

Pivot — rotation; C1–C2. Hinge — like a door; elbow. Saddle — trapezium to metacarpal 1, the thumb. Plane — gliding; between the tarsals. Condyloid — the radiocarpal wrist. Ball-and-socket — all planes; hip and shoulder, the only two in the body.

26Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What every synovial joint has

Back

Hyaline cartilage on the articular surfaces · a two-layer capsule with a synovial membrane secreting synovial fluid into the joint cavity · ligaments of dense regular connective tissue · bursae where things rub.

27Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

Uniaxial, biaxial, multiaxial

Back

Movement in one, two or several directions. A multiaxial joint such as the hip allows anterior–posterior, medial–lateral and rotational movement.

28Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Flexion and extension — plane and joints

Back

Sagittal (anterior–posterior) plane. Flexion decreases the angle / narrows the joint space; extension increases it. Shoulder, hip, elbow, knee, wrist and the digit joints. For the head and spine, anterior bending is flexion.

29Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

Abduction and adduction — plane and joints

Back

Coronal (medial–lateral) plane. Abduction away from the midline — including spreading the fingers or toes; adduction toward or across it. Shoulder, hip, wrist, and the digit joints.

30Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual

Medial vs lateral rotation

Back

Medial (internal) turns the limb's anterior surface toward the midline; lateral (external) turns it away. Upper limb at the shoulder, lower limb at the hip.

31Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Sprain — and why it hurts more than it should

Back

Damage to a ligament, from overstretching to a tear. Ligaments are dense in pain receptors sensitive to stretching and swelling, so the injury may be less severe than the pain suggests. Ice first, then heat.

32Lab 7flashcardBlock 6
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Osteoarthritis vs rheumatoid arthritis

Back

Osteoarthritis — wear; cartilage degenerates until bones grind; weight-bearing joints; partly preventable by weight control and exercise. Rheumatoid — autoimmune attack on the synovial membranes; permanent.

Lab 8 — Muscular

Week 8 · study page · 28 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 28 flashcards · 1 diagrams, 9 labels · Labs 7 and 8 both ran in the single Monday 09/28 period. "We're doing both in lab as well, Monday… it's an awful lot to get done, so much labeling."

1Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which four properties does all muscle tissue share?

Answer: a

Excitable — responds to a stimulus. Contractible — shortens. Distensible (the chapter says extensible) — stretches. Elastic — returns to its resting length. There is no fifth property, and "distensible" and "extensible" are the same one. Voluntary control is not on the list — it is what separates skeletal muscle from the other two.

2Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Besides movement, what three things does muscle tissue do?

Answer: a

The lab's general paragraph on muscle tissue lists movement, support, energy storage as glycogen, and heat production — and it explains the heat: it is the by-product of the constant ATP production, aerobic and anaerobic, that contraction costs. Shivering is the body using that on purpose. Whalen's Ch. 4 deck adds the same two functions the textbook's tissue chapter leaves out.

3Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where is cardiac muscle found?

Answer: b

The walls of the heart and nowhere else. The diaphragm and the upper oesophagus are skeletal muscle — which is why curare and botulinum toxin stop breathing — and the great vessels have smooth muscle in their walls. Cardiac muscle's job is one thing: contract to pump blood.

4Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual

Which of these is a job of smooth muscle?

Answer: c

Smooth muscle is involuntary and it moves food, moves secretions, gives involuntary control of respiration, and regulates blood flow in the arteries by contracting. It is in the walls of vessels, of the digestive and urinary systems, and in the iris. Options a and d are skeletal; option b is cardiac.

5Lab 8Activity 2
  • lab manual

Which connective tissue sheath wraps a fascicle?

Answer: b

Epimysium wraps the whole muscle; perimysium wraps a fascicle; endomysium wraps one muscle fiber. All three merge at the ends of the muscle to form the tendon. These three names are the lab's — Chapter 6 says only "a membrane of fibrous connective tissue". The sarcolemma is the fiber's plasma membrane, not a sheath.

6Lab 8Activity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Put the organisational levels in order, outside in.

Answer: a

Muscle (in epimysium) → fascicle (in perimysium) → muscle fiber, which is one cell (in endomysium) → myofibril → sarcomere, the functional unit. The commonest slip is putting fiber above fascicle: a fiber is a single cell, and a fascicle is a bundle of them.

7Lab 8Activity 2
  • lab manual

What is a triad, and what is it for?

Answer: b

A T-tubule flanked by sarcoplasmic reticulum on either side — three membranes in section. The arrangement increases the contact area between the sarcolemma and the calcium store, so the arriving signal and the calcium release happen close together. The lab's image for a T-tubule is a finger pushed into a water balloon.

8Lab 8Activity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where does the enzyme ATPase sit?

Answer: a

The myosin head carries ATPase, which binds and breaks down ATP — which is why the head is the part that both cocks and detaches. The base of the myosin molecule attaches to a central M protein and the molecule extends toward the ends of the sarcomere. Fast-twitch cells owe their speed to carrying a faster form of this same enzyme.

9Lab 8Activity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

How is the thin filament built, and what is on it?

Answer: b

Actin is globular proteins in two strands, attached to proteins in the Z disc, extending toward the M line and partially overlapping the myosin. Each subunit carries a binding site specific for the myosin heads, and tropomyosin overlies those sites with troponin interspersed along it. Option a describes myosin, the thick filament.

10Lab 8Activity 2
  • lab manual

Reading across one sarcomere, which sequence of bands is right?

Answer: b

Lighter I bands at the ends, beside the Z discs; the darker A band in the middle, with the H zone and M line at its centre. Option a is that inverted. The bands are the lab's vocabulary — Chapter 6 names only the Z line — so this is a lab-exam labelling question.

11Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Two of the three muscle types are striated and two are involuntary. Which is neither?

Answer: c

Smooth muscle is the only one that is neither striated nor voluntary. Cardiac is striated but involuntary. Skeletal is striated and voluntary. They are not the same two, which is what makes the question work. Nuclei then settle the striated pair: many at the edge = skeletal, one in the middle = cardiac.

12Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual

How are cardiac cells joined to their neighbours?

Answer: b

Intercalated discs, which carry gap junctions — the discs strengthen the tissue and the junctions speed conduction through the heart, so the wall contracts as one. Smooth muscle has gap junctions without intercalated discs (option c), and skeletal fibers are joined to nothing at all and contract end to end (option a).

13Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual

Why does a skeletal muscle fiber have many nuclei along its edge?

Answer: a

Immature muscle cells fuse during development into a single long fiber, and their nuclei end up spaced along its periphery — which is what a cell that can run the length of a whole muscle needs. Option c is the tempting structural guess, but myofibrils are protein bundles, not compartments with nuclei; glycogen is stored in the sarcoplasm.

14Lab 8Activity 1
  • lab manual

Why is smooth muscle not striated?

Answer: b

Striations come from the orderly arrangement of actin and myosin inside sarcomeres. Smooth muscle has both proteins but arranges its myofilaments differently, so there are no bands — and that is also why it can shorten in several directions at once rather than only end to end.

15Lab 8Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook
