What shortens during contraction, and what does not?

Answer: c

Actin slides along myosin, the overlap increases, and the sarcomere shortens — the filaments themselves do not change length. When many sarcomeres shorten, the whole muscle contracts. This is the single most-tested misconception on the topic, and both the lab and the chapter state it in the same words.

16Lab 8Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the resting sarcomere, what state are the myosin heads in?

Answer: c

At rest the heads have already split ATP into ADP + P_i_, and that energy has swivelled them out toward the Z lines — cocked, like a pistol. The power stroke releases that stored energy, which is why ATP does not power the pull. Option a is rigor mortis, where there is no ATP to detach the heads.

17Lab 8Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is the correct order of the cross-bridge cycle?

Answer: a

1 attachment — the cocked heads bind the nearest actin. 2 power stroke — stored energy releases, the heads swing back and pull actin toward the midline; ADP and P_i_ leave. 3 detachment — new ATP binds and the head lets go. 4 reactivation — the head splits that ATP and re-cocks. The cycle repeats hundreds of times a second.

18Lab 8Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Rigor mortis happens because of what?

Answer: b

After death calcium leaks out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and starts contraction — but ATP production has stopped, and it takes an ATP to break a cross-bridge. Stiff by 3–4 hours; it passes after 2–3 days as actin and myosin break down, which is option d describing the end of rigor, not its cause. If ATP powered the pull rather than the release, a dead muscle would go limp.

19Lab 8Activity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Calcium is the switch. What exactly does it switch?

Answer: a

At rest the troponin–tropomyosin complex covers the myosin-binding sites on actin. Ca2+ binds troponin, troponin changes shape, and tropomyosin is shifted off the sites so myosin can bind. Relaxation happens when membrane pumps clear the calcium back out and the complex re-covers the sites. Options b and d describe ATP's jobs, not calcium's.

20Lab 8Activity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Put the neuromuscular junction steps in order.

Answer: a

1 A nerve impulse reaches the junction. 2 Acetylcholine is released from small packets in the neuron tip. 3 It diffuses across the gap and binds receptors on the muscle cell membrane, creating an electrochemical message. 4 That message runs along the membrane, into the T-tubules, to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases calcium. Calcium is always last — it is the switch, not the signal.

21Lab 8Activity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A muscle cell can be 30 cm long. What solves the problem of reaching its middle?

Answer: b

Transverse tubules are tiny cylindrical pockets of the muscle cell's plasma membrane reaching deep into it. They carry the signal — not the calcium — from the surface to virtually every sarcomere. That is the exam framing the lab sets up, and it is why a triad puts sarcoplasmic reticulum right beside a T-tubule.

22Lab 8Activity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Three poisons break three different steps of the neuromuscular drawing. Which pairing is right?

Answer: b

Curare stops acetylcholine binding to its receptor. Botulinum toxin stops acetylcholine being released. Both give flaccid paralysis and both kill by paralysing the diaphragm, which is skeletal muscle. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the opposite failure — a defective dystrophin gene lets too much calcium in, and it kills the cell.

23Lab 8Activity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

How big is a motor unit, and how does size relate to control?

Answer: a

A motor unit is a motor neuron and all the muscle cells it stimulates, and all of them contract together — about 150 cells on average. Size is inversely related to precision: an eye-muscle neuron may control 3 cells; a calf-muscle neuron thousands. Recruitment is how the nervous system raises contraction strength — by stimulating more motor units.

24Lab 8Activity 4
  • lab manual

What decides a muscle's action?

Answer: b

The lab is explicit: the action of the muscle depends entirely on its location and the attachment points to the bone — so "as you learn the muscles, pay attention to where they attach. This will help you learn how they function." Options c and d describe how a muscle is used or how hard it pulls, not which movement it produces.

25Lab 8Activity 4
  • lab manual

Origin and insertion are told apart how?

Answer: b

The origin is the point of attachment on the fixed bone — the one that does not move when the muscle contracts. The insertion is on the mobile bone. The distinction is functional, not positional, which is why option a is the intuitive wrong answer. The lab also sets the scope: "you will need to know their functions. You will not need to know every origin and insertion for this course."

26Lab 8Activity 4
  • lab manual

The biceps brachii flexes the forearm. What are the brachialis and brachioradialis to it?

Answer: b

A main muscle causing a specific action is the prime mover; muscles causing the same action as the prime mover are synergists. The lab's worked example is exactly this: the biceps brachii flexes the lower arm, and the brachioradialis (in the forearm) and the brachialis (deep to the biceps) are both synergists that aid the motion. Muscle groups causing opposite actions are antagonistic.

27Lab 8Activity 4
  • lab manual

Which pairing of agonist, antagonist and movement is right?

Answer: c

The hamstrings — three muscles of the posterior compartment of the thigh — flex the leg; the quadriceps femoris — four muscles of the anterior compartment — extend it. The arm pair runs the same way: biceps brachii, anterior compartment, flexes the forearm; triceps brachii, posterior compartment, extends it. The compartment tells you the action, which is the lab's point about attachment.

28Lab 8Activity 4
  • lab manual

A muscle's name carries information. What does "biceps brachii" tell you?

Answer: b

The lab's own worked example of why the Latin roots are worth learning: bi- means two, cep means head, and brachii means arm — so the name tells you the muscle is in the arm and has two origins. Other roots on its table: maximus largest, medius medium, minimus smallest, longus long, brevis short, rectus straight, externus outside, internus inside, uni / bi / tri / quad for one, two, three and four.

1Lab 8short answerActivity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Compare the functions of the three muscle tissue types, and say where each is found.

Model answer

All three share four properties: excitable (responds to stimuli), contractible (shortens), distensible or extensible (stretches) and elastic (returns to resting length), and in all three an electrical signal along the membrane starts the contraction. Beyond movement, muscle tissue also provides support, stores energy as glycogen, and produces heat — heat being the by-product of the constant ATP production, aerobic and anaerobic, that contraction costs, which is what shivering exploits. Skeletal. Movement, including facial expression · posture against gravity · support and protection of internal organs (the abdominal wall and pelvic floor) · moving blood and lymph by pushing on veins and lymphatic vessels · generating heat that warms the body above most environmental temperatures. Found attached to bones and around the body's entrance points — limbs, trunk, head and neck, plus the pharynx, oesophagus, diaphragm and some voluntary sphincters. Cardiac. Contracts to pump blood. In the walls of the heart, and nowhere else. Smooth. Involuntary movement — moves food, gives involuntary control of respiration, moves secretions, and regulates blood flow in the arteries by contracting. In the walls of vessels, of the digestive and urinary systems, and in the iris. What separates them: only skeletal muscle is voluntary; cardiac and smooth have gap junctions and skeletal does not, which is how a sheet of cells reacts as one to a single signal — the heart wall contracting together, and peristalsis; and skeletal and cardiac fibers contract end to end while smooth muscle shortens in multiple directions at once.

Four shared properties, then each type's jobs and locations, then the three things that separate them. The functions of cardiac and smooth muscle are lab material with no chapter behind them — Chapter 6 is skeletal-only and says so — which is exactly why this is a lab question.

2Lab 8short answerActivity 2
  • lab manual

Describe the organisation of a skeletal muscle from the outside in, and name the structures inside one fiber.

Model answer

The nest, each level in its own connective tissue covering. The whole muscle is wrapped in epimysium; inside it, fibers are bundled into fascicles, each wrapped in perimysium; inside a fascicle are the muscle fibers — the muscle cells — each wrapped in endomysium. All three sheaths merge and condense at the ends of the muscle to form the tendon. Inside a myofibril run the sarcomeres, arranged end to end, and the sarcomere is the functional unit. Inside one fiber. Its plasma membrane is the sarcolemma and its cytoplasm the sarcoplasm; the myofibrils lie in the sarcoplasm and are what make the cell look striated. The sarcoplasmic reticulum is specialised endoplasmic reticulum and it stores the calcium that starts contraction. A T-tubule is an invagination of the sarcolemma, diving in and around the myofibrils — a finger pushed into a water balloon — and sarcoplasmic reticulum on both sides of one makes a triad, which increases the contact area between the membrane and the calcium store.

The nest in order with all three sheaths correctly placed, the tendon point, then the fiber's own named structures. Origin, insertion and antagonistic pairs are not this topic — that is §6.2 on the chapter tab; this activity's three objectives are the organisational relationship, the sarcomere, and identifying the structures of the cell.

3Lab 8short answerActivity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the sarcomere in detail — the filaments, the regulatory proteins and the bands.

Model answer

The sarcomere is cylindrical and runs Z line to Z line, built from thin filaments (actin) and thick filaments (myosin). Myosin is thick and fibrous with globular heads; the head carries the enzyme ATPase, which binds and breaks down ATP, and the base attaches to a central M protein, the molecule extending toward the ends of the sarcomere. Actin is globular proteins in two strands, attached to proteins in the Z disc, extending toward the M line and partially overlapping the myosin; each subunit carries a binding site specific for the myosin heads. Tropomyosin overlies those binding sites, with troponin interspersed along it — the two together regulate access to the sites. The bands, across one sarcomere: a lighter I band, then the darker A band with the H zone and M line at its centre, then a lighter I band — Z disc to Z disc. When the muscle contracts the overlap between actin and myosin increases and the sarcomere shortens; the filaments themselves do not change length.

A labelling question in prose. Myosin's ATPase head and M-protein base, actin's two strands on the Z disc, tropomyosin with troponin interspersed, and the I/A/H/M band order are the lab's own named structures — the chapter names only the Z line.

4Lab 8short answerActivity 4
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Explain the sliding filament theory, including what switches it on and what powers it.

Model answer

The model in one sentence: a muscle contracts when actin filaments slide along myosin filaments, increasing the overlap and shortening the sarcomere; when many sarcomeres shorten, the whole muscle contracts — and the filaments do not shorten, the sarcomere does. At rest the myosin heads have already split ATP into ADP + P_i_, and the stored energy has swivelled them out toward the Z lines — cocked, like a pistol. Step 1, cross-bridge attachment: the heads bind the nearest actin filament, bridging thick and thin — hence cross-bridge. Step 2, the power stroke: the stored energy is released, the heads swing back to their bent positions and pull the actin toward the midline of the sarcomere; ADP and P_i_ leave the head. Step 3, detachment: new ATP binds the heads and they let go of actin. Step 4, reactivation: the heads split that ATP and store the energy, cocking again. The cycle repeats hundreds of times a second. What switches it on: calcium. At rest the troponin–tropomyosin complex covers the myosin-binding sites on actin; Ca2+ binds troponin, which changes shape and shifts tropomyosin off the sites so myosin can bind. Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum and released when the signal arrives; relaxation happens when membrane pumps clear the calcium back out and the complex re-covers the sites. Calcium and ATP do different jobs: calcium uncovers the sites; ATP cocks the head and, in a separate step, detaches it. The pull is powered by an earlier ATP split, not by the ATP that binds in step 3 — and rigor mortis is the proof: after death calcium leaks out and starts contraction, but with no ATP the cross-bridges cannot be broken, so the body stiffens within 3–4 hours and only relaxes after 2–3 days as actin and myosin break down.

The sentence, then four steps in order, then calcium's role, then the calcium-versus-ATP distinction with rigor mortis as the discriminating case. Saying ATP powers the power stroke is the error that makes rigor mortis inexplicable.

5Lab 8short answerActivity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the neuromuscular junction step by step, and explain what the T-tubules are for.

Model answer

One. A nerve impulse reaches the neuromuscular junction — the junction between the tip of a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle cell. Two. The impulse causes the release of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter, from small packets (synaptic vesicles) in the neuron tip. Three. Acetylcholine diffuses across a small gap and binds receptors on the muscle cell membrane, changing its permeability and creating an electrochemical message like a nerve impulse. Four. The message runs along the plasma membrane, into the T-tubules, then to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, opening channels that release calcium ions — and the cross-bridge cycle takes over. What the T-tubules are for: they are tiny cylindrical pockets of the muscle cell's plasma membrane reaching into the cell, and they carry the signal from the surface deep inside, to virtually every sarcomere. They carry the signal, not the calcium — the calcium comes out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum beside them, which is why a triad puts the two membranes in contact. The exam framing is: how does a surface signal reach the middle of a 30 cm cell? A motor unit is a motor neuron and all the muscle cells it stimulates, all contracting together — about 150 cells on average, though an eye-muscle neuron may control 3 and a calf-muscle neuron thousands; recruitment raises contraction strength by stimulating more motor units.

Four steps in order with acetylcholine, the receptor, the T-tubule and the sarcoplasmic reticulum named, then the T-tubule's purpose stated as the signal, not the calcium. The motor-unit paragraph is the lab's "if the topic runs long" material and earns if there is room.

6Lab 8short answerActivity 4
  • lab manual

Explain prime mover, synergist and antagonist, using the lab's two worked pairs.

Model answer

A muscle's action depends entirely on its location and its attachment points — the origin on the bone that stays fixed, the insertion on the bone that moves. A prime mover is the main muscle causing a specific action. Synergists are muscles that cause the same action as the prime mover and aid the motion. Antagonists are muscle groups that cause the opposite action. The arm. The biceps brachii is the prime mover for flexing the forearm; the brachialis, deep to it in the upper arm, and the brachioradialis, in the forearm, are its synergists. Its antagonist is the triceps brachii, in the posterior compartment of the arm, which extends the forearm. The thigh. The hamstrings — a group of three in the posterior compartment — flex the leg. Their antagonist is the quadriceps femoris, a group of four in the anterior compartment, which extends it. The pattern in both: anterior compartment flexes, posterior compartment extends, and the two groups are antagonists of each other. Note the lab's scope statement: "You will need to know their functions. You will not need to know every origin and insertion for this course."

Define all three terms, then use both pairs. The mark that separates a full answer is the compartment generalisation — anterior flexes, posterior extends — because that is what the lab means by "pay attention to where they attach".

1Lab 8label the diagramThe three muscle tissue types, down the microscope

Name every numbered structure before you open anything.

  1. 1name it

    Skeletal muscle fiber

    Long cylindrical fibers lying in parallel groups, bundled into fascicles. Voluntary — the only one.

  2. 2name it

    Peripheral nuclei

    Many per fiber, along the edge — because immature muscle cells fused during development into one long cell.

  3. 3name it

    Striations

    Prominent. They come from the orderly arrangement of actin and myosin inside the sarcomeres.

  4. 4name it

    Cardiac muscle cell

    Short and branched, and found in the walls of the heart and nowhere else. Striated, but involuntary.

  5. 5name it

    Intercalated disc

    The end-to-end join between cardiac cells, carrying gap junctions. They strengthen the tissue and speed conduction, so the heart wall contracts as one.

  6. 6name it

    Central nucleus

    One, in the middle — which is what separates cardiac from skeletal, since both are striated. (Note: Table 4.3 says flatly "one nucleus" where the chapter text hedges with "typically only one".)

  7. 7name it

    Smooth muscle cell

    Short, spindle-shaped with tapered ends, one nucleus per fiber, each cell touching several others at once. Involuntary.

  8. 8name it

    No striations

    Smooth muscle's myofilaments are not arranged in sarcomeres, so there are no bands — and it can shorten in several directions at once rather than only end to end.

  9. 9name it

    Gap junctions

    Join smooth muscle cells (and cardiac cells, inside the intercalated discs). They let a sheet of cells react as one to a single signal — how peristalsis works. Skeletal muscle has none.

1Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The four properties of all muscle tissue

Back

Excitable · contractible · distensible (extensible) · elastic. An electrical signal along the membrane starts the contraction. There is no fifth property, and voluntary control is not one of them.

2Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Muscle tissue's jobs beyond movement

Back

Support · energy storage as glycogen · heat production. Heat is the by-product of the constant ATP production contraction costs — and shivering uses it on purpose.

3Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Skeletal muscle — the five functions

Back

Movement (including facial expression) · posture · supports and protects internal organs (abdominal wall, pelvic floor) · moves blood and lymph by squeezing veins and lymphatics · generates heat.

4Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where is skeletal muscle, besides the limbs?

Back

Around the body's entrance points (mouth, anus), and in the pharynx, oesophagus and diaphragm, plus some voluntary sphincters. The diaphragm being skeletal is why curare and botulism kill.

5Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

Smooth muscle — jobs and locations

Back

Moves food · involuntary control of respiration · moves secretions · regulates blood flow by narrowing arteries. In the walls of vessels, the digestive and urinary systems, and the iris.

6Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

What separates the three types?

Back

Only skeletal is voluntary. Cardiac and smooth have gap junctions; skeletal does not. Skeletal and cardiac contract end to end; smooth shortens in multiple directions at once.

7Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

The three muscle types, down the microscope

Back

Skeletal — long cylinders, many peripheral nuclei, prominent striations, joined to nothing. Cardiac — short, branched, one central nucleus, striated, intercalated discs. Smooth — short, spindle-shaped with tapered ends, one nucleus, no striations, gap junctions.

8Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

Why do two of the three show striations?

Back

The bands come from the orderly arrangement of actin and myosin inside sarcomeres. Smooth muscle arranges its myofilaments differently, so no bands — and it can shorten in several directions at once.

9Lab 8flashcardActivity 1
  • lab manual

Why does a skeletal fiber have many nuclei?

Back

Immature muscle cells fuse during development into one long fiber, and the nuclei end up spaced along its edge — for a cell that can run the length of a whole muscle.

10Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

Epimysium, perimysium, endomysium

Back

Epi → the whole muscle. Peri → a fascicle. Endo → one fiber. All three merge at the ends of the muscle to form the tendon.

11Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The nest, outside in

Back

Muscle → fascicle → muscle fiber (one cell) → myofibril → sarcomere. The sarcomere is the functional unit; myofibrils are sarcomeres end to end.

12Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

Sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum

Back

Sarcolemma — the fiber's plasma membrane. Sarcoplasm — its cytoplasm, holding the myofibrils. Sarcoplasmic reticulum — specialised ER that stores the calcium.

13Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

T-tubule and triad

Back

A T-tubule is an invagination of the sarcolemma diving in around the myofibrils — a finger pushed into a water balloon. Sarcoplasmic reticulum on both sides of one is a triad, increasing the contact area between membrane and calcium store.

14Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

Myosin, in detail

Back

Thick and fibrous, with globular heads. The head carries ATPase, which binds and breaks down ATP. The base attaches to a central M protein and extends toward the ends of the sarcomere.

15Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

Actin, in detail

Back

Globular proteins in two strands, attached to proteins in the Z disc, extending toward the M line and partially overlapping the myosin. Each subunit carries a myosin-binding site.

16Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Tropomyosin and troponin

Back

Tropomyosin overlies the myosin-binding sites on actin, with troponin interspersed along it. Together they regulate access to the sites.

17Lab 8flashcardActivity 2
  • lab manual

The bands across one sarcomere

Back

I band (light) · A band (dark), with the H zone and M line at its centre · I band (light) — Z disc to Z disc.

18Lab 8flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The sliding filament model, in one sentence

Back

Actin slides along myosin, the overlap increases, and the sarcomere shortens. The filaments do not shorten — the sarcomere does.

19Lab 8flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What state is a resting myosin head in?

Back

Cocked — it has already split ATP into ADP + P_i_, and the stored energy has swivelled it out toward the Z lines, like a pistol ready to fire.

20Lab 8flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The four steps of the cross-bridge cycle

Back

1 Attachment — heads bind actin. 2 Power stroke — stored energy releases, heads swing back pulling actin inward; ADP and P_i_ leave. 3 Detachment — new ATP binds and the head lets go. 4 Reactivation — the head splits it and re-cocks. Hundreds of times a second.

21Lab 8flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Calcium's job vs ATP's job

Back

Calcium uncovers the binding sites. ATP cocks the head and, in a separate step, detaches it. The pull is powered by an earlier ATP split, not by the ATP that binds in step 3.

22Lab 8flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Rigor mortis — why it proves the point

Back

After death calcium leaks out and starts contraction, but ATP production stops — and it takes ATP to break a cross-bridge. Stiff by 3–4 hours, relaxing after 2–3 days as actin and myosin break down. If ATP powered the pull, a dead muscle would go limp.

23Lab 8flashcardActivity 3
  • lab manual
  • textbook

How does a muscle relax?

Back

Membrane pumps clear the calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the troponin–tropomyosin complex re-covers the binding sites.

24Lab 8flashcardActivity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The neuromuscular junction, four steps

Back

1 Nerve impulse arrives. 2 Acetylcholine released from packets in the neuron tip. 3 It diffuses the gap and binds receptors on the muscle membrane, creating an electrochemical message. 4 The message runs into the T-tubules → sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium.

25Lab 8flashcardActivity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What do T-tubules carry?

Back

The signal, not the calcium — from the surface deep inside, to virtually every sarcomere. That is how a surface signal reaches the middle of a 30 cm cell.

26Lab 8flashcardActivity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Three ways to break the junction

Back

Botulinum toxin — acetylcholine is not released. Curare — acetylcholine cannot bind. Duchenne muscular dystrophy — the opposite: too much calcium enters and kills the cell. The first two both kill by paralysing the diaphragm.

27Lab 8flashcardActivity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Motor unit

Back

A motor neuron and all the muscle cells it stimulates — all contracting together. About 150 cells on average; an eye-muscle neuron may control 3, a calf-muscle neuron thousands.

28Lab 8flashcardActivity 5
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Recruitment

Back

The nervous system raises the strength of contraction by stimulating more motor units. Fine control means small motor units.
